cer.phenomenon: In a crash test at 48 km/h (about 30 mph), an unbelted crash test dummy continues forward at the car's original speed and strikes the steering wheel with significant force. A belted dummy decelerates with the car and experiences much lower forces. The unbelted dummy's head hits the windshield approximately 0.05 seconds after the car contacts the barrier.
cer.claim_starter: Based on Newton's First Law, I claim that the unbelted dummy continues forward because...
cer.evidence_source: Use the concept of inertia and the time delay (0.05 s) between the car stopping and the dummy hitting the windshield to calculate the distance the dummy traveled inside the car.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because according to Newton's First Law, the dummy's body has inertia and will continue moving at ___ unless a ___ acts on it. The seatbelt provides this force for the belted dummy, but the unbelted dummy's only 'force' is the ___, which is why injuries are so severe.

lessons.title: Newton's Second Law — F = ma (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: apply Newton's Second Law to calculate the net force, mass, or acceleration of an object and explain the relationship between these three quantities
lessons.circle_prompt: What's easier to push — an empty shopping cart or a full one? A beach ball or a bowling ball? Why? What does this tell us about the relationship between force and mass?
lessons.do_now: Two identical forces push two different objects. Object A has a mass of 2 kg and Object B has a mass of 10 kg. Which object accelerates more? By how much? Show your reasoning.
materials: Dynamics carts and track (1 set per group)
Spring scales or force sensors (1 per group)
Masses (100 g, 200 g, 500 g — sets per group)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Newton's Second Law — F = ma. Show a clip of a race between a sports car and a freight truck, both with the same engine horsepower. Ask: Why does the sports car win? Both have the same force — what's different? Students predict the relationship between force, mass, and acceleration before seeing the equation.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Newton's Second Law — F = ma. Lab investigation: Groups use a dynamics cart on a track. Part 1 — Keep mass constant, vary the applied force (1 rubber band, 2 rubber bands, 3 rubber bands), measure acceleration (from distance and time). Part 2 — Keep force constant (same rubber band stretch), vary the mass (add 200 g, 400 g, 600 g), measure acceleration. Groups graph Force vs. Acceleration and Acceleration vs. Mass.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Newton's Second Law — F = ma. Present Newton's Second Law: F_net = ma. Analyze the lab data: Force vs. Acceleration is linear (slope = mass). Acceleration vs. Mass is inverse. Rearrange the equation for each variable: a = F_net/m, m = F_net/a, F_net = ma. Define the unit of force: 1 Newton = 1 kg·m/s^2. Work through three practice problems covering each rearrangement.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Newton's Second Law — F = ma. Multi-force problems: A 1500 kg car has an engine force of 4500 N forward and friction of 500 N backward. Students calculate net force and acceleration. Then: What happens to the acceleration if the car picks up 4 passengers (total added mass 300 kg)? Students solve and compare.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Newton's Second Law — F = ma. Exit ticket: A 0.145 kg baseball is pitched at 40 m/s. The batter hits it, and it leaves the bat at 50 m/s in the opposite direction. The bat is in contact with the ball for 0.002 s. Calculate the acceleration and the average force on the ball.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a three-column organizer: 'Find Force → F = ma,' 'Find Acceleration → a = F/m,' 'Find Mass → m = F/a.' Include a worked example for each. Use color-coding for each variable.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the dynamics cart lab and all practice problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Analyze the non-constant force case: What happens when the force depends on position (like a spring)? Explore qualitatively how F = ma still applies at every instant. Calculate the acceleration of a rocket as it burns fuel and loses mass.
differentiation.ell: Provide a visual F = ma triangle (cover the variable you're solving for). Use hands-on lab experience as primary learning before mathematical formalism. Provide bilingual problem glossary.
differentiation.iep: Provide the F = ma triangle on a laminated card. Break multi-step problems into single-step sub-problems. Allow calculator use throughout. Reduce the number of practice problems to focus on one rearrangement at a time.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how Katherine Johnson, a Black mathematician at NASA, used F = ma and related equations to calculate trajectories for the Mercury and Apollo missions. Her hand calculations were so trusted that John Glenn refused to fly until she personally verified the computer's orbital calculations.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'Newton's Second Law': A heavier object has less acceleration when the same force is applied because___. Both a truck and a car experience the same braking force, but___. The net force on the object is 20 N and its mass is 4 kg, so___.

vocabulary.definition: The acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass; F_net = ma
A relationship where one quantity increases as the other increases by the same factor (e.g., double the force → double the acceleration, if mass is constant)

Section 4: Net Force with Multiple Forces Acting

cer.phenomenon: A 70 kg sprinter accelerates from rest to 10 m/s in 1.5 seconds at the start of a race. A 2000 kg car also accelerates from rest to 10 m/s but takes 4.0 seconds.
cer.claim_starter: Based on Newton's Second Law, I claim that the sprinter generates a greater acceleration than the car, but the car requires a greater net force because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the acceleration and net force for both the sprinter and the car using a = Δv/Δt and F = ma.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because while the sprinter's acceleration is ___ m/s^2 compared to the car's ___ m/s^2, the net force on the car (___ N) is much greater than on the sprinter (___ N). This illustrates the role of ___ in Newton's Second Law.

lessons.title: Newton's Third Law and Action-Reaction Pairs (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: identify Newton's Third Law action-reaction force pairs and explain why they do not cancel each other out
lessons.circle_prompt: If you push against a wall, does the wall push back? How do you know? What evidence do you have?
lessons.do_now: Two ice skaters face each other and push off. Skater A has a mass of 50 kg and Skater B has a mass of 80 kg. Who moves faster after the push? Why? Draw a diagram.
materials: Two spring scales hooked together (1 pair per group)
Two dynamics carts with Velcro or spring bumpers
Skateboards or rolling chairs (2, for teacher demo)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Newton's Third Law and Action-Reaction Pairs. Teacher demonstration: Two students sit in rolling chairs facing each other. Student A pushes Student B. Ask: What happens to both students? (Both move apart.) Why does Student A roll backward when they pushed Student B forward? Students discuss in pairs before the formal explanation.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Newton's Third Law and Action-Reaction Pairs. Activity 1: Students hook two spring scales together and pull. They observe that both scales always read the same value regardless of who pulls harder or whether one person holds still. Activity 2: Two dynamics carts with a compressed spring between them are released simultaneously. Students compare how far each cart travels for equal masses and unequal masses.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Newton's Third Law and Action-Reaction Pairs. Present Newton's Third Law: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. Clarify common misconceptions: (1) Action-reaction pairs act on DIFFERENT objects, so they never cancel. (2) The forces are equal in magnitude even if the objects have different masses — but the accelerations differ because a = F/m. Identify action-reaction pairs in examples: person walking (foot pushes ground backward, ground pushes foot forward), rocket propulsion, swimming.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Newton's Third Law and Action-Reaction Pairs. Students receive scenario cards and must identify the action-reaction pair for each: (1) A hammer hits a nail. (2) The Earth pulls you down with gravity. (3) A rocket expels exhaust gases. (4) You lean against a wall. For each, students name both forces, what object each acts on, and whether the objects have the same acceleration.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Newton's Third Law and Action-Reaction Pairs. Exit ticket: A 1000 kg car rear-ends a 3000 kg truck. According to Newton's Third Law, which vehicle experiences a greater force during the collision? Which experiences greater acceleration? Explain both answers.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a Newton's Third Law template: 'Object A exerts a force on Object B → Object B exerts an equal and opposite force on Object A.' Fill in the blanks for each scenario. Include a common misconception correction sheet.
differentiation.on_level: Complete spring scale activity and scenario card analysis as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Analyze the 'horse and cart' paradox: If the horse pulls the cart with the same force the cart pulls the horse, how does the system ever accelerate? Resolve using free body diagrams for each object separately.
differentiation.ell: Use physical demonstrations for every action-reaction pair. Provide a visual action-reaction pair diagram template with arrows and labels in English and native language. Use consistent color coding (red arrow = action, blue arrow = reaction).
differentiation.iep: Provide a pre-printed list of action-reaction pairs with one force identified and space for the student to fill in the other. Use the spring scale activity as the primary assessment tool. Simplify the exit ticket to multiple choice.

lessons.crse_connection: Explore how rocket propulsion — a direct application of Newton's Third Law — enabled the contributions of Mary Jackson, NASA's first Black female engineer, who worked on wind tunnel experiments that tested how air flows over spacecraft. Discuss how her work required understanding action-reaction forces between air molecules and surfaces.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'action-reaction': When you jump, the ground pushes you up because___. The forces in an action-reaction pair are equal and opposite, but they don't cancel because___. A rocket pushes exhaust gases downward, so___.

vocabulary.definition: For every action force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force; the two forces act on different objects
The contact force exerted by a surface perpendicular to the object resting on it; the reaction to the object pressing on the surface

explain.description: Address common misconceptions from practice; model problem-solving strategies. Building on previous days: Present Newton's Third Law: For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. Clarify common misconceptions: (1) Action-reaction pairs act on DIFFERENT objects, so they never cancel. (2) The forces are equal in magnitude even if the objects have different masses — but the accelerations differ because a = F/m. Identify action-reaction pairs in examples: person walking (foot pushes ground backward, ground pushes foot forward), rocket propulsion, swimming.

elaborate.description: CER activity connecting evidence to claims about the topic. Building on previous days: Students receive scenario cards and must identify the action-reaction pair for each: (1) A hammer hits a nail. (2) The Earth pulls you down with gravity. (3) A rocket expels exhaust gases. (4) You lean against a wall. For each, students name both forces, what object each acts on, and whether the objects have the same acceleration.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket with application-level problems requiring multi-step reasoning. Building on previous days: Exit ticket: A 1000 kg car rear-ends a 3000 kg truck. According to Newton's Third Law, which vehicle experiences a greater force during the collision? Which experiences greater acceleration? Explain both answers.

differentiation.approaching: Review key concepts from the full sequence before assessment. Provide a Newton's Third Law template: 'Object A exerts a force on Object B → Object B exerts an equal and opposite force on Object A.' Fill in the blanks for each scenario. Include a common misconception correction sheet.
differentiation.on_level: Complete spring scale activity and scenario card analysis as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Complete extension challenge connecting to real-world applications. Analyze the 'horse and cart' paradox: If the horse pulls the cart with the same force the cart pulls the horse, how does the system ever accelerate? Resolve using free body diagrams for each object separately.
differentiation.ell: Use physical demonstrations for every action-reaction pair. Provide a visual action-reaction pair diagram template with arrows and labels in English and native language. Use consistent color coding (red arrow = action, blue arrow = reaction).
differentiation.iep: Provide a pre-printed list of action-reaction pairs with one force identified and space for the student to fill in the other. Use the spring scale activity as the primary assessment tool. Simplify the exit ticket to multiple choice.

lessons.crse_connection: Explore how rocket propulsion — a direct application of Newton's Third Law — enabled the contributions of Mary Jackson, NASA's first Black female engineer, who worked on wind tunnel experiments that tested how air flows over spacecraft. Discuss how her work required understanding action-reaction forces between air molecules and surfaces.

vocabulary.definition: Two forces that are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and act on different objects as described by Newton's Third Law

cer.phenomenon: A 2000 kg SUV collides head-on with a 800 kg compact car. Both drivers report different experiences: the compact car driver is severely injured while the SUV driver walks away with minor bruises. cer.claim_starter: Based on Newton's Third Law, I claim that both vehicles experience the same magnitude of force during the collision, but the outcomes differ because...
cer.evidence_source: Apply Newton's Third Law to identify the forces and Newton's Second Law (a = F/m) to calculate the acceleration experienced by each vehicle during the collision.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because Newton's Third Law guarantees the forces are ___, but since the compact car has a ___ mass, it experiences a ___ acceleration (and deceleration), which results in greater injury risk. This is why vehicle safety standards consider ___.

lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: draw a free body diagram showing all forces acting on an object and calculate the net force to predict the object's acceleration
lessons.circle_prompt: Think of a time when you felt pulled in multiple directions at once — responsibilities, choices, people wanting different things. How did you figure out which way to go? Forces on objects work similarly.
lessons.do_now: A 5 kg box sits on a table. Draw all the forces acting on the box. Are the forces balanced or unbalanced? How do you know?
materials: Free body diagram template sheets (printed, 6 per page)
Toy cars and string for pulling demos

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Free Body Diagrams and Net Force Calculations. Show the sample Regents question from the bungee jumping cluster: 'Which vector diagram correctly models the forces acting on the bungee jumper standing on the platform?' Display the four choices. Ask students to vote before instruction. Reveal that this exact type of question appears on the Regents exam.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Free Body Diagrams and Net Force Calculations. Scenario stations: Students rotate through four stations, each with a physical setup. Station 1 — A book resting on a table. Station 2 — A mass hanging from a spring scale. Station 3 — A cart being pulled across the table with a string (include friction). Station 4 — A mass hanging from two strings at angles. At each station, students draw a free body diagram and label all forces with arrows proportional to magnitude.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Free Body Diagrams and Net Force Calculations. Teach the free body diagram procedure: (1) Identify the object. (2) Draw it as a dot. (3) Identify all contact forces (normal, friction, tension, applied) and field forces (gravity). (4) Draw arrows from the dot in the direction of each force, scaled to relative magnitude. (5) Choose a coordinate system. (6) Sum forces in each direction: F_net,x = ΣFx and F_net,y = ΣFy. Work through a horizontal pulling problem and a hanging mass problem.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Free Body Diagrams and Net Force Calculations. evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Free Body Diagrams and Net Force Calculations. differentiation.advanced: Solve problems involving forces at angles requiring component decomposition. Analyze a system with two connected objects (Atwood machine) using separate FBDs for each object.

differentiation.iep: Provide a FBD template with force arrows pre-drawn for common scenarios; students label and calculate magnitudes. Break net force calculation into steps: 'Add all forces pointing right. Add all forces pointing left. Subtract to find net force.' Allow extended time.

cer.phenomenon: An elevator contains a person standing on a bathroom scale. When the elevator is at rest on the ground floor, the scale reads 700 N. As the elevator begins to accelerate upward, the scale reads 840 N. As the elevator moves upward at constant velocity, the scale reads 700 N again. As the elevator decelerates near the top floor, the scale reads 560 N.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the free body diagram analysis, I claim that the scale reading changes because the scale measures the normal force, not the true weight, and this normal force changes when...
cer.evidence_source: Draw a free body diagram for the person during each phase (at rest, accelerating up, constant velocity, decelerating). Calculate the net force and acceleration in each case.

lessons.title: Weight, Mass, and the Force of Gravity (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: distinguish between mass and weight, calculate the weight of an object using F_g = mg, and explain how weight changes with location while mass stays constant
lessons.circle_prompt: If you could visit any planet or moon in the solar system, where would you go? Would you weigh more or less there? Would you have more or less mass?
lessons.do_now: A 70 kg astronaut stands on Earth where g = 9.81 m/s^2. Calculate their weight. Then calculate their weight on the Moon where g = 1.62 m/s^2. Did their mass change?

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Weight, Mass, and the Force of Gravity. Show a clip of astronauts on the International Space Station floating and 'weightless.' Ask: Have the astronauts lost mass? Have they lost weight? Are they truly weightless? (They are in free fall — the ISS and astronauts fall together, so there is no normal force, creating the sensation of weightlessness.) Students discuss the surprising answer.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Weight, Mass, and the Force of Gravity. Students measure the same object's mass on a triple-beam balance (in grams/kg) and its weight on a spring scale (in Newtons). They do this for five objects of different mass. They plot Weight (N) vs. Mass (kg) on graph paper. The slope of the line should be approximately 9.81 — students calculate it and recognize this as g.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Weight, Mass, and the Force of Gravity. Define weight: F_g = mg, where g is the gravitational field strength (9.81 N/kg on Earth). Mass is intrinsic (amount of matter, in kg) and does not change with location. Weight is a force (in N) and changes depending on the local value of g. Demonstrate: the same 1 kg mass weighs 9.81 N on Earth, 1.62 N on the Moon, and 24.79 N on Jupiter. Complete a 'Weight on Other Worlds' table as a class.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Weight, Mass, and the Force of Gravity. Students calculate their own weight on Earth, the Moon, Mars, and Jupiter using the planetary gravity data card. Then they solve: An object weighs 50 N on Earth. What is its mass? What would it weigh on Mars (g = 3.71 m/s^2)? If you wanted an object to weigh 100 N on Mars, what mass would it need?

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Weight, Mass, and the Force of Gravity. Exit ticket: (1) What is the mass of an object that weighs 196 N on Earth? (2) Would this object have the same mass on the Moon? (3) Would it have the same weight? Calculate its weight on the Moon (g = 1.62 m/s^2).

differentiation.approaching: Provide a Mass vs. Weight comparison chart with fill-in blanks. Pre-organize the 'Weight on Other Worlds' table with formulas visible. Include a conversion helper: 'To find weight from mass, multiply by g.'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the graphing lab and planetary weight calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research why g varies slightly at different locations on Earth (altitude, latitude, local geology). Calculate how much their weight changes between sea level and the top of Mount Everest.
differentiation.ell: Use visual weight vs. mass comparison posters with images of scales (spring scale = weight in N, balance = mass in kg). Provide sentence frames for explaining the difference. Include native language vocabulary cards.
differentiation.iep: Provide a Weight = mass x g card with examples. Use a simple two-step template for all problems: 'Step 1: Identify mass and g. Step 2: Multiply.' Reduce the planetary calculations to two planets. Allow calculator use throughout.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how understanding weight vs. mass is critical for space missions, including the contributions of Dr. Mae Jemison, the first African American woman in space, who conducted experiments on weightlessness and bone loss aboard the Space Shuttle Endeavour in 1992.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'weight' and 'mass': An astronaut on the Moon can jump higher than on Earth because___. Mass and weight are related, but they are not the same thing because___. The gravitational field strength on Jupiter is 24.79 m/s^2, so a 50 kg person would weigh___.

vocabulary.definition: The gravitational force acting on an object; F_g = mg; a vector quantity measured in Newtons directed toward the center of the attracting body
The force of gravity per unit mass at a given location; on Earth's surface, g = 9.81 N/kg (equivalent to 9.81 m/s^2)
The condition in which an object experiences no normal force; occurs during free fall, not due to the absence of gravity

cer.phenomenon: A produce company ships fruit from Earth to a hypothetical Moon colony. On Earth, they pack 100 kg of apples into a crate. A customer on the Moon colony weighs the crate on a spring scale and reads only 162 N, which corresponds to 16.5 kg on Earth. The customer claims they were shortchanged. The company insists they shipped 100 kg.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the difference between mass and weight, I claim that both the company and the customer can be correct because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the weight of 100 kg of apples on the Moon (g = 1.62 m/s^2) and explain why a spring scale calibrated for Earth would give a misleading reading on the Moon.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because a spring scale measures ___, not mass. On the Moon, 100 kg has a weight of only ___ N, which a scale calibrated for Earth would incorrectly report as ___ kg. To accurately measure mass on the Moon, the customer should use a ___ instead.

lessons.title: Friction — Static and Kinetic (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: distinguish between static and kinetic friction, calculate friction forces using Ff = mu * F_N, and predict how friction affects the motion of objects
lessons.circle_prompt: What surfaces are the most slippery you have ever walked on? What made them slippery? What did you do differently to walk safely?
lessons.do_now: A 10 kg box sits on a rough floor. You push it with 20 N of force and it does not move. Then you push with 40 N and it starts sliding. What was the maximum static friction? Is kinetic friction larger or smaller than static friction?
materials: Wooden blocks with different surfaces (smooth, rough, sandpaper-covered)
Masses to place on blocks (200 g, 500 g, 1 kg)
Various surface materials (glass, cardboard, rubber mat, wax paper)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Friction — Static and Kinetic. Show a video of curling — the sport where players slide a stone across ice and sweepers brush the ice ahead of it. Ask: Why do they sweep? What effect does sweeping have on friction? How can changing friction change the outcome of the game? This introduces friction as something that can be measured and manipulated.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Friction — Static and Kinetic. Lab investigation: Students pull a wooden block at constant speed across different surfaces using a spring scale to measure kinetic friction force. They vary the normal force by adding masses on top of the block. Students create a data table of F_friction vs. F_normal for each surface and graph the results. The slope of each line is the coefficient of kinetic friction (mu_k).

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Friction — Static and Kinetic. Define friction: a contact force that opposes the relative motion (or attempted motion) between surfaces. Static friction (Ff <= mu_s * F_N) prevents motion and adjusts up to a maximum. Kinetic friction (Ff = mu_k * F_N) acts on sliding objects and is constant. Key relationships: mu_s > mu_k for the same surfaces; friction depends on normal force and surface type, NOT on surface area. Connect to lab data.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Friction — Static and Kinetic. Multi-step problem: A 20 kg box is pushed across a floor (mu_k = 0.30) with a force of 100 N horizontally. Students draw the FBD, calculate F_N (= mg = 196 N), kinetic friction (= 0.30 x 196 = 58.8 N), net force (= 100 - 58.8 = 41.2 N), and acceleration (= 41.2/20 = 2.06 m/s^2). Then: What minimum force is needed to start the box moving if mu_s = 0.40?

cer.phenomenon: On a dry road, a car traveling at 25 m/s can stop in approximately 32 m. On a wet road, the same car at the same speed requires approximately 64 m to stop. On an icy road, the stopping distance increases to approximately 160 m. The car's mass and brakes are identical in all three cases.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the relationship between friction and stopping distance, I claim that road conditions primarily affect stopping distance by changing...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the coefficient of kinetic friction for each road condition using the kinematic equation vf^2 = vi^2 + 2ad and F_friction = mu * mg.

lessons.title: Inclined Planes (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: resolve gravitational force into components parallel and perpendicular to an inclined plane and calculate the acceleration of an object on a frictionless or frictional incline
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever tried to walk up or push something up a steep hill? What made it harder as the hill got steeper? At what angle would it become impossible?
lessons.do_now: A 5 kg block sits on a ramp tilted at 30 degrees. Draw the force of gravity straight down. Now try to split that gravity arrow into two parts: one along the ramp and one into the ramp surface. Which part tries to slide the block down?

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Inclined Planes. Show images of San Francisco's steepest streets (grades up to 31.5%) and ask: Why do cars sometimes slide on these streets? What forces are acting? Then show a video of a truck failing to climb an icy hill. Ask: What angle would make it impossible for any vehicle to climb, even without ice?

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Inclined Planes. Groups place a wooden block on an adjustable ramp and slowly increase the angle until the block begins to slide. They measure this critical angle (angle of repose). Then they set the ramp to 20, 30, and 40 degrees and use a spring scale to measure the force needed to hold the block stationary on the ramp at each angle. Students note the pattern: steeper angle → more force needed.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Inclined Planes. Teach the inclined plane force decomposition: gravity splits into F_parallel = mg sin(theta) along the ramp and F_perpendicular = mg cos(theta) into the surface. The normal force equals F_perpendicular (not mg!). For a frictionless incline: a = g sin(theta). With friction: a = g sin(theta) - mu_k * g cos(theta). Draw the full FBD on the incline with rotated coordinate axes. Work through a complete example: 8 kg block on a 37-degree incline with mu_k = 0.20.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Inclined Planes. Students solve: A 50 kg skier starts from rest at the top of a 25-degree slope that is 100 m long. If mu_k = 0.10, what is the skier's acceleration? How fast are they going at the bottom? How long does the run take?

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Inclined Planes. Exit ticket: A 4.0 kg block is on a frictionless 30-degree incline. (a) What is F_parallel? (b) What is F_perpendicular? (c) What is the normal force? (d) What is the acceleration down the ramp?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a color-coded inclined plane FBD template: red arrow for gravity (straight down), green for F_parallel (along ramp, downhill), blue for F_perpendicular (into surface), purple for normal force (out of surface). Include the formulas next to each arrow.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the ramp exploration and incline calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Determine the angle at which the block begins to slide and use it to calculate the coefficient of static friction (tan(theta_c) = mu_s). Analyze a block being pushed UP an incline against both gravity and friction.
differentiation.ell: Use the physical ramp extensively before introducing equations. Provide step-by-step visual guides showing how to decompose the gravity vector. Label diagrams in English and native language.
differentiation.iep: Provide a pre-drawn inclined plane FBD with forces labeled and formulas written next to each. Break problems into: 'Step 1: Find F_parallel. Step 2: Find F_perpendicular. Step 3: Find normal force. Step 4: Find friction. Step 5: Find net force. Step 6: Find acceleration.' Allow calculator use throughout.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how the ancient Egyptians used inclined planes (ramps) to build the pyramids, and how the Inca built steep road systems through the Andes mountains with switchback ramps. Both civilizations understood intuitively that ramps reduce the force needed to move heavy objects — the same physics students calculate today.

Both F_parallel and F_perpendicular come from gravity, but they act in different directions, so___. The ramp angle was increased from 20 to 40 degrees, so the block's acceleration___.

cer.phenomenon: A moving company must slide a 200 kg piano down a ramp from a second-floor apartment. The ramp is 6 m long and the second floor is 3 m above the ground (30-degree angle). Without friction, the piano would accelerate dangerously. They lay a carpet on the ramp (mu_k = 0.45) and the piano slides down slowly and controllably.
cer.claim_starter: Based on inclined plane analysis, I claim that the carpet reduces the piano's acceleration to a safe level because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the acceleration of the piano without friction (a = g sin 30) and with friction (a = g sin 30 - mu_k * g cos 30). Compare both values and calculate the piano's speed at the bottom in each case.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because without friction the acceleration would be ___ m/s^2, reaching a speed of ___ m/s at the bottom, but with the carpet's friction the acceleration is reduced to ___ m/s^2, resulting in a manageable speed of ___ m/s.

lessons.title: Circular Motion and Centripetal Force (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: explain that an object moving in a circle is accelerating, identify the centripetal force keeping it in circular motion, and calculate centripetal acceleration and force
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever been on a merry-go-round, a spinning ride at an amusement park, or taken a sharp turn in a car? What did you feel? Which direction were you pulled?
lessons.do_now: Tie a small object to a string and swing it in a horizontal circle above your head. If you let go of the string, which direction does the object fly — outward, inward, or tangent to the circle? Try it (safely) and observe.
materials: Small masses on strings (1 per student, for safe spinning)
Rubber stoppers and glass tubes for centripetal force apparatus (1 per group)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Circular Motion and Centripetal Force. Show a video of a car making a sharp turn — a coffee cup on the dashboard slides to the outside of the turn. Ask: What force pushes the cup outward? (Trick question — no force pushes it outward! The cup continues in a straight line due to inertia while the car turns underneath it. The cup appears to slide outward from the car's frame of reference.) This challenges the common 'centrifugal force' misconception.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Circular Motion and Centripetal Force. Lab activity: Students swing a rubber stopper in a horizontal circle using the centripetal force apparatus (stopper on string through a glass tube, with hanging masses providing the centripetal force). They vary the radius (string length) and the speed (number of revolutions per time) and observe how the hanging mass needed to maintain circular motion changes. Students record data on force, radius, and period.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Circular Motion and Centripetal Force. Define centripetal acceleration: ac = v^2/r, always directed toward the center of the circle. Centripetal force: Fc = mac = mv^2/r, also toward the center. Emphasize: centripetal force is not a new type of force — it is the name for whatever force provides the center-directed acceleration (tension, gravity, friction, normal force). Examples: the Moon orbits Earth (gravity is centripetal force), a car turns (friction is centripetal force), a ball on a string (tension is centripetal force).

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Circular Motion and Centripetal Force. Problem: A 1000 kg car makes a turn on a flat road with radius 50 m at 15 m/s. (a) What centripetal acceleration does the car experience? (b) What centripetal force is needed? (c) What provides this force? (friction) (d) What is the minimum coefficient of friction needed? Students solve and discuss what happens if mu is too low (the car skids outward).

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Circular Motion and Centripetal Force. lessons.title: Momentum — The Measure of Motion (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: calculate the momentum of an object and explain why momentum depends on both mass and velocity
lessons.circle_prompt: Which would be harder to stop — a truck moving slowly or a bicycle moving fast? What about the truck and bicycle moving at the same speed? What factors matter when trying to stop something?
lessons.do_now: A 0.145 kg baseball traveling at 40 m/s and a 7.0 kg bowling ball traveling at 2.0 m/s both head toward you. Which one has more momentum? Which one would you rather try to catch? Why might your answers differ?
materials: Various balls (tennis, baseball, basketball, bowling ball — or equivalent masses)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Momentum — The Measure of Motion. Show a side-by-side comparison: a ping-pong ball fired at 1000 m/s vs. a bowling ball rolling at 1 m/s. Which has more momentum? Students calculate both (p = mv) and are surprised that the bowling ball's momentum (7 x 1 = 7 kg·m/s) far exceeds the ping-pong ball's (0.0027 x 1000 = 2.7 kg·m/s). This introduces momentum as the quantity that combines mass AND velocity.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Momentum — The Measure of Motion. Groups rank 8 objects by momentum: (1) a 1500 kg car at 30 m/s, (2) a 100 kg sprinter at 10 m/s, (3) a 0.058 kg tennis ball at 60 m/s, (4) a 0.145 kg baseball at 40 m/s, (5) a 7.26 kg shot put at 14 m/s, (6) a 0.005 kg bullet at 900 m/s, (7) an 80 kg person walking at 1.5 m/s, (8) a 75,000 kg loaded semi-truck at 25 m/s. Students calculate, rank, and discuss which they would least want to be hit by and why 'most momentum' doesn't always mean 'most dangerous.'

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Momentum — The Measure of Motion. Define momentum: p = mv, a vector quantity with the same direction as velocity, measured in kg·m/s. Key properties: momentum is proportional to both mass and velocity, it has a direction, and changing momentum requires a force over time (preview of impulse). Show that Newton originally wrote his Second Law as F = Δp/Δt (rate of change of momentum), not F = ma. Work through examples including a direction change: a ball bouncing off a wall.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Momentum — The Measure of Motion. Direction matters problem: A 0.4 kg ball moves east at 10 m/s and bounces off a wall, returning west at 8 m/s. Calculate the change in momentum. (Students must recognize that the direction change means Δp = p_final - p_initial = (-3.2) - (4.0) = -7.2 kg·m/s, not 0.8.) Discuss why this is larger than if the ball simply stopped.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Momentum — The Measure of Motion. Exit ticket: A 70 kg hockey player skates north at 8 m/s. (a) What is the player's momentum? (b) A 90 kg player skates south at 6 m/s. What is their momentum? (c) Which player has greater momentum magnitude? (d) If they collide head-on, what is the total momentum of the system?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a momentum calculation template: p = m x v, with units clearly shown (kg x m/s = kg·m/s). Include a direction reminder: 'Momentum is a vector — include direction.' Pre-set up the ranking activity with a calculation table.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the momentum ranking activity and direction-change problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research and present on the concept of momentum in special relativity (relativistic momentum) and explain why objects cannot reach the speed of light.
differentiation.ell: Use physical demonstrations with rolling balls of different masses and speeds. Provide a visual momentum comparison chart with bar diagrams. Include bilingual vocabulary and sentence frames.
differentiation.iep: Provide a p = mv reference card with worked examples. Focus on magnitude calculations before introducing direction. Reduce the ranking activity to 5 objects. Allow calculator use throughout.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how understanding momentum is essential in sports analysis — from cricket bowling speeds to NFL tackle physics. Highlight how Dr. Stefan Duma, a biomechanical engineer, uses momentum calculations to design safer football helmets, and how recent research has focused on protecting youth athletes in underserved communities where outdated equipment is common.

A bullet and a bowling ball can have the same momentum, but the bullet travels much faster because___. The ball bounced off the wall and reversed direction, so the change in momentum was ___ than if it had simply stopped.

A system with no external net forces acting on it; the total momentum of an isolated system is conserved

cer.phenomenon: In bowling, a 7.26 kg ball traveling at 8.0 m/s strikes a 1.5 kg pin at rest. After the collision, the pin flies backward at 12 m/s while the ball continues forward at a reduced speed. A common misconception is that the lighter pin must have less momentum than the heavier ball.
cer.claim_starter: Based on momentum calculations, I claim that the pin's momentum after the collision is ___ compared to the ball's change in momentum because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the ball's initial momentum, the pin's final momentum, and the ball's change in momentum. Compare the magnitudes.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the pin's momentum after the collision (p = ___ x ___ = ___ kg·m/s) is related to the ball's ___ in momentum, which connects to the idea that momentum is ___ between objects during interactions.

lessons.title: Impulse and the Impulse-Momentum Theorem (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: calculate impulse as force multiplied by time, apply the impulse-momentum theorem (J = Delta p), and explain how increasing collision time decreases the force experienced
lessons.circle_prompt: Would you rather fall onto concrete or a mattress? Jump from a height and land stiff-legged or bend your knees? Why? What is your body doing differently in each case?
lessons.do_now: A 0.5 kg ball drops and hits the ground, changing its velocity from -5 m/s to +3 m/s in 0.02 seconds. What is the change in momentum? What average force did the ground exert on the ball?
materials: Various padding materials (bubble wrap, foam, towels, newspaper)
Containers for egg drop (cups, bags, boxes)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Impulse and the Impulse-Momentum Theorem. Teacher demonstration: Drop an egg onto a hard surface (it breaks). Then drop an identical egg from the same height onto a thick foam pad (it survives). Ask: Both eggs experienced the same change in momentum (same mass, same velocity change). So why did one break and the other didn't? The difference must be in the FORCE — which depends on the TIME of the collision.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Impulse and the Impulse-Momentum Theorem. Engineering challenge: Groups design a container using provided padding materials that will protect an egg dropped from 2 m. Before dropping, each group must calculate: (a) the egg's velocity at impact (using free fall), (b) the change in momentum, and (c) the average force if the collision time is 0.01 s (no padding) vs. 0.1 s (with padding). After predictions, groups test their designs.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Impulse and the Impulse-Momentum Theorem. Define impulse: J = F * Delta t (force x time), measured in N·s. State the Impulse-Momentum Theorem: J = Delta p, meaning F * Delta t = m * Delta v. Key insight: for a given change in momentum, increasing the collision time DECREASES the force: F = Delta p / Delta t. Show the graphical interpretation: impulse is the area under a Force-time graph. Work through an airbag calculation: same Delta p, but airbag extends time from 0.005 s to 0.05 s.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Impulse and the Impulse-Momentum Theorem. Real-world applications analysis: Students explain the physics behind: (1) Why cars have crumple zones. (2) Why boxers roll with punches. (3) Why gymnasts bend their knees on landing. (4) Why there are padded walls behind the goals in ice hockey. For each, students identify what changes (time), what stays the same (impulse/momentum change), and what decreases (force).

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Impulse and the Impulse-Momentum Theorem. Exit ticket: A 60 kg person jumps from a 1.0 m ledge. (a) Calculate their velocity just before hitting the ground. (b) Calculate the impulse needed to stop them. (c) If they land stiff-legged (Delta t = 0.01 s), what is the average force? (d) If they bend their knees (Delta t = 0.3 s), what is the average force?

differentiation.approaching: Provide the Impulse-Momentum Theorem as a visual equation chain: F x t = m x Delta v. Include a 'big time = small force' diagram showing the inverse relationship. Pre-calculate the egg's impact velocity for the engineering challenge.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the egg drop engineering challenge and impulse calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Analyze a Force-time graph with non-constant force (triangular or parabolic shape) and calculate impulse as the area under the curve. Compare impulse from an airbag Force-time graph to a rigid steering wheel graph.
differentiation.ell: Use the egg drop as primary instruction — the physical experience makes the abstract concept concrete. Provide a visual impulse-momentum chain: 'Larger time → Smaller force → Less damage.' Include bilingual vocabulary.
differentiation.iep: Provide the impulse formula on a reference card. Focus on the conceptual relationship (longer time = less force) before calculations. Break the exit ticket into two separate problems. Allow calculator use throughout.

lessons.crse_connection: Explore the physics of traditional martial arts techniques — karate practitioners break boards by maximizing force (short contact time), while aikido practitioners redirect an opponent's momentum over a longer time to reduce injury. Connect to how these cultural practices from Japan and East Asia embody impulse-momentum physics.

lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can apply and compare concepts and calculate impulse as force multiplied by time, apply the impulse-momentum theorem (J = Delta p), and explain how increasing collision time decreases the force experienced
lessons.circle_prompt: Share one connection you made between yesterday's topic and something in your daily life.
lessons.do_now: Recall from yesterday: explain one key idea from yesterday about how to define and describe key concepts related to: calculate impulse as force multiplied by time, apply the impulse-momentum theorem (J = Delta p), and explain how increasing collision time decreases the force experienced.
materials: Various padding materials (bubble wrap, foam, towels, newspaper)
Containers for egg drop (cups, bags, boxes)

engage.description: Review warm-up connecting Day 1 vocabulary to a new example or context. Continuing: Teacher demonstration: Drop an egg onto a hard surface (it breaks). Then drop an identical egg from the same height onto a thick foam pad (it survives). Ask: Both eggs experienced the same change in momentum (same mass, same velocity change). So why did one break and the other didn't? The difference must be in the FORCE — which depends on the TIME of the collision.

explore.description: Structured practice — students work through increasingly complex problems with scaffolds. Continuing: Engineering challenge: Groups design a container using provided padding materials that will protect an egg dropped from 2 m. Before dropping, each group must calculate: (a) the egg's velocity at impact (using free fall), (b) the change in momentum, and (c) the average force if the collision time is 0.01 s (no padding) vs. 0.1 s (with padding). After predictions, groups test their designs.

explain.description: Mini-lesson addressing patterns from practice; introduce additional complexity. Continuing: Define impulse: J = F * Delta t (force x time), measured in N·s. State the Impulse-Momentum Theorem: J = Delta p, meaning F * Delta t = m * Delta v. Key insight: for a given change in momentum, increasing the collision time DECREASES the force: F = Delta p / Delta t. Show the graphical interpretation: impulse is the area under a Force-time graph. Work through an airbag calculation: same Delta p, but airbag extends time from 0.005 s to 0.05 s.

elaborate.description: Partner work on application problems with real-world contexts. Continuing: Real-world applications analysis: Students explain the physics behind: (1) Why cars have crumple zones. (2) Why boxers roll with punches. (3) Why gymnasts bend their knees on landing. (4) Why there are padded walls behind the goals in ice hockey. For each, students identify what changes (time), what stays the same (impulse/momentum change), and what decreases (force).

evaluate.description: Formative assessment — students solve 2-3 problems independently and self-check. Continuing: Exit ticket: A 60 kg person jumps from a 1.0 m ledge. (a) Calculate their velocity just before hitting the ground. (b) Calculate the impulse needed to stop them. (c) If they land stiff-legged (Delta t = 0.01 s), what is the average force? (d) If they bend their knees (Delta t = 0.3 s), what is the average force?

differentiation.approaching: Provide completed examples from Day 1 as reference. Provide the Impulse-Momentum Theorem as a visual equation chain: F x t = m x Delta v. Include a 'big time = small force' diagram showing the inverse relationship. Pre-calculate the egg's impact velocity for the engineering challenge.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the egg drop engineering challenge and impulse calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Analyze a Force-time graph with non-constant force (triangular or parabolic shape) and calculate impulse as the area under the curve. Compare impulse from an airbag Force-time graph to a rigid steering wheel graph.
differentiation.ell: Use the egg drop as primary instruction — the physical experience makes the abstract concept concrete. Provide a visual impulse-momentum chain: 'Larger time → Smaller force → Less damage.' Include bilingual vocabulary.
differentiation.iep: Provide the impulse formula on a reference card. Focus on the conceptual relationship (longer time = less force) before calculations. Break the exit ticket into two separate problems. Allow calculator use throughout.

lessons.crse_connection: Explore the physics of traditional martial arts techniques — karate practitioners break boards by maximizing force (short contact time), while aikido practitioners redirect an opponent's momentum over a longer time to reduce injury. Connect to how these cultural practices from Japan and East Asia embody impulse-momentum physics.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'Force-Time Graph': Write three sentences — 'Force-Time Graph... because ___.' / 'Force-Time Graph... but ___.' / 'Force-Time Graph... so ___.'

vocabulary.definition: The impulse on an object equals its change in momentum: F * Delta t = m * Delta v = Delta p
A graph showing force on the y-axis and time on the x-axis; the area under the curve equals the impulse

cer.phenomenon: Two identical crash test dummies in identical cars hit a wall at 50 km/h (13.9 m/s). Car A has a rigid steel frame and comes to a stop in 0.05 s. Car B has engineered crumple zones and comes to a stop in 0.5 s. Both drivers have a mass of 75 kg. The dummy in Car A experiences severe 'injuries' while the dummy in Car B survives with minor damage.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the impulse-momentum theorem, I claim that the crumple zone reduces the peak force by a factor of approximately ___ because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the impulse (change in momentum) for both dummies — it is the same. Then calculate the average force in each car using F = Delta p / Delta t.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because both dummies experience the same impulse of ___ N·s (since Delta p = m * Delta v = ___), but Car A's force is ___ N while Car B's force is only ___ N. The crumple zone increased the collision time by a factor of ___, which reduced the force by the same factor because ___.

lessons.title: Conservation of Momentum (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: apply the law of conservation of momentum to calculate unknown velocities before or after a collision in an isolated system
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever played pool or billiards? What happens when the cue ball hits another ball straight on? What about at an angle? Is anything 'lost' in the collision?
lessons.do_now: A 2 kg cart moving at 3 m/s collides with a stationary 1 kg cart. After the collision, the 2 kg cart moves at 1 m/s in the same direction. What is the velocity of the 1 kg cart after the collision? (Hint: total momentum before = total momentum after.)
materials: Dynamics carts with spring bumpers (2 per group)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Conservation of Momentum. Show a Newton's cradle in action. Ask: When one ball swings in and hits, why does exactly one ball swing out the other side? Why not two balls at half the speed? Students predict and discuss. Introduce the idea that something is conserved — total momentum of the system does not change if no external forces act.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Conservation of Momentum. Lab investigation: Groups perform cart collisions on a dynamics track. They measure velocities before and after collision (using photogates or distance/time). Trial 1: equal mass carts, one at rest. Trial 2: unequal mass carts, one at rest. Trial 3: both carts moving toward each other. For each trial, students calculate total momentum before and after and compare.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Conservation of Momentum. State the Law of Conservation of Momentum: In an isolated system (no external net force), total momentum before an interaction equals total momentum after. Mathematical form: m1v1i + m2v2i = m1v1f + m2v2f. Derive from Newton's Third Law: during the collision, F_12 = -F_21, so Delta p_1 = -Delta p_2, meaning the total change in momentum is zero. Work through two examples: a collision where both objects are initially moving, and an explosion (person throwing a ball).

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Conservation of Momentum. Recoil problem: A 60 kg astronaut floating at rest in space throws a 5 kg toolbox at 3 m/s away from the space station. What is the astronaut's velocity after the throw? Students apply conservation of momentum with initial momentum = 0 and recognize this is the same physics as rocket propulsion.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Conservation of Momentum. Exit ticket: A 10 kg bowling ball moving at 6 m/s strikes a 1.5 kg pin at rest. After the collision, the bowling ball moves at 5.2 m/s in the same direction. (a) What is the total momentum before the collision? (b) What is the pin's velocity after the collision? (c) Is momentum conserved? Show your work.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a conservation of momentum equation template with labeled slots: m1*v1i + m2*v2i = m1*v1f + m2*v2f. Include a checklist: 'Is one object at rest? Set that v = 0. Are they moving in opposite directions? Make one velocity negative.' Walk through one worked example before independent practice.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the collision lab and conservation of momentum calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Analyze a multi-object collision (three objects) and verify conservation of momentum. Calculate the percentage of kinetic energy lost in each lab trial to classify the collision type (preview of elastic/inelastic).
differentiation.ell: Use the physical cart collisions as primary instruction. Provide a visual before/after diagram template where students draw and label velocities. Include bilingual vocabulary and a labeled equation template.
differentiation.iep: Provide the conservation equation on a reference card with an example. Pre-fill 'before' values in the equation and let students solve for the unknown 'after' value. Reduce to two-object, one-at-rest problems only. Allow calculator use.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the physics of car collisions and how conservation of momentum is used in accident reconstruction — a field that intersects with social justice when determining fault in crashes. Highlight how bias in accident investigations has historically affected communities of color and how objective physics-based reconstruction can promote fairness.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'conservation of momentum': Total momentum is conserved in a collision because___. The bowling ball slows down after hitting the pin, but the total momentum of the system doesn't change because___. The astronaut was initially at rest and threw the toolbox forward, so the astronaut must move___.

vocabulary.definition: In an isolated system with no external net force, the total momentum before an interaction equals the total momentum after
Forces from outside the system (e.g., friction with the ground, gravity if not accounted for); these CAN change the total momentum

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: The Law of Conservation of Momentum

vocabulary.definition: A system in which no external net forces act; only internal forces between objects within the system are present
The backward motion of one object when another is propelled forward; an application of conservation of momentum starting from rest

cer.phenomenon: In a football game, a 100 kg linebacker running east at 5 m/s tackles a 80 kg running back moving east at 7 m/s. After the tackle, both players move together (they stick together). A referee flags the play and claims the running back was moving forward before the tackle.
cer.claim_starter: Based on conservation of momentum, I claim that after the tackle, both players move ___ at ___ m/s because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the total momentum before the collision (both moving east, so add). Use m1v1i + m2v2i = (m1 + m2)vf to find the final velocity.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the total momentum before is ___ + ___ = ___ kg·m/s eastward. Since they stick together, vf = ___/(___ + ___) = ___ m/s eastward. The positive (eastward) direction confirms the running back's forward motion was sufficient to carry both players ___.

lessons.title: Elastic and Inelastic Collisions (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: classify collisions as elastic, inelastic, or perfectly inelastic and determine whether kinetic energy is conserved in each type
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about different types of collisions you have seen — a bouncy ball vs. a lump of clay, bumper cars vs. a car crash. What is different about each? Does anything get 'used up' in some collisions?
lessons.do_now: Two 1 kg carts collide on a frictionless track. Before: Cart A moves at 4 m/s, Cart B is at rest. After: Cart A is at rest, Cart B moves at 4 m/s. Calculate the total kinetic energy before and after. Was kinetic energy conserved?
materials: Dynamics carts with magnetic bumpers (elastic) and Velcro bumpers (inelastic)
Happy ball and sad ball (same size, different bounce)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Elastic and Inelastic Collisions. Drop a 'happy ball' (bouncy) and a 'sad ball' (non-bouncy, same size and appearance) from the same height. The happy ball bounces high while the sad ball barely bounces. Ask: Both had the same momentum change (from moving down to stopping). But one bounces and one doesn't. What's different? Where did the energy go in the sad ball? Introduce the idea that momentum is always conserved, but kinetic energy may not be.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Elastic and Inelastic Collisions. Groups perform two types of collisions on the dynamics track: (1) Magnetic bumper carts (elastic-like — they bounce apart) and (2) Velcro bumper carts (perfectly inelastic — they stick together). For each, students measure velocities before and after, calculate total momentum (should be conserved in both), and calculate total kinetic energy before and after (conserved only in elastic).

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Elastic and Inelastic Collisions. Define three collision types: (1) Perfectly elastic — objects bounce apart, both momentum and KE conserved (ideal case: billiard balls). (2) Inelastic — objects separate but KE is not conserved; some KE converts to heat, sound, deformation. (3) Perfectly inelastic — objects stick together; maximum KE loss (but momentum still conserved). Key formula for perfectly inelastic: m1v1i + m2v2i = (m1 + m2)vf. For elastic collisions between equal masses with one at rest: objects exchange velocities.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Elastic and Inelastic Collisions. Problem: A 1500 kg car traveling at 20 m/s rear-ends a 1000 kg car at rest. (a) If they stick together (perfectly inelastic), find the final velocity. (b) Calculate KE before and after. (c) What percentage of KE was lost? (d) Where did the lost energy go? (heat, sound, deformation of the metal)

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Elastic and Inelastic Collisions. Exit ticket: Two objects collide. Object A (3 kg) moves at 5 m/s east. Object B (2 kg) moves at 3 m/s west. They stick together. (a) Find the final velocity. (b) Is this elastic or inelastic? (c) Calculate the KE lost.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a collision type comparison chart: Elastic (bounce, KE conserved), Inelastic (separate, KE not conserved), Perfectly Inelastic (stick, max KE loss). Include worked examples for each type.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the collision lab comparing elastic and inelastic collisions and solve both types of problems.
differentiation.advanced: Solve a fully elastic collision algebraically (two equations: conservation of momentum and conservation of KE) to find both final velocities. Analyze the percentage of energy lost as a function of mass ratio in perfectly inelastic collisions.
differentiation.ell: Use the physical cart demonstrations as primary instruction. Provide a visual collision comparison poster with arrows and labels. Color-code: green = elastic (all KE kept), red = perfectly inelastic (max KE lost). Include bilingual vocabulary.
differentiation.iep: Focus on perfectly inelastic collisions only (stick together — one equation, one unknown). Provide the combined formula on a reference card. Break KE calculations into single steps. Allow calculator use throughout.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how collision physics is used in car safety ratings by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and how access to safer vehicles is an equity issue — families in lower-income communities often drive older cars with fewer safety features. Connect to how physics knowledge empowers consumers to make informed safety decisions.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'elastic' and 'inelastic': In a perfectly inelastic collision, the objects stick together, so the final velocity is found by___. Momentum is conserved in all collisions, but kinetic energy is only conserved in ___ collisions because___. The sad ball lost most of its kinetic energy on impact because___.

vocabulary.definition: A collision in which both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved; objects bounce apart with no permanent deformation
A collision in which the objects stick together after impact; momentum is conserved but the maximum amount of kinetic energy is lost
A permanent change in shape resulting from a collision; represents energy transferred from kinetic energy to internal energy

Section 3: Kinetic Energy — Sometimes Conserved, Sometimes Not
Section 5: Where Does the Lost Kinetic Energy Go?

lessons.do_now: Review: Based on yesterday's lesson, explain one key idea from yesterday about how to define and identify key concepts related to: classify collisions as elastic, inelastic, or perfectly inelastic and determine whether kinetic energy is conserved in each type.
materials: Dynamics carts with magnetic bumpers (elastic) and Velcro bumpers (inelastic)
Happy ball and sad ball (same size, different bounce)

engage.description: Brief review of Day 1 concepts through a warm-up problem or quick discussion. Building on previous days: Drop a 'happy ball' (bouncy) and a 'sad ball' (non-bouncy, same size and appearance) from the same height. The happy ball bounces high while the sad ball barely bounces. Ask: Both had the same momentum change (from moving down to stopping). But one bounces and one doesn't. What's different? Where did the energy go in the sad ball? Introduce the idea that momentum is always conserved, but kinetic energy may not be.

explore.description: Students work through practice problems or applications in pairs or small groups. Building on previous days: Groups perform two types of collisions on the dynamics track: (1) Magnetic bumper carts (elastic-like — they bounce apart) and (2) Velcro bumper carts (perfectly inelastic — they stick together). For each, students measure velocities before and after, calculate total momentum (should be conserved in both), and calculate total kinetic energy before and after (conserved only in elastic).

explain.description: Address common misconceptions from practice; model problem-solving strategies. Building on previous days: Define three collision types: (1) Perfectly elastic — objects bounce apart, both momentum and KE conserved (ideal case: billiard balls). (2) Inelastic — objects separate but KE is not conserved; some KE converts to heat, sound, deformation. (3) Perfectly inelastic — objects stick together; maximum KE loss (but momentum still conserved). Key formula for perfectly inelastic: m1v1i + m2v2i = (m1 + m2)vf. For elastic collisions between equal masses with one at rest: objects exchange velocities.

elaborate.description: CER activity connecting evidence to claims about the topic. Building on previous days: Problem: A 1500 kg car traveling at 20 m/s rear-ends a 1000 kg car at rest. (a) If they stick together (perfectly inelastic), find the final velocity. (b) Calculate KE before and after. (c) What percentage of KE was lost? (d) Where did the lost energy go? (heat, sound, deformation of the metal)

evaluate.description: Exit ticket with application-level problems requiring multi-step reasoning. Building on previous days: Exit ticket: Two objects collide. Object A (3 kg) moves at 5 m/s east. Object B (2 kg) moves at 3 m/s west. They stick together. (a) Find the final velocity. (b) Is this elastic or inelastic? (c) Calculate the KE lost.

differentiation.approaching: Review key concepts from the full sequence before assessment. Provide a collision type comparison chart: Elastic (bounce, KE conserved), Inelastic (separate, KE not conserved), Perfectly Inelastic (stick, max KE loss). Include worked examples for each type.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the collision lab comparing elastic and inelastic collisions and solve both types of problems.
differentiation.advanced: Complete extension challenge connecting to real-world applications. Solve a fully elastic collision algebraically (two equations: conservation of momentum and conservation of KE) to find both final velocities. Analyze the percentage of energy lost as a function of mass ratio in perfectly inelastic collisions.
differentiation.ell: Use the physical cart demonstrations as primary instruction. Provide a visual collision comparison poster with arrows and labels. Color-code: green = elastic (all KE kept), red = perfectly inelastic (max KE lost). Include bilingual vocabulary.
differentiation.iep: Focus on perfectly inelastic collisions only (stick together — one equation, one unknown). Provide the combined formula on a reference card. Break KE calculations into single steps. Allow calculator use throughout.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how collision physics is used in car safety ratings by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and how access to safer vehicles is an equity issue — families in lower-income communities often drive older cars with fewer safety features. Connect to how physics knowledge empowers consumers to make informed safety decisions.
lessons.hochman_activity: Kernel sentence expansion using 'Kinetic Energy (KE)': Start with 'Kinetic Energy (KE) is important.' Expand by adding when, where, why, and how details to create a complex sentence that demonstrates understanding of the concept.

vocabulary.definition: A collision in which momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not; some KE is converted to heat, sound, or deformation
The energy of motion; KE = 1/2 mv^2; measured in Joules (J)

guided_notes_outline: Section 2: Momentum Is ALWAYS Conserved (in isolated systems)
Section 4: Perfectly Inelastic Collisions — Objects Stick Together

cer.phenomenon: In a physics lab, two identical 1.0 kg carts collide on a frictionless track. In Trial 1 (magnetic bumpers), Cart A at 2.0 m/s hits Cart B at rest; after, Cart A stops and Cart B moves at 2.0 m/s. In Trial 2 (Velcro bumpers), Cart A at 2.0 m/s hits Cart B at rest; after, both move together at 1.0 m/s.
cer.claim_starter: Based on energy analysis, I claim that Trial 1 is elastic and Trial 2 is perfectly inelastic because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate total KE before and after for both trials. Compare the results.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because in Trial 1, KE_before = ___ J and KE_after = ___ J (they are ___). In Trial 2, KE_before = ___ J and KE_after = ___ J (___% of KE was lost). Both trials conserve momentum (___ kg·m/s), but only Trial 1 conserves ___.

lessons.title: 2D Collisions Introduction and Real-World Applications (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: apply conservation of momentum in two dimensions by analyzing the x- and y-components separately and connect momentum concepts to real-world safety design
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever played pool, air hockey, or marbles? When you hit a ball at an angle, it doesn't go straight — it goes off to the side. Why? What determines the angle?
lessons.do_now: A 1.0 kg ball moving east at 5 m/s hits a stationary 1.0 kg ball. After the collision, ball 1 moves northeast at 3.5 m/s at 45 degrees above east. In which direction must ball 2 move to conserve momentum? Sketch the situation.
materials: Flat surface with grid paper taped to it
Carbon paper for marking collision paths

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: 2D Collisions Introduction and Real-World Applications. Show an overhead view of a pool break shot in slow motion. Ask: How does the cue ball 'know' which direction to send each ball? Does the total momentum of all the balls equal the cue ball's original momentum? Establish that conservation of momentum applies in every direction simultaneously — we analyze x and y components separately.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: 2D Collisions Introduction and Real-World Applications. Marble collision lab: Students roll a marble into a stationary marble on a flat surface with carbon paper underneath to record paths. They vary the angle of impact (head-on, 30-degree offset, 60-degree offset). Students measure the angle between the two paths after collision. For equal-mass elastic collisions, they discover the paths are always 90 degrees apart.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: 2D Collisions Introduction and Real-World Applications. Teach 2D momentum conservation: momentum is conserved independently in the x-direction AND the y-direction. Write two equations: m1v1xi + m2v2xi = m1v1xf + m2v2xf AND m1v1yi + m2v2yi = m1v1yf + m2v2yf. Work through one example: a 2 kg object moving east at 4 m/s collides with a 1 kg stationary object. After, the 2 kg object moves at 30 degrees north of east at 3 m/s. Find the 1 kg object's speed and direction using component analysis.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: 2D Collisions Introduction and Real-World Applications. Safety engineering design challenge: Students are given data about a car collision at an intersection (car A heading north, car B heading east) and must use 2D momentum conservation to determine pre-crash speeds from post-crash wreckage movement. This is real accident reconstruction physics. Groups present their analysis.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: 2D Collisions Introduction and Real-World Applications. Exit ticket: A 5 kg ball moving east at 3 m/s collides with a 5 kg ball at rest. After the collision, ball 1 moves at 2.1 m/s at 45 degrees north of east. Find the x- and y-components of ball 2's final velocity.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a 2D momentum template with separate x and y columns. Pre-draw the before/after diagram and label the components. Include a component calculation helper: 'vx = v cos(theta), vy = v sin(theta).'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the marble collision lab and 2D momentum calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Solve the full accident reconstruction problem independently. Analyze whether the collision was elastic by calculating total KE before and after in 2D.
differentiation.ell: Use the marble lab as primary instruction — students see 2D collisions before calculating them. Provide labeled vector diagrams with bilingual annotations. Use graph paper overlays to make component analysis visual.
differentiation.iep: Simplify to cases where one object is initially at rest and final velocities are at common angles (30, 45, 60 degrees). Provide a component calculation card with trig values for these angles. Allow extended time.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how forensic physics — using momentum conservation to reconstruct car accidents — is used in the justice system. Explore how Dr. Hugh DeHaven, inspired by surviving a plane crash in WWI, pioneered crash survivability research that led to mandatory seatbelts. His work saved millions of lives and was eventually extended to protect all road users.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using '2D collision': Momentum must be conserved in both the x- and y-directions because___. Before the collision, there was no y-component of momentum, but after the collision one ball moves north, so the other must move ___ because___. Pool players use the physics of 2D collisions, so an experienced player can predict___.

vocabulary.definition: A collision in which objects move in a plane (two dimensions) rather than along a single line; momentum is conserved independently in each direction
A collision where the objects do not hit head-on but at an angle, causing motion in two dimensions after impact

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Why 2D? — When Collisions Don't Happen Head-On
Section 3: Conservation of Momentum in the y-Direction
