vocabulary.definition: The process of breaking vectors into x- and y-components to apply conservation of momentum in each direction independently
The use of physics principles (especially conservation of momentum) to determine pre-collision velocities from post-collision evidence

Section 4: Solving 2D Collision Problems Step by Step

cer.phenomenon: At an intersection, a 1500 kg Car A traveling north collides with a 2000 kg Car B traveling east. The cars lock together and slide northeast at 10 m/s at 37 degrees north of east. Police need to determine if either car was speeding (speed limit: 20 m/s or about 45 mph).
cer.claim_starter: Based on 2D conservation of momentum analysis, I claim that Car ___ was speeding because...
cer.evidence_source: Use component analysis: In the x-direction, only Car B had momentum before the collision: m_B * v_Bi = (m_A + m_B) * vf * cos(37). In the y-direction, only Car A had momentum: m_A * v_Ai = (m_A + m_B) * vf * sin(37). Solve for each car's pre-collision speed.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because solving the x-equation gives Car B's speed as ___ m/s and solving the y-equation gives Car A's speed as ___ m/s. Comparing each to the 20 m/s speed limit shows that Car ___ was exceeding the limit, which contributed to the collision.

lessons.title: Momentum Unit Review and Safety Engineering Design Challenge (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: design and evaluate a device that minimizes the force on an object during a collision by applying the impulse-momentum theorem and conservation of momentum
lessons.circle_prompt: If you could redesign one safety feature in everyday life — a helmet, a car bumper, playground equipment, a phone case — what would it be? What physics principle would guide your design?
lessons.do_now: Quick review: (a) What is the impulse on a 1200 kg car that changes velocity from 25 m/s to 0? (b) If the collision takes 0.1 s, what is the average force? (c) If an airbag extends the time to 0.5 s, what is the new average force?
materials: Egg drop engineering materials (foam, bubble wrap, cardboard, tape, rubber bands, straws, cotton balls)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Momentum Unit Review and Safety Engineering Design Challenge. Show a compilation video of automotive crash test footage — comparing a 1960s car crash test (devastating) with a modern car (survival). Ask: What changed in 60 years? Students brainstorm: crumple zones, airbags, seatbelts, energy-absorbing materials. All are applications of the impulse-momentum theorem. Today, students will design their own safety device.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Momentum Unit Review and Safety Engineering Design Challenge. Engineering design challenge (HS-PS2-3 aligned): Groups design a protective container for an egg dropped from 3 m. Constraints: can only use provided materials, total padding mass cannot exceed 100 g, container must be no larger than 15 cm in any dimension. Before building, groups must submit a written prediction: (a) estimated collision time, (b) calculated average force on the egg, (c) explanation of how their design increases collision time. Then they build, test, and evaluate.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Momentum Unit Review and Safety Engineering Design Challenge. Groups present their results: which designs survived and why. Teacher connects successful designs to physics principles: materials that compress slowly increase collision time, multiple layers of padding distribute force over a larger area. Relate to HS-PS2-3 — evaluating a device that minimizes force during a collision.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Momentum Unit Review and Safety Engineering Design Challenge. Comprehensive review: Students work through a Regents-style question cluster involving momentum. A scenario presents two bumper car collisions — one where the cars bounce off (elastic) and one where they lock together (perfectly inelastic). Students apply conservation of momentum, calculate impulse, and compare forces using the impulse-momentum theorem.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Momentum Unit Review and Safety Engineering Design Challenge. Exit ticket: A 0.50 kg ball moving at 6.0 m/s east collides with a 0.30 kg ball moving at 4.0 m/s west. They stick together. (a) Find the final velocity. (b) Calculate the kinetic energy lost. (c) Classify the collision type. (d) If the collision lasted 0.01 s, what average force did each ball experience?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a unit review checklist: 'Can I calculate momentum? Impulse? Apply conservation of momentum? Identify collision types? Calculate KE before and after?' Include a formula sheet and one worked example per topic.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the engineering design challenge and comprehensive review problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: After the egg drop, students redesign for a stricter constraint (50 g padding, 4 m drop). They must use quantitative analysis to justify their redesign choices. Write a formal engineering report with physics calculations.
differentiation.ell: Partner ELL students with strong English speakers during the design challenge. Provide a visual review guide with diagrams for each problem type. Allow use of all reference materials during practice.
differentiation.iep: Provide a condensed review focusing on the three core skills: p = mv, J = F*t = Delta p, and m1v1i + m2v2i = (m1+m2)vf. Include worked examples for each. Allow extended time and calculator use for all assessments.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how the physics of collision safety has global equity implications — helmet design for motorcycle riders in Southeast Asia, where motorcycles are the primary transportation, must account for different crash scenarios than helmets designed for American car-centric roads. Explore how engineers are designing affordable safety equipment for communities worldwide.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences integrating unit vocabulary: The egg survived the 3-meter drop because our design increased the collision time by___. Momentum was conserved in the bumper car collision, but kinetic energy was not because___. The crumple zone increased the stopping time from 0.05 s to 0.5 s, so the average force decreased by a factor of___.

vocabulary.definition: In an isolated system, total momentum before = total momentum after; applies to all collisions regardless of type
A collision where objects stick together; momentum is conserved but maximum kinetic energy is lost

cer.phenomenon: A company designs two phone cases: Case A is a rigid plastic shell (collision time when dropped: 0.005 s) and Case B is a soft silicone case with air pockets (collision time: 0.05 s). A 0.20 kg phone is dropped from 1.5 m onto a hard floor. With Case A, the screen cracks. With Case B, the phone is undamaged.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the impulse-momentum theorem, I claim that Case B protects the phone better because it reduces the peak force by a factor of ___ by...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the phone's velocity at impact (from free fall), the impulse needed to stop it, and the average force for each case. Compare the forces to the known screen breaking force.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because both cases deliver the same impulse of ___ N·s, but Case A's force of ___ N exceeds the screen's breaking threshold while Case B's force of ___ N does not. The silicone air pockets work by increasing ___, which is the same principle behind ___.

units.anchoring_phenomenon: A compass needle always points north, even though nothing visible is pushing or pulling it. Meanwhile, rubbing a balloon on your hair makes it stick to the wall. Both of these involve invisible forces that act at a distance — how can objects exert forces on each other without touching?
essential_questions: How do gravitational and electrostatic forces depend on mass, charge, and distance?
What are fields and how do they explain forces that act at a distance?
How are electric currents and magnetic fields related?
units.crse_theme: Students explore the contributions of diverse scientists to our understanding of fundamental forces — from Ibn al-Haytham's early work on optics and forces in the Islamic Golden Age, to Benjamin Banneker's astronomical calculations using gravitational principles, to Nikola Tesla's (Serbian-American) and Lewis Howard Latimer's (African American) contributions to electromagnetism and electrical engineering.

formative: Gravitational and electrostatic force calculation sets
summative: Investigation: Electromagnetism — Current and Magnetic Fields

investigations: Investigation 5: Investigating the Relationship Between Electric Current and Magnetic Fields

lessons.title: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: apply Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation to calculate the gravitational force between two masses and explain how the force depends on mass and distance
lessons.circle_prompt: What keeps the Moon orbiting Earth and Earth orbiting the Sun? Is there a string? A push? If nothing is touching them, how can there be a force?
lessons.do_now: The Moon is about 384,000 km from Earth. If we could somehow double that distance, what do you think would happen to the gravitational pull between them — cut in half? Cut to a quarter? Stay the same? Make a prediction and explain.
materials: Physics Reference Table (NYSED) — contains gravitational constant G
Solar system data card (masses and distances)
Gravitational force simulation (PhET or similar) on devices

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation. Tell the (likely apocryphal) story of Newton watching an apple fall and wondering: Does the same force that pulls the apple to the ground also pull the Moon toward Earth? Show an animation of the apple falling and the Moon orbiting, both pulled by the same type of force. Ask: If gravity reaches the Moon, does it reach the Sun? Other galaxies? How far does it go? (Answer: infinitely, but it gets weaker.)

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation. Simulation exploration: Students use a PhET gravity simulation to explore how gravitational force changes as they: (1) Double mass 1 while keeping mass 2 and distance constant, (2) Double mass 2, (3) Double the distance, (4) Triple the distance. They record the force for each trial and look for the mathematical pattern before the formula is revealed.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation. Present Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation: Fg = Gm1m2/r^2 where G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N·m^2/kg^2. Break down the equation: force is directly proportional to each mass (double one mass → double the force) and inversely proportional to the SQUARE of the distance (double the distance → force drops to 1/4). Work through calculations: (1) Force between Earth and Moon. (2) Force between two students sitting 1 m apart (surprisingly tiny — explains why we don't feel gravity pulling us toward each other).

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation. Proportional reasoning problems (Regents style): If the distance between two objects is tripled, by what factor does the gravitational force change? (1/9) If one mass is doubled and the distance is halved, by what factor does the force change? (8x) Students solve using the equation structure without plugging in specific numbers.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation. Exit ticket: (a) Calculate the gravitational force between a 70 kg person and Earth (mass = 5.98 x 10^24 kg, radius = 6.37 x 10^6 m). (b) Compare this to the person's weight (mg). (c) Explain why these two values should be the same.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a labeled equation card: Fg = Gm1m2/r^2 with each variable defined and units listed. Include a proportional reasoning guide: 'If mass doubles → force doubles. If distance doubles → force is 1/4.' Pre-load the PhET simulation with guided questions.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the simulation exploration and both calculation and proportional reasoning problems.
differentiation.advanced: Derive the surface gravitational acceleration (g = GM/R^2) from F = Gm1m2/r^2 and F = mg. Calculate g on the surface of Mars, Jupiter, and the Moon. Explain why g varies slightly across Earth's surface.
differentiation.ell: Use the PhET simulation as primary instruction — visual and interactive before mathematical. Provide a bilingual formula card with labeled diagrams showing m1, m2, and r. Use sentence frames for proportional reasoning explanations.
differentiation.iep: Provide a calculator tutorial for scientific notation entry. Focus on proportional reasoning questions (no plug-in calculations needed). Reduce problem set. Provide a worked example for the exit ticket format.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Benjamin Banneker, a free Black man in the 1700s who used Newtonian gravitational principles to predict astronomical events and published an almanac. His scientific achievements challenged prevailing racist beliefs about intellectual capacity. vocabulary.definition: Every object with mass attracts every other object with mass; Fg = Gm1m2/r^2

cer.phenomenon: The International Space Station orbits Earth at an altitude of approximately 408 km above the surface. Astronauts aboard the ISS experience 'weightlessness,' leading many people to believe there is no gravity in space. However, at 408 km altitude, the gravitational field strength is approximately 8.7 m/s^2 — only about 11% less than on the surface (9.81 m/s^2).
cer.claim_starter: Based on calculations using Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation, I claim that astronauts on the ISS are NOT beyond Earth's gravity because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate g at the ISS altitude using g = GM/r^2 where r = Earth's radius + 408 km. Compare to g at the surface.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because at 408 km altitude, g = ___ m/s^2, which is ___% of the surface value. The astronauts feel weightless not because gravity is absent, but because the ISS and astronauts are in ___, so there is no ___ force. This is the same principle as ___.

lessons.title: Gravitational Fields (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: describe and draw gravitational field lines around a mass and calculate the gravitational field strength at any distance from a mass
lessons.circle_prompt: How does Earth 'reach out' and pull on the Moon without touching it? If you could see the invisible influence that gravity creates in space, what would it look like?
lessons.do_now: Calculate the gravitational field strength at the surface of Mars (mass = 6.42 x 10^23 kg, radius = 3.39 x 10^6 m). Compare to Earth's 9.81 N/kg. How much would a 70 kg person weigh on Mars?
materials: Iron filings and magnets (for field visualization analogy)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Gravitational Fields. Sprinkle iron filings around a bar magnet on an overhead projector or document camera. The filings align to show the invisible field. Ask: Gravity also creates an invisible field around every mass. How do you think gravitational field lines would look around Earth? Students sketch predictions.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Gravitational Fields. Students draw gravitational field lines around: (1) a single planet (arrows pointing inward, evenly spaced around the planet, getting farther apart as distance increases), (2) two equal-mass planets near each other (field lines show attraction between them), (3) a large planet near a small moon (more field lines from the larger mass). Students compare their diagrams and develop field-drawing rules.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Gravitational Fields. Define gravitational field: a region of space where a mass experiences a gravitational force. Field strength: g = F/m = GM/r^2, measured in N/kg (equivalent to m/s^2). Field line rules: (1) point toward the mass (gravity is always attractive), (2) closer spacing = stronger field, (3) never cross. Show how the field concept explains action at a distance: a mass creates a field, and another mass responds to the local field — no need for direct contact.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Gravitational Fields. Students calculate g at various distances from Earth: at the surface (r = R), at 2R, 3R, and 10R. They graph g vs. r and observe the inverse-square decay. They also calculate the point between Earth and the Moon where the gravitational fields are equal and opposite (the Lagrange point L1).

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Gravitational Fields. Exit ticket: (a) Draw the gravitational field lines around Earth. (b) At what distance from Earth's center would the gravitational field strength be 1/4 of its surface value? (c) Is there any location in the universe where the gravitational field is truly zero? Explain.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a gravitational field line drawing guide with rules and examples. Include a worked example of g = GM/r^2 with clear steps for scientific notation arithmetic.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the field diagram drawings and field strength calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research and present on Lagrange points — the five positions in a two-body gravitational system where a small object can maintain a stable position. Calculate the location of L1 between Earth and the Sun.
differentiation.ell: Use the iron filing demonstration as a visual anchor for the field concept. Provide step-by-step diagrams for drawing field lines. Include bilingual field vocabulary cards.
differentiation.iep: Focus on the conceptual understanding of fields (arrows point toward mass, closer = stronger). Simplify calculations to one surface-gravity problem. Allow use of calculator and formula card.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how the concept of a 'field' was revolutionary — Michael Faraday, a self-educated son of a blacksmith with no formal education, developed the field concept that transformed physics. His story demonstrates that scientific genius is not limited by social class or educational background.
lessons.hochman_activity: Appositive sentences: Students write sentences embedding definitions. Example: 'The gravitational field, a region of space where a mass experiences a gravitational force, exists around every object with mass.' Students write two more using 'field strength' and 'inverse square law.'

vocabulary.definition: A region of space surrounding a mass where another mass would experience a gravitational force; represented by field lines pointing toward the mass
Lines drawn to represent the direction and relative strength of a field; for gravity, they point toward the mass and are closer together where the field is stronger

cer.phenomenon: Scientists recently detected gravitational waves — ripples in the gravitational field — from two black holes merging 1.3 billion light-years away. The LIGO detector measured a change in distance smaller than 1/1000th the width of a proton. Before this detection, some people doubted that gravitational fields were real physical entities (as opposed to just mathematical tools).
cer.claim_starter: Based on the detection of gravitational waves, I claim that gravitational fields are real physical entities because...
cer.evidence_source: The LIGO detection shows that changes in massive objects (merging black holes) produce disturbances that propagate through the gravitational field at the speed of light and can be measured at great distances.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because if gravitational fields were merely mathematical constructs, they could not carry ___ through space. The fact that gravitational waves travel at ___ and were detected ___ years after the merger demonstrates that the field is a physical entity that can store and transmit ___.

lessons.title: Coulomb's Law and Electric Charge (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: apply Coulomb's Law to calculate the electrostatic force between two charged objects and compare the mathematical structure of Coulomb's Law to Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever gotten a shock from touching a doorknob in winter, or had your hair stand up after pulling off a sweater? What causes static electricity? Why does it seem worse in winter?
lessons.do_now: Rub a balloon on your hair and hold it near small pieces of paper. What happens? Now hold it near a stream of water from a faucet. What happens? In both cases, what type of force is at work?
materials: Pith balls or aluminum foil balls on strings

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Coulomb's Law and Electric Charge. Demo: Charge two balloons by rubbing with wool. Hold them near each other — they repel. Hold a charged balloon near a neutral wall — it attracts. Ask: Why does the same balloon sometimes repel and sometimes attract? Introduce the two types of charge: positive and negative. Like charges repel, opposite charges attract. The force depends on the amount of charge and the distance.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Coulomb's Law and Electric Charge. Charge exploration stations: Station 1 — Rub two strips of tape on the desk and peel them off (both positive); bring them together (repel). Then stick one tape on top of another, peel apart (opposite charges); bring together (attract). Station 2 — Charge a balloon and bring it near an electroscope; observe the leaves. Station 3 — Charge a balloon and observe its effect on a thin stream of water. Students record observations about attraction, repulsion, and the effect of distance.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Coulomb's Law and Electric Charge. Present Coulomb's Law: Fe = kq1q2/r^2 where k = 8.99 x 10^9 N·m^2/C^2. Compare directly to Newton's Law of Gravitation: both are inverse-square laws, both depend on a property of the objects (mass or charge), but gravity is always attractive while electric force can attract or repel. Calculate example: force between two charges of 1 C separated by 1 m (enormously large — 9 billion N!). Then calculate force between an electron and proton in a hydrogen atom.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Coulomb's Law and Electric Charge. Side-by-side comparison table: Students fill in a Venn diagram comparing gravitational and electrostatic forces. Similarities: inverse square, depend on properties of objects, act at a distance, described by fields. Differences: gravity always attracts / electric can repel, gravity depends on mass / electric on charge, electric force is enormously stronger than gravity for subatomic particles.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Coulomb's Law and Electric Charge. Exit ticket: Two charges of +3.0 x 10^-6 C and -5.0 x 10^-6 C are separated by 0.20 m. (a) Calculate the electrostatic force between them. (b) Is the force attractive or repulsive? (c) If the distance is doubled, what is the new force?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a labeled Coulomb's Law equation card parallel to the gravity equation card. Include a 'like/unlike charges' visual guide. Pre-organize the comparison table with column headers filled in.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the charge exploration stations and Coulomb's Law calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the ratio of the electrostatic force to the gravitational force between a proton and electron. Discuss why, despite gravity being so much weaker, it dominates on large scales (hint: most large objects are electrically neutral).
differentiation.ell: Use physical demonstrations at each station. Provide a bilingual charge vocabulary card with visual icons (+ for positive, - for negative, arrows for attract/repel). Use the gravity/electric comparison table as a visual organizer.
differentiation.iep: Focus on the conceptual comparison between gravitational and electrostatic forces. Provide the Coulomb's Law equation on a reference card with units labeled. Break calculations into single steps. Reduce the exit ticket to two parts.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Charles-Augustin de Coulomb's experiments and how his work was influenced by earlier observations of static electricity by ancient Greeks (amber and fur) and Chinese scholars. Also highlight the contributions of Benjamin Franklin — emphasizing that his famous kite experiment (if it happened as described) was extremely dangerous and should not be replicated.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'electrostatic force': Two positive charges repel each other because___. Both gravity and electrostatic forces follow an inverse-square law, but the electrostatic force is much stronger because___. The two charges were brought closer together, so the force between them___.

cer.phenomenon: A Van de Graaff generator charges a person's hair, making each strand stand up and separate from the others. The person's hair spreads out in all directions, roughly forming a sphere. The more charge the generator delivers, the farther apart the hair strands spread.
cer.claim_starter: Based on Coulomb's Law, I claim that the hair strands spread apart because...
cer.evidence_source: Each hair strand acquires the same sign of charge (positive). Apply Coulomb's Law: like charges repel, and the force depends on the magnitude of charge and the distance between strands.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because each charged hair strand repels every other strand with a force described by Fe = ___. Since all strands have the ___ sign of charge, they repel and spread apart until the repulsive force is balanced by ___. More charge from the generator increases ___, causing the hair to spread ___.

lessons.title: Electric Fields and Electric Potential (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: draw electric field lines around point charges, calculate electric field strength, and explain electric potential as the energy per unit charge at a point in an electric field
lessons.circle_prompt: If you could see the invisible forces around a charged object — like seeing the wind — what would it look like? Would it look the same around a positive charge and a negative charge?
lessons.do_now: Draw the gravitational field lines around Earth (arrows pointing inward). Now draw what you think the electric field lines look like around a single positive charge. How are they similar? How are they different?
materials: Colored pencils (red for positive, blue for negative)
Grass seeds in oil (for field line visualization, if available)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Electric Fields and Electric Potential. If available, show a real-time electric field visualization using grass seeds floating in oil between charged electrodes. Students observe the seeds aligning along field lines. If not available, show a simulation. Ask: The seeds are showing us something invisible — the electric field. What rules do the field lines follow? Students compare to gravitational field lines.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Electric Fields and Electric Potential. Drawing activity: Students draw electric field lines for: (1) a single positive charge (lines radiate outward), (2) a single negative charge (lines point inward), (3) a positive-negative pair (dipole — lines from + to -), (4) two positive charges (lines repel between them, creating a region of weak field). For each, students identify regions of strong and weak fields based on line spacing.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Electric Fields and Electric Potential. Define electric field: E = F/q = kQ/r^2, measured in N/C. Direction: the direction a positive test charge would move. Introduce electric potential: V = W/q (work per unit charge), measured in Volts (J/C). Potential difference (voltage) drives current. Connect: the electric field points from high potential to low potential, just as a ball rolls from high to low altitude. An electron in an electric field gains KE as it moves from low to high potential.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Electric Fields and Electric Potential. Students calculate: (a) The electric field strength 0.30 m from a +2.0 x 10^-6 C charge. (b) The force on an electron placed at that point. (c) If an electron is released from rest in this field, describe its motion (accelerates toward the positive charge). Discuss: An electron accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V gains how much kinetic energy? (KE = qV = 1.6 x 10^-17 J)

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Electric Fields and Electric Potential. Exit ticket: (a) Draw the electric field lines between a +Q and -Q charge (dipole). (b) Where is the field strongest? (c) A charge of +3.0 x 10^-6 C is in a uniform electric field of 500 N/C. What force does it experience?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a field line drawing rule card: 'Lines start on + and end on -. Closer lines = stronger field. Lines never cross.' Include a formula card with E = kQ/r^2 and F = qE side by side.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the field drawing activity and electric field calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the electric field at a point due to two charges using vector addition of fields. Analyze equipotential lines and their relationship to field lines (always perpendicular).
differentiation.ell: Use color-coded drawings extensively (red for +, blue for -, green arrows for field direction). Provide a step-by-step field-drawing guide with examples. Include bilingual vocabulary cards with labeled diagrams.
differentiation.iep: Focus on field line drawing rules (qualitative) before calculations. Provide a pre-drawn dipole field with labels for students to annotate. Simplify calculations to single-charge field problems. Allow formula card and calculator.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how electric field concepts are fundamental to medical technology — from EKGs (measuring the heart's electric field) to defibrillators. Highlight how Dr. Levi Watkins Jr., a Black cardiac surgeon, performed the first implantation of an automatic defibrillator in a human patient in 1980, saving countless lives through the application of electric field physics.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'electric field': Electric field lines point away from positive charges because___. Gravitational and electric fields are both described by inverse-square laws, but electric field lines can point either inward or outward because___. The electron was placed in a strong electric field, so it experienced a ___ and accelerated toward___.

vocabulary.definition: A region of space where a charged object experiences an electric force; E = F/q = kQ/r^2; measured in N/C; direction is the direction a positive test charge would move
The difference in electric potential between two points; determines the work done on a charge moving between those points; V = W/q

cer.phenomenon: During a thunderstorm, the bottom of a cloud becomes negatively charged and the ground beneath it becomes positively charged (by induction). The electric field between the cloud and ground can reach 3 x 10^6 N/C — the breakdown strength of air. At this point, lightning strikes, transferring about 5 Coulombs of charge in about 0.001 seconds through a potential difference of about 300 million Volts.
cer.claim_starter: Based on electric field and potential analysis, I claim that lightning occurs when the electric field exceeds air's breakdown strength because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the energy transferred during a lightning strike using W = qV and the average current using I = q/t. Compare the electric field to air's breakdown value.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because normally air is an ___, but when the electric field exceeds ___ N/C, the air molecules become ___ and conduct electricity. The energy transferred is W = ___ x ___ = ___ J, which is equivalent to ___. The enormous current of ___ A for ___ s is what makes lightning so destructive.

lessons.title: Comparing Gravitational and Electrostatic Forces (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: compare and contrast gravitational and electrostatic forces using mathematical representations and predict how changes in mass, charge, or distance affect each force
lessons.circle_prompt: Gravity and electricity are two of the four fundamental forces in nature. Which one do you think is stronger? Which one affects your daily life more? How would the world be different without one of them?
lessons.do_now: Complete this comparison: Fg = Gm1m2/r^2 and Fe = kq1q2/r^2. What is the same about these two equations? What is different? List at least three similarities and two differences.

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Comparing Gravitational and Electrostatic Forces. Pose the question: The electrostatic force between a proton and electron in a hydrogen atom is about 10^39 times stronger than the gravitational force between them. If electric force is SO much stronger, why does gravity — not electricity — hold the solar system together? Students brainstorm in pairs. (Answer: large objects are electrically neutral, so electric forces cancel, but mass never cancels — there is no 'negative mass.')

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Comparing Gravitational and Electrostatic Forces. Side-by-side calculation challenge: Students calculate both the gravitational and electrostatic force for three scenarios: (1) Between a proton and electron at 5.3 x 10^-11 m. (2) Between two 1.0 C charges at 1 m (hypothetical). (3) Between Earth and a 1 kg object at Earth's surface (gravity only). They compute the ratio Fe/Fg for scenario 1 and verify it is approximately 10^39.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Comparing Gravitational and Electrostatic Forces. Create a comprehensive comparison table with students: Property → Gravitational / Electrostatic. Law: both inverse-square. Property of matter: mass / charge. Always attractive? Yes / No (can repel). Strength: weakest of four fundamental forces / much stronger. Field lines: always point toward mass / point toward negative, away from positive. Dominates at: large scales (planets, stars) / small scales (atoms, molecules). Then practice Regents-style proportional reasoning: 'If the charge on one object is tripled and the distance between them is doubled, by what factor does the electrostatic force change?'

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Comparing Gravitational and Electrostatic Forces. Regents practice cluster: Students work through a set of 6 comparison questions mixing gravitational and electrostatic forces. Questions require identifying which law to use, proportional reasoning, and conceptual explanations. Include at least one question about field line diagrams and one about force direction.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Comparing Gravitational and Electrostatic Forces. Exit ticket: (a) Two identical charged spheres are 0.5 m apart. If one sphere's charge is doubled and the distance is tripled, by what factor does the force change? (b) Explain one reason why gravity, not electrostatic force, holds planets in orbit.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a pre-filled comparison table with one column completed (gravitational) and blanks for the student to fill in the electrostatic column. Include a proportional reasoning formula card showing how to handle 'doubled,' 'tripled,' 'halved' changes.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the comparison calculations and Regents practice set as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research the other two fundamental forces (strong nuclear and weak nuclear) and add them to the comparison table. Discuss the hierarchy of forces and why physicists seek a Grand Unified Theory.
differentiation.ell: Use the comparison table as a visual organizer for all content. Provide bilingual comparison vocabulary (attract/repel, stronger/weaker, toward/away). Use color-coding throughout: blue for gravity, red for electrostatic.
differentiation.iep: Focus on qualitative comparison (similarities and differences list) before calculations. Provide proportional reasoning as multiple choice. Reduce the Regents practice set to 3 questions. Allow all references.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how understanding the relative strengths of forces is essential for modern technology — from the atomic force microscope (AFM) invented in 1986, which uses electrostatic forces to image surfaces at the atomic level, to gravitational wave detectors. Highlight how these technologies have been developed by international, diverse teams of scientists.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences comparing forces: Gravity is always attractive because___. Both gravitational and electrostatic forces follow an inverse-square law, but electrostatic force can be either attractive or repulsive because___. Large astronomical objects are electrically neutral, so the dominant force between planets is___.

vocabulary.definition: A pattern shared by both gravitational and electrostatic forces where the force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between objects
The condition of having equal amounts of positive and negative charge, resulting in zero net charge; explains why large objects do not experience net electrostatic forces

lessons.title: Comparing Gravitational and Electrostatic Forces (Day 2 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can apply and analyze my understanding to compare and contrast gravitational and electrostatic forces using mathematical representations and predict how changes in mass, charge, or distance affect each force
lessons.circle_prompt: Share one connection you made between yesterday's topic and something in your daily life.
lessons.do_now: Review: Based on yesterday's lesson, explain one key idea from yesterday about how to define and identify key concepts related to: compare and contrast gravitational and electrostatic forces using mathematical representations and predict how changes in mass, charge, or distance affect each force.

engage.description: Brief review of Day 1 concepts through a warm-up problem or quick discussion. Building on previous days: Pose the question: The electrostatic force between a proton and electron in a hydrogen atom is about 10^39 times stronger than the gravitational force between them. If electric force is SO much stronger, why does gravity — not electricity — hold the solar system together? Students brainstorm in pairs. (Answer: large objects are electrically neutral, so electric forces cancel, but mass never cancels — there is no 'negative mass.')

explore.description: Students work through practice problems or applications in pairs or small groups. Building on previous days: Side-by-side calculation challenge: Students calculate both the gravitational and electrostatic force for three scenarios: (1) Between a proton and electron at 5.3 x 10^-11 m. (2) Between two 1.0 C charges at 1 m (hypothetical). (3) Between Earth and a 1 kg object at Earth's surface (gravity only). They compute the ratio Fe/Fg for scenario 1 and verify it is approximately 10^39.

explain.description: Address common misconceptions from practice; model problem-solving strategies. Building on previous days: Create a comprehensive comparison table with students: Property → Gravitational / Electrostatic. Law: both inverse-square. Property of matter: mass / charge. Always attractive? Yes / No (can repel). Strength: weakest of four fundamental forces / much stronger. Field lines: always point toward mass / point toward negative, away from positive. Dominates at: large scales (planets, stars) / small scales (atoms, molecules). Then practice Regents-style proportional reasoning: 'If the charge on one object is tripled and the distance between them is doubled, by what factor does the electrostatic force change?'

elaborate.description: CER activity connecting evidence to claims about the topic. Building on previous days: Regents practice cluster: Students work through a set of 6 comparison questions mixing gravitational and electrostatic forces. Questions require identifying which law to use, proportional reasoning, and conceptual explanations. Include at least one question about field line diagrams and one about force direction.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket with application-level problems requiring multi-step reasoning. Building on previous days: Exit ticket: (a) Two identical charged spheres are 0.5 m apart. If one sphere's charge is doubled and the distance is tripled, by what factor does the force change? (b) Explain one reason why gravity, not electrostatic force, holds planets in orbit.

differentiation.approaching: Review key concepts from the full sequence before assessment. Provide a pre-filled comparison table with one column completed (gravitational) and blanks for the student to fill in the electrostatic column. Include a proportional reasoning formula card showing how to handle 'doubled,' 'tripled,' 'halved' changes.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the comparison calculations and Regents practice set as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Complete extension challenge connecting to real-world applications. Research the other two fundamental forces (strong nuclear and weak nuclear) and add them to the comparison table. Discuss the hierarchy of forces and why physicists seek a Grand Unified Theory.
differentiation.ell: Use the comparison table as a visual organizer for all content. Provide bilingual comparison vocabulary (attract/repel, stronger/weaker, toward/away). Use color-coding throughout: blue for gravity, red for electrostatic.
differentiation.iep: Focus on qualitative comparison (similarities and differences list) before calculations. Provide proportional reasoning as multiple choice. Reduce the Regents practice set to 3 questions. Allow all references.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how understanding the relative strengths of forces is essential for modern technology — from the atomic force microscope (AFM) invented in 1986, which uses electrostatic forces to image surfaces at the atomic level, to gravitational wave detectors. Highlight how these technologies have been developed by international, diverse teams of scientists.
lessons.hochman_activity: Kernel sentence expansion using 'Proportional Reasoning': Start with 'Proportional Reasoning is important.' Expand by adding when, where, why, and how details to create a complex sentence that demonstrates understanding of the concept.

vocabulary.definition: The four basic forces in nature: gravitational, electromagnetic, strong nuclear, and weak nuclear; all other forces are manifestations of these four
A problem-solving approach that determines how a quantity changes when one or more variables are multiplied by a factor, without plugging in specific numbers

guided_notes_outline: Section 2: Similarities — Inverse-Square, Field Models, Action at a Distance
Section 4: Proportional Reasoning Practice for Both Forces

cer.phenomenon: A small piece of paper (about 0.001 kg) sits on a table. The entire Earth (6 x 10^24 kg) pulls it downward with the gravitational force. A small charged plastic comb (with perhaps 10^-8 C of charge) can pick up the paper, overcoming Earth's gravitational pull. The comb has a mass billions of times less than Earth.
cer.claim_starter: Based on force comparisons, I claim that the electrostatic force from the comb can overcome Earth's gravitational force because...
cer.evidence_source: Estimate the gravitational force on the paper (F = mg). Estimate the electrostatic force between the comb and the induced charge on the paper using Coulomb's Law with reasonable assumptions. Compare the magnitudes.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the gravitational force on the paper is only ___ N, while the electrostatic force, even with a tiny charge, can be ___ because the constant k (___ N·m^2/C^2) is enormously larger than G (___ N·m^2/kg^2). This everyday observation demonstrates that the electrostatic force is fundamentally ___ than gravity.

lessons.title: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: describe the magnetic field around a bar magnet and a current-carrying wire, and explain the relationship between electric current and magnetic fields
lessons.circle_prompt: Magnets are on your refrigerator, in your phone, in your earbuds, and inside every electric motor. Where else do you encounter magnets? What would life be like without them?
lessons.do_now: A compass needle always points north. What is a compass needle made of, and why does it point north? What does this tell us about Earth itself?
materials: Iron filings and paper (for field visualization)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism. Place a bar magnet under a sheet of paper and sprinkle iron filings on top. The filings reveal the magnetic field pattern. Ask: What do these field lines tell us? Where is the field strongest? Students observe that the field lines go from the north pole to the south pole and are most concentrated near the poles.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism. Two-part investigation: Part 1 — Students place small compasses around a bar magnet and draw the field lines by following the compass needle direction. They map the complete field. Part 2 — Students connect a straight wire to a battery (with a switch) and place compasses around the wire. When current flows, the compass needles deflect, showing that electric current creates a magnetic field. Students observe the circular field pattern around the wire.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism. Present the connection between electricity and magnetism: (1) Hans Christian Oersted discovered in 1820 that electric current deflects a compass needle. (2) A straight current-carrying wire creates circular magnetic field lines (use the right-hand rule: thumb points in current direction, fingers curl in field direction). (3) A solenoid (coil of wire) creates a field that looks like a bar magnet's field — north and south poles form at each end. (4) Adding an iron core strengthens the electromagnet dramatically. Draw diagrams for each case.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism. Build an electromagnet: Students wrap insulated wire (20-30 turns) around a large iron nail and connect it to a battery. They test its strength by counting how many paper clips it can pick up. Then they investigate: How does the number of coils affect the strength? How does adding a second battery in series affect it? Students connect observations to the physics: more current and more turns = stronger magnetic field.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Magnetic Fields and Electromagnetism. Exit ticket: (a) Draw the magnetic field around a straight current-carrying wire viewed from the end (current coming out of the page). Use the right-hand rule to determine the field direction. (b) What three changes could you make to strengthen an electromagnet?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a magnetic field drawing guide with examples for bar magnets, straight wires, and solenoids. Include a step-by-step right-hand rule guide with illustrations. Pre-label the compass mapping sheet.
differentiation.on_level: Complete both investigations (compass mapping and current/compass) and the electromagnet building activity.
differentiation.advanced: Research the relationship between the strength of the magnetic field around a wire and the current (B = mu_0 * I / 2*pi*r). Calculate the field strength at different distances from a current-carrying wire. Investigate the magnetic field inside a solenoid.
differentiation.ell: Use hands-on activities as primary instruction. Provide visual right-hand rule diagrams with step-by-step illustrations. Include bilingual vocabulary cards. Use the compass and iron filing activities to make the invisible field visible.
differentiation.iep: Focus on the hands-on investigations. Provide a pre-drawn magnetic field template for bar magnets and straight wires for students to annotate. Simplify the exit ticket to drawing from a template. Allow partner work for the electromagnet activity.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how Nikola Tesla, a Serbian-American immigrant, developed the alternating current (AC) system that powers the modern world, overcoming opposition from Thomas Edison. Also highlight Lewis Howard Latimer, an African American inventor who worked with both Edison and Bell, and who improved the carbon filament for light bulbs and drafted the patent drawings for Bell's telephone. Both men's work depended on understanding electromagnetism.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'electromagnetism': A compass needle deflects near a current-carrying wire because___. Permanent magnets always have both a north and south pole, but electromagnets can be turned on and off because___. Adding more coils of wire and an iron core strengthened the electromagnet, so___.

vocabulary.definition: A region of space where a magnetic material or moving charge experiences a magnetic force; represented by field lines from north to south poles outside the magnet
A method to determine the direction of the magnetic field around a current: point the thumb in the direction of conventional current flow, and the fingers curl in the direction of the magnetic field

Section 4: Solenoids and Electromagnets

cer.phenomenon: In a junkyard, a crane uses a powerful electromagnet to lift old cars weighing over 1000 kg. The operator can pick up cars by turning the electromagnet on and drop them by turning it off. A permanent magnet strong enough to lift a car would be impractically large and could never release the car.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the properties of electromagnets, I claim that electromagnets are superior to permanent magnets for this application because...
cer.evidence_source: Compare the properties of electromagnets (variable strength, can be turned on/off, strength controlled by current) to permanent magnets (fixed strength, always on, cannot release objects on demand).
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because an electromagnet's field strength can be ___ by adjusting the ___, and it can be completely turned ___ to release the car. The electromagnet in a junkyard crane typically uses a large ___ and an iron core with ___ turns of wire to generate the enormous force needed.

lessons.title: Electromagnetic Induction and Unit Review (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: explain how a changing magnetic field induces an electric current (Faraday's Law) and connect this principle to real-world technologies including generators and transformers
lessons.circle_prompt: Almost all the electricity you use — from the outlets in your home to the charger for your phone — was generated using magnetism. How can a magnet produce electricity? Isn't that the opposite of what we learned yesterday?
lessons.do_now: Yesterday you learned that electric current creates a magnetic field. Today's question: Can a magnetic field create electric current? Predict what would happen if you moved a magnet in and out of a coil of wire connected to a light bulb.
materials: Coils of wire (50-100 turns, 1 per group)
Galvanometers or sensitive ammeters (1 per group)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Electromagnetic Induction and Unit Review. Teacher demonstration: Connect a coil of wire to a galvanometer. Hold a magnet still inside the coil — no current. Push the magnet in — current appears. Pull it out — current reverses. Hold it still again — no current. Ask: What is the pattern? When does current flow? Students deduce that current flows only when the magnetic field is CHANGING (magnet moving relative to the coil).

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Electromagnetic Induction and Unit Review. Students replicate the demonstration and investigate: (1) Does moving faster produce more current? (Yes.) (2) Does a stronger magnet produce more current? (Yes.) (3) Does more coils produce more current? (Yes.) (4) Does it matter which direction you move the magnet? (Yes — current reverses.) Students record observations and formulate a general rule for when and how much current is induced.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Electromagnetic Induction and Unit Review. Present Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction: A changing magnetic field through a coil induces a voltage (and therefore current if the circuit is complete). Larger changes, faster changes, and more coils produce more induced voltage. This is the basis of: (1) Electric generators — spinning a coil in a magnetic field (or spinning a magnet near a coil) produces AC electricity. (2) Transformers — changing current in one coil induces voltage in a nearby coil. (3) The fundamental symmetry: current → magnetic field (Oersted) AND changing magnetic field → current (Faraday).

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Electromagnetic Induction and Unit Review. Students use a hand-crank generator to light an LED. They observe that cranking faster produces brighter light (more voltage and current). Discuss how this is the same principle used in power plants — coal, natural gas, nuclear, wind, and hydroelectric plants ALL spin a generator. The source of energy differs, but the physics is the same: changing magnetic fields induce current. Brief unit review: students complete a graphic organizer connecting gravity, electrostatics, and magnetism.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Electromagnetic Induction and Unit Review. Exit ticket: (a) Describe two ways to increase the current induced in a coil when moving a magnet nearby. (b) Explain why a magnet held still inside a coil produces no current. (c) Name one real-world device that uses electromagnetic induction and explain how it works.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a cause-and-effect organizer: 'Changing magnetic field → Induced current.' Include a list of factors that increase induced current (faster motion, stronger magnet, more coils). Provide a technology connection chart matching each device (generator, transformer) to the physics principle.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the induction investigation and hand-crank generator activity. Work through unit review problems.
differentiation.advanced: Research Lenz's Law (the induced current opposes the change that created it) and explain why the magnet feels resistance when pushed into the coil. Discuss the implications of Lenz's Law for energy conservation.
differentiation.ell: Use the physical magnet-and-coil demonstration as the primary learning experience. Provide a visual Faraday's Law summary with before/during/after diagrams. Include bilingual vocabulary and a technology connections visual.
differentiation.iep: Focus on the hands-on investigation and the conceptual rule: 'Changing magnetic field = induced current. Steady magnetic field = no current.' Simplify the exit ticket to yes/no and short-answer format. Allow partner work.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Michael Faraday's remarkable story — born into poverty, with little formal education, he became one of the greatest experimental scientists in history through self-teaching and mentorship. His discovery of electromagnetic induction made modern civilization possible. Also discuss how access to electricity remains an equity issue globally, with over 700 million people lacking reliable electricity, disproportionately affecting communities in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'electromagnetic induction': Moving a magnet through a coil produces current because___. A stationary magnet inside a coil produces no current, but a moving magnet does because___. Electromagnetic induction is the basis of all electrical generators, so virtually all electricity we use is produced by___.

vocabulary.definition: The process of generating an electric current by changing the magnetic field through a coil of wire; discovered by Michael Faraday in 1831
A device that converts mechanical energy to electrical energy using electromagnetic induction; a coil rotates in a magnetic field, inducing alternating current
Electric current produced by a changing magnetic field; flows only while the magnetic field is changing, not when it is steady

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Faraday's Discovery — Changing Magnetic Fields Create Current
Section 3: Generators — How Power Plants Make Electricity
Section 5: Unit Review — Connecting Gravity, Electrostatics, and Magnetism

lessons.title: Work as Energy Transfer (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: calculate the work done on an object by a force, including cases where the force is at an angle to the displacement
lessons.circle_prompt: What does the word 'work' mean to you in everyday life? How might a physicist define 'work' differently? Think of a time you worked really hard physically — were you always moving something?
lessons.do_now: A student pushes a 10 kg box across the floor with 50 N of force for 3 meters. Another student holds a 10 kg box above their head for 30 seconds without moving. Who did more work in the physics sense? Explain your reasoning.
materials: Smooth surfaces and rough surfaces (cardboard, sandpaper)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Work as Energy Transfer. Display two images: (1) A person pushing a heavy box across a room. (2) A person holding a heavy box perfectly still above their head, sweating and straining. Ask: Who is doing more work? Students vote — most will say the person holding the box. Reveal that in physics, only the person pushing the box does work, because work requires displacement in the direction of the force.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Work as Energy Transfer. Groups use spring scales to pull a 1 kg mass across a table at constant speed over 1.0 m. They record the force and calculate W = Fd. Then they pull the same mass up a ramp (at an angle) to the same height and record the force and distance along the ramp. Students compare the work done in each case and discover that W = Fd cos(theta) accounts for the angle between force and displacement.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Work as Energy Transfer. Define work: W = Fd cos(theta), where theta is the angle between the force and displacement vectors. Units: Joules (J) = N·m. Key cases: theta = 0 degrees (force parallel to displacement, maximum work), theta = 90 degrees (force perpendicular, zero work — like carrying a box horizontally while gravity pulls down), theta = 180 degrees (force opposes displacement, negative work — like friction). Work through three practice problems: pushing a lawn mower at an angle, lifting a weight vertically, and friction slowing a sliding object.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Work as Energy Transfer. A 40 kg child pulls a 15 kg sled with a rope that makes a 30-degree angle with the horizontal. The tension in the rope is 40 N and the child pulls the sled 100 m. Students calculate the work done by the child on the sled, the work done by gravity, and the work done by the normal force.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Work as Energy Transfer. Exit ticket: A 60 N force is applied to a box at 45 degrees above the horizontal. The box moves 8.0 m along the floor. Calculate the work done by the applied force. Then explain why the normal force does zero work.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a work calculation flowchart: Step 1 — Identify F and d. Step 2 — Find angle between F and d. Step 3 — Plug into W = Fd cos(theta). Include a cosine value reference card for common angles (0, 30, 45, 60, 90 degrees).
differentiation.on_level: Complete the spring scale exploration and all practice problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate work done by a variable force using the area under a Force vs. Displacement graph. Analyze the work done during the compression of a spring where force changes with position.
differentiation.ell: Provide visual diagrams showing force and displacement vectors with the angle clearly labeled for each problem. Use color-coding: blue arrow = force, red arrow = displacement, green arc = angle. Include bilingual vocabulary card.
differentiation.iep: Provide a W = Fd cos(theta) reference card with a diagram. Break multi-step problems into single calculations. Provide a calculator tutorial for the cosine function. Allow use of the common angles reference card on assessments.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Emilie du Chatelet, an 18th-century French physicist who demonstrated that energy is proportional to velocity squared (not just velocity), laying groundwork for the concept of kinetic energy. Despite her contributions, she was often overshadowed by her male contemporaries, including Voltaire.

Both pushing and lifting require effort, but only one involves work when the box moves horizontally because___. dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

materials: Dynamics carts and track (1 set per group)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Kinetic Energy and the Work-Energy Theorem. Show two video clips: (1) A bowling ball rolling slowly toward pins. (2) A tennis ball fired from a machine at high speed. Ask: Which would you rather be hit by? Why? Both can knock things over — what determines how much damage a moving object can do? Introduce kinetic energy as the quantity that captures this idea.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Kinetic Energy and the Work-Energy Theorem. Students use dynamics carts with motion sensors. Part 1: Keep mass constant (0.5 kg), vary speed (0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 m/s). Calculate KE for each trial. Graph KE vs. v and KE vs. v^2. Part 2: Keep speed constant (1.0 m/s), vary mass (0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 kg). Calculate KE and graph KE vs. m. Students identify: KE depends on the square of velocity but linearly on mass.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Kinetic Energy and the Work-Energy Theorem. Formalize: KE = 1/2 mv^2. Point out the squared velocity term — doubling speed quadruples KE. This is why highway accidents are so much more dangerous than parking lot accidents. Introduce the work-energy theorem: W_net = delta KE = KE_f - KE_i. If positive net work is done, KE increases (object speeds up). If negative net work is done, KE decreases (object slows down). Work through two examples: (1) A 1200 kg car accelerates from 10 m/s to 25 m/s — find the net work done. (2) A braking force does -8000 J of work on a 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s — find the final speed.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Kinetic Energy and the Work-Energy Theorem. Application: A 0.145 kg baseball is pitched at 40 m/s toward a batter. The batter hits the ball, and it leaves the bat at 45 m/s in the opposite direction. Use the work-energy theorem to find the net work done on the ball by the bat. Then, if the bat was in contact for 0.5 cm, calculate the average force.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Kinetic Energy and the Work-Energy Theorem. Exit ticket: A 70 kg sprinter starts from rest and reaches 10 m/s. (a) Calculate the change in kinetic energy. (b) How much net work was done on the sprinter? (c) If the sprinter covered 15 m during this acceleration, what was the average net force?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a KE calculation template with blanks: KE = 1/2 (___ kg)(___ m/s)^2 = ___ J. Include a work-energy theorem summary card: 'Net work = final KE - initial KE. Positive net work = speeds up. Negative net work = slows down.'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the dynamics cart exploration and all work-energy theorem problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Derive KE = 1/2 mv^2 from W = Fd and the kinematics equations. Analyze how stopping distance depends on the square of speed and explain the physics behind speed limits in school zones.
differentiation.ell: Use bar diagrams to visually represent KE before and after work is done. Provide bilingual vocabulary cards with visual models. Use color-coded energy bars (red = KE before, blue = KE after, green = work done).
differentiation.iep: Provide a step-by-step problem-solving template for work-energy theorem problems. Allow use of formula card on assessments. Reduce the number of practice problems and focus on single-step KE calculations before multi-step problems.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the physics of car crashes and how kinetic energy relates to vehicle safety. Examine how crash test ratings impact different communities — lower-income families often drive older vehicles with fewer safety features.

dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

materials: Springs of different spring constants (2-3 per group)
Ring stands and clamps for hanging springs

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Gravitational and Elastic Potential Energy. Show the bungee jumping cluster from the Regents sampler (Macau Tower, 233 m). Ask: When the jumper stands on the platform, they have zero kinetic energy. When they reach the lowest point, they also have zero kinetic energy. But they moved 200 m. Where did the energy go during the fall, and where is it stored at the bottom? Students brainstorm in pairs.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Gravitational and Elastic Potential Energy. Station 1 — Gravitational PE: Students hold masses at different heights (0.5 m, 1.0 m, 1.5 m, 2.0 m) and calculate PE = mgh for each. They verify that PE depends linearly on height by graphing PE vs. h. Station 2 — Elastic PE: Students hang masses from a spring, measure the stretch (x), and calculate PE = 1/2 kx^2 using the spring constant k (provided on a tag or measured by students). They graph PE vs. x and PE vs. x^2.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Gravitational and Elastic Potential Energy. Define potential energy as stored energy due to position or configuration. Gravitational PE: PE_g = mgh, where h is measured relative to a chosen reference point. The choice of reference point is arbitrary but must be consistent. Elastic PE: PE_s = 1/2 kx^2, where k is the spring constant (N/m) and x is the displacement from equilibrium. Connect to Hooke's Law: F = kx (from Unit 3). Work through examples: (1) A 60 kg bungee jumper on a 233 m platform — calculate PE_g. (2) A spring with k = 200 N/m compressed 0.15 m — calculate PE_s.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Gravitational and Elastic Potential Energy. Regents connection: Students solve the bungee jumping sampler question — calculating the change in gravitational PE for a 60 kg jumper riding an elevator from the ground to a 233 m platform. Then they draw an energy bar chart showing PE_g, PE_s, and KE at the platform, during free fall (before cord stretches), and at the lowest point.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Gravitational and Elastic Potential Energy. Exit ticket: A spring with k = 400 N/m is compressed 0.25 m and launches a 0.1 kg ball straight up. (a) Calculate the elastic PE stored in the spring. (b) If all this energy converts to gravitational PE, how high does the ball rise?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a side-by-side comparison chart: Gravitational PE (PE = mgh, depends on height, reference point matters) vs. Elastic PE (PE = 1/2 kx^2, depends on stretch/compression, equilibrium is reference). Include a worked example for each.
differentiation.on_level: Complete both station activities and energy bar chart problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Derive PE_s = 1/2 kx^2 from the area under a Force vs. Displacement graph for a spring. Analyze how gravitational PE changes for objects at very large distances from Earth where g is not constant.
differentiation.ell: Use physical demonstrations at each station — students see and feel the spring stretching and masses being lifted before calculating. Provide bilingual energy vocabulary cards with diagrams showing energy storage.
differentiation.iep: Color-coded formula cards: green for PE_g = mgh, blue for PE_s = 1/2 kx^2. Break the exit ticket into single-variable calculation steps. Provide pre-labeled energy bar chart templates.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how the Inca civilization used gravitational potential energy concepts in their terrace farming system — moving water downhill through precisely engineered channels. Connect to modern hydroelectric power, which converts gravitational PE of water to electrical energy, and discuss how dam construction affects indigenous communities worldwide.

Both gravitational and elastic PE are forms of stored energy, but they depend on different factors because___. The spring was compressed 0.20 m and has a spring constant of 300 N/m, so the elastic PE stored is___.
