cer.phenomenon: A 60 kg bungee jumper stands on a platform 233 m above the ground at the Macau Tower. The unstretched bungee cord is 50 m long. The jumper falls 200 m to the lowest point, coming momentarily to rest. At the lowest point, the cord has stretched 150 m beyond its natural length.
cer.claim_starter: Based on energy analysis, I claim that at the lowest point, all of the jumper's original gravitational PE has been converted to elastic PE stored in the bungee cord because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the gravitational PE at the platform (relative to the lowest point). Calculate the elastic PE stored in the cord at maximum stretch using the given stretch distance. Compare the two values.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because at the platform the jumper has ___ J of gravitational PE and zero KE, while at the lowest point the jumper has zero KE and zero gravitational PE (relative to that point), so the ___ J must be stored as ___ in the cord.

lessons.title: Conservation of Mechanical Energy (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: apply the law of conservation of energy to solve problems involving the transformation between kinetic and potential energy in systems without significant friction
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever been on a roller coaster, a swing, or a skateboard ramp? Describe the moment when you felt the fastest. Was it always at the lowest point? Why do you think that is?
lessons.do_now: A 2 kg ball is dropped from 10 m. What is its speed just before hitting the ground? Use conservation of energy, not kinematics equations.

dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

materials: Hot Wheels track with loop (1 per group)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Conservation of Mechanical Energy. Set up a Hot Wheels track with a hill and a loop. Release a car from the top of the hill. Ask: How do we know the car will make it through the loop? What if we release it from a lower point? Students predict the minimum release height needed to complete the loop. Introduce conservation of energy as the tool that lets us make this prediction without knowing anything about forces or acceleration along the curved path.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Conservation of Mechanical Energy. Students set up tracks with a hill and a loop. They release a marble from various heights and record whether it completes the loop. They measure the loop diameter and calculate the minimum height using conservation of energy: mgh = mgh_top + 1/2 mv^2_top. Key insight: mass cancels — the result is independent of mass. Students test with marbles of different sizes to confirm.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Conservation of Mechanical Energy. Formalize the law of conservation of mechanical energy: In the absence of non-conservative forces (friction, air resistance), the total mechanical energy remains constant. KE_i + PE_i = KE_f + PE_f. Demonstrate using energy bar charts for three scenarios: (1) Ball dropped from height h — PE converts to KE. (2) Ball launched upward — KE converts to PE. (3) Pendulum — continuous KE/PE exchange. Work through two quantitative problems from the Regents bungee cluster style.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Conservation of Mechanical Energy. A 65 kg skier starts from rest at the top of a 40 m hill and slides to the bottom (no friction). (a) Find the speed at the bottom. (b) The skier then goes up a second hill 25 m high. Find the speed at the top of the second hill. (c) What is the maximum height of a hill the skier could clear? Students draw energy bar charts for each position.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Conservation of Mechanical Energy. Exit ticket: A 0.5 kg ball on a frictionless track is released from a height of 3.0 m. At the bottom of the track, it enters a vertical loop of radius 0.8 m. (a) What is the ball's speed at the bottom of the loop? (b) What is its speed at the top of the loop?

differentiation.approaching: Provide an energy conservation problem-solving template: Step 1 — Identify initial and final positions. Step 2 — List the energy types at each position (KE, PE_g, PE_s). Step 3 — Write the equation KE_i + PE_i = KE_f + PE_f. Step 4 — Substitute and solve. Include pre-drawn energy bar chart templates.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the loop investigation and all conservation of energy problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Analyze what happens when friction IS present: Where does the 'lost' energy go? Calculate the work done by friction using W_friction = KE_f + PE_f - KE_i - PE_i. Design a roller coaster on paper that satisfies given constraints (max speed, loop clearance) using conservation of energy.
differentiation.ell: Use energy bar charts as a visual intermediary before writing equations. Color-code energy types consistently (yellow = KE, blue = PE_g, green = PE_s). Provide sentence frames: 'At position ___, the energy is stored as ___. At position ___, the energy has transformed into ___.'
differentiation.iep: Provide a laminated conservation of energy equation card. Use the bar chart as the primary tool — students fill in bars before writing equations. Break problems into steps: 'First find PE_i, then set equal to KE_f, then solve for v.' Reduce the number of problems.

lessons.crse_connection: Analyze the physics of roller coasters, connecting to the contributions of John Allen, considered the 'dean of roller coaster designers,' and discuss how amusement park physics disproportionately affects communities near theme parks. Examine how energy conservation principles are used in designing sustainable transportation systems in cities around the world.

A ball released from 5 m high on a frictionless track will reach the same height on the other side, but if there is friction it will not because___. A force (like friction) that depends on path and converts mechanical energy to thermal energy; when present, mechanical energy is not conserved

cer.topic: Conservation of Energy on a Roller Coaster
cer.phenomenon: A roller coaster car (mass 500 kg with passengers) starts from rest at the top of the first hill (height 45 m). The second hill is 30 m high. The third hill is 38 m high. After the third hill, the track is level, and brakes bring the car to rest over a distance of 25 m. A rider notices they feel fastest at the bottom of the first valley and slowest at the top of the third hill.
cer.claim_starter: Based on conservation of energy, I claim that the rider's observations are correct because the speed at any point depends on...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the speed at the bottom of the first valley, the top of the second hill, the top of the third hill, and determine the braking force needed to stop the car on the level section.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because conservation of energy gives v = sqrt(2g(h_initial - h_point)), so the lowest point (h = 0) gives the ___ speed of ___ m/s, while the highest subsequent point (h = ___ m) gives the ___ speed of ___ m/s.

lessons.title: Energy Transformations and Dissipation (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: trace energy transformations through a system, identify where energy is dissipated as thermal energy, and explain why perpetual motion machines are impossible
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about the energy transformations in your morning routine — your alarm goes off, you turn on a light, eat breakfast, walk to school. How many energy conversions can you count?
lessons.do_now: A bouncy ball is dropped from 2 m. It bounces back to only 1.5 m. Where did the missing energy go? Is energy conserved? Explain the difference between energy conservation and mechanical energy conservation.

dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer
PS3.D: Energy in Chemical Processes and Everyday Life

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Energy Transformations and Dissipation. Challenge: Can anyone build a machine that runs forever without any energy input? Show images of famous perpetual motion machine designs from history. Students discuss in pairs why each would fail. Reveal: Every machine eventually stops because energy is dissipated as thermal energy through friction, sound, and deformation.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Energy Transformations and Dissipation. Station rotation (3 stations, 4 min each). Station 1 — Bouncing ball: Drop a ball from a measured height 5 times, record the rebound height each time. Calculate the fraction of energy retained per bounce. Station 2 — Hand generator: Crank a generator to light a bulb. Feel the bulb get warm. Trace the energy chain: chemical (food) -> kinetic (arm) -> electrical (generator) -> light + thermal (bulb). Station 3 — Rubber band: Rapidly stretch and un-stretch a thick rubber band 20 times, then touch it to your lip. It is warm — mechanical energy converted to thermal.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Energy Transformations and Dissipation. Formalize energy dissipation: In real systems, mechanical energy is always converted to thermal energy through friction, air resistance, and deformation. Total energy is still conserved (First Law of Thermodynamics), but the useful mechanical energy decreases. Introduce efficiency: efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input x 100%. Discuss the energy chain of a car: chemical (gasoline) -> thermal (combustion) -> kinetic (pistons) -> kinetic (wheels), with large losses at each step (typical car: ~25% efficient).

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Energy Transformations and Dissipation. A bouncy ball dropped from 2.0 m rebounds to 1.6 m. Students calculate: (a) The fraction of mechanical energy retained per bounce. (b) The energy dissipated per bounce for a 0.05 kg ball. (c) The height after 3 bounces. (d) The efficiency of one bounce as a percentage.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Energy Transformations and Dissipation. Exit ticket: A light bulb converts 100 J of electrical energy into 5 J of light and 95 J of thermal energy. (a) What is the efficiency of the bulb? (b) Is energy conserved in this process? (c) Why are LED bulbs considered more efficient?

differentiation.approaching: Provide an energy transformation chain template with arrows and boxes. Students fill in the energy form at each stage. Include an efficiency formula card with a worked example.
differentiation.on_level: Complete all three stations and efficiency calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research the efficiency of different power plants (coal, natural gas, nuclear, solar) and create a comparison chart. Analyze why the theoretical maximum efficiency of a heat engine is limited by the Carnot efficiency.
differentiation.ell: Use physical stations as primary learning — students experience energy transformations before abstracting. Provide an energy transformation visual chain with icons (flame, arrow, light bulb, thermometer) and bilingual labels.
differentiation.iep: Pre-label energy transformation charts with some boxes filled in. Reduce station data collection to 3 bounces instead of 5. Provide a calculator walkthrough for efficiency calculations.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how energy efficiency and access are social justice issues. Examine how lower-income communities often pay higher percentages of their income on energy bills and have older, less efficient appliances. Highlight the work of Lisa Jackson, former EPA administrator, in promoting energy efficiency standards that disproportionately benefit underserved communities.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'energy dissipation': A bouncing ball never returns to its original height because___. Total energy is always conserved in a closed system, but mechanical energy is not because___. The car engine converts only 25% of gasoline's chemical energy to useful kinetic energy, so the remaining 75%___.

vocabulary.definition: The conversion of useful mechanical energy into thermal energy (heat) through friction, air resistance, or deformation
The ratio of useful energy output to total energy input, expressed as a percentage; always less than 100% for real machines
A hypothetical device that operates indefinitely without an energy source; impossible due to energy dissipation

lessons.do_now: Review: Based on yesterday's lesson, explain one key idea from yesterday about how to define and identify key concepts related to: trace energy transformations through a system, identify where energy is dissipated as thermal energy, and explain why perpetual motion machines are impossible.

dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer
PS3.D: Energy in Chemical Processes and Everyday Life

engage.description: Brief review of Day 1 concepts through a warm-up problem or quick discussion. Building on previous days: Challenge: Can anyone build a machine that runs forever without any energy input? Show images of famous perpetual motion machine designs from history. Students discuss in pairs why each would fail. Reveal: Every machine eventually stops because energy is dissipated as thermal energy through friction, sound, and deformation.

explore.description: Students work through practice problems or applications in pairs or small groups. Building on previous days: Station rotation (3 stations, 4 min each). Station 1 — Bouncing ball: Drop a ball from a measured height 5 times, record the rebound height each time. Calculate the fraction of energy retained per bounce. Station 2 — Hand generator: Crank a generator to light a bulb. Feel the bulb get warm. Trace the energy chain: chemical (food) -> kinetic (arm) -> electrical (generator) -> light + thermal (bulb). Station 3 — Rubber band: Rapidly stretch and un-stretch a thick rubber band 20 times, then touch it to your lip. It is warm — mechanical energy converted to thermal.

explain.description: Address common misconceptions from practice; model problem-solving strategies. Building on previous days: Formalize energy dissipation: In real systems, mechanical energy is always converted to thermal energy through friction, air resistance, and deformation. Total energy is still conserved (First Law of Thermodynamics), but the useful mechanical energy decreases. Introduce efficiency: efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input x 100%. Discuss the energy chain of a car: chemical (gasoline) -> thermal (combustion) -> kinetic (pistons) -> kinetic (wheels), with large losses at each step (typical car: ~25% efficient).

elaborate.description: CER activity connecting evidence to claims about the topic. Building on previous days: A bouncy ball dropped from 2.0 m rebounds to 1.6 m. Students calculate: (a) The fraction of mechanical energy retained per bounce. (b) The energy dissipated per bounce for a 0.05 kg ball. (c) The height after 3 bounces. (d) The efficiency of one bounce as a percentage.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket with application-level problems requiring multi-step reasoning. Building on previous days: Exit ticket: A light bulb converts 100 J of electrical energy into 5 J of light and 95 J of thermal energy. (a) What is the efficiency of the bulb? (b) Is energy conserved in this process? (c) Why are LED bulbs considered more efficient?

differentiation.approaching: Review key concepts from the full sequence before assessment. Provide an energy transformation chain template with arrows and boxes. Students fill in the energy form at each stage. Include an efficiency formula card with a worked example.
differentiation.on_level: Complete all three stations and efficiency calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Complete extension challenge connecting to real-world applications. Research the efficiency of different power plants (coal, natural gas, nuclear, solar) and create a comparison chart. Analyze why the theoretical maximum efficiency of a heat engine is limited by the Carnot efficiency.
differentiation.ell: Use physical stations as primary learning — students experience energy transformations before abstracting. Provide an energy transformation visual chain with icons (flame, arrow, light bulb, thermometer) and bilingual labels.
differentiation.iep: Pre-label energy transformation charts with some boxes filled in. Reduce station data collection to 3 bounces instead of 5. Provide a calculator walkthrough for efficiency calculations.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how energy efficiency and access are social justice issues. Examine how lower-income communities often pay higher percentages of their income on energy bills and have older, less efficient appliances. Highlight the work of Lisa Jackson, former EPA administrator, in promoting energy efficiency standards that disproportionately benefit underserved communities.
lessons.hochman_activity: Kernel sentence expansion using 'Energy Transformation': Start with 'Energy Transformation is important.' Expand by adding when, where, why, and how details to create a complex sentence that demonstrates understanding of the concept.

vocabulary.definition: The internal energy of an object due to the random motion of its particles; increased when mechanical energy is dissipated
The conversion of energy from one form to another (e.g., chemical to thermal to kinetic in a car engine)

guided_notes_outline: Section 2: Energy Dissipation — Where Does the Lost Energy Go?
Section 4: Why Perpetual Motion Machines Are Impossible

cer.phenomenon: A standard incandescent light bulb converts approximately 5% of electrical energy to visible light and 95% to thermal energy. A compact fluorescent bulb (CFL) converts about 20% to visible light. An LED bulb converts about 40% to visible light. A household uses 30 light bulbs for an average of 5 hours per day, each consuming 60 W (incandescent), 13 W (CFL), or 8 W (LED) to produce the same amount of light.
cer.claim_starter: Based on efficiency data, I claim that switching from incandescent to LED bulbs significantly reduces energy waste and cost because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the daily energy consumption for each bulb type (in kWh). Calculate the annual cost at $0.15 per kWh. Determine how much energy is wasted as heat for each type.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because LED bulbs use only ___ W compared to ___ W for incandescent, saving ___ kWh per year and $___ annually, while producing the same light output. This is because the LED converts ___% of energy to light compared to only ___% for incandescent.

lessons.title: Power (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: calculate power as the rate at which work is done or energy is transferred, and compare the power output of different systems
lessons.circle_prompt: Two students carry identical backpacks to the same floor of the building. One takes the stairs and arrives in 30 seconds. The other takes the elevator and arrives in 60 seconds. Who did more work? Who was more powerful? What is the difference?
lessons.do_now: A motor does 5000 J of work in 10 seconds. A second motor does 5000 J of work in 25 seconds. Both do the same work. What is different about them? Calculate a quantity that captures this difference.

dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Power. Compare two cars: both can reach 100 km/h, but a sports car does it in 4 seconds while a minivan takes 12 seconds. Ask: If they reach the same speed and have similar mass, they gain similar kinetic energy. What is the sports car better at? Introduce power as the rate of doing work or transferring energy.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Power. Staircase power lab: Students measure their mass (using a bathroom scale), the height of a flight of stairs, and the time it takes to walk up and then run up the stairs. They calculate the work done (W = mgh) and the power output (P = W/t) for each trial. Students compare their walking power to their running power and rank classmates by power output.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Power. Define power: P = W/t = Fd/t = Fv. Units: Watts (W) = J/s. 1 horsepower = 746 W. Discuss the difference between energy and power: A 100 W bulb and a 60 W bulb can both emit the same total energy — the 100 W bulb just does it faster. Work through examples: (1) An elevator motor lifts 800 kg a height of 20 m in 30 s — find the power. (2) A cyclist maintains a speed of 8 m/s against a friction force of 40 N — find the power.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Power. A 1200 kg car accelerates from rest to 30 m/s in 8 seconds. (a) Calculate the kinetic energy gained. (b) Calculate the average power output. (c) Express this in horsepower. (d) If the engine is 25% efficient, how much total chemical energy (from fuel) was used?

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Power. Exit ticket: A crane lifts a 2000 kg steel beam 15 m in 45 seconds at constant speed. (a) Calculate the work done by the crane. (b) Calculate the power of the crane in watts and horsepower.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a power formula reference card showing P = W/t and P = Fv side by side with unit reminders (W in Joules, t in seconds, P in Watts). Include a step-by-step example for the staircase lab calculation.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the staircase power lab and all practice problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research the power output of various energy sources (human body, car engine, power plant, the Sun) and create a powers-of-ten comparison chart. Calculate the average power output of a sprinter during a 100 m dash using work-energy theorem.
differentiation.ell: Use the physical staircase activity as the primary learning experience. Provide a bilingual vocabulary card with diagrams showing the difference between energy (how much) and power (how fast). Sentence frames for comparisons.
differentiation.iep: Pre-fill the staircase lab data table with column headers and units. Provide a step-by-step calculation guide. Allow use of the formula card on assessments.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how James Watt, a Scottish engineer, defined horsepower to market his steam engine to mine owners. Connect to how the Industrial Revolution transformed labor — and how power generation has always been tied to social power, from coal mines employing child workers in England to modern debates about renewable energy access in developing nations.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'power': Two students may do the same amount of work climbing stairs, but the faster student has more power because___. A 100 W light bulb and a 60 W light bulb both produce light, but the 100 W bulb uses more energy per second because___. The crane lifted the beam 15 m in 45 seconds, so its power output was___.

vocabulary.definition: The rate at which work is done or energy is transferred; P = W/t, measured in Watts
A unit of power; 1 hp = 746 W; originally defined by James Watt

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: What Is Power? — Rate of Doing Work
Section 3: Units of Power — Watts and Horsepower

cer.phenomenon: In the 2009 World Championships, Usain Bolt ran 100 m in 9.58 seconds with a mass of 86 kg. In the same competition, a weightlifter performed a clean and jerk, lifting 200 kg to a height of 2.0 m in 1.5 seconds. Both are considered elite athletes.
cer.claim_starter: Based on power calculations, I claim that the weightlifter actually generates more instantaneous power than Bolt, even though Bolt appears more explosive, because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate Bolt's average kinetic energy at the finish (using v = d/t as an approximation) and his average power output. Calculate the weightlifter's work (W = mgh) and power output.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the weightlifter's power output is approximately ___ W, while Bolt's average power is approximately ___ W. However, Bolt's peak power during the acceleration phase is ___ because ___.

lessons.title: Simple Machines and Mechanical Advantage (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: calculate the ideal mechanical advantage and efficiency of simple machines and explain how machines trade force for distance while conserving energy
lessons.circle_prompt: What tools or machines do you use regularly that make tasks easier — a ramp for moving heavy objects, a bottle opener, scissors, a pulley? How do they actually help you?
lessons.do_now: A 200 N box must be lifted 1.5 m onto a truck. You could lift it straight up, or push it up a 4.5 m ramp. Calculate the work done in each case (ignoring friction). What does the ramp change, and what stays the same?
materials: Pulleys (single and compound, 1 set per group)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Simple Machines and Mechanical Advantage. Show images of the Egyptian pyramids and ask: How did workers move 2.5-ton stone blocks to a height of 146 m without modern cranes? Display illustrations of ramps, levers, and rollers used in ancient construction. Machines do not reduce the amount of work — they make it possible by reducing the force needed.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Simple Machines and Mechanical Advantage. Groups compare the force needed to lift a 1 kg mass straight up versus pulling it up ramps at different angles. They measure the input force (spring scale reading) and input distance (ramp length) for each angle. Students calculate: Work_input = F_input x d_input and Work_output = F_gravity x height. They compute efficiency = W_out/W_in x 100% and IMA = d_input/d_output for each ramp.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Simple Machines and Mechanical Advantage. Define simple machines: devices that change the direction or magnitude of a force. Ideal Mechanical Advantage (IMA) = distance_input / distance_output. Actual Mechanical Advantage (AMA) = Force_output / Force_input. Efficiency = AMA/IMA x 100% = Work_out/Work_in x 100%. Key principle: a machine cannot multiply energy — it trades force for distance. Briefly overview six simple machines: lever, inclined plane, wedge, screw, wheel and axle, pulley.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Simple Machines and Mechanical Advantage. Pulley system challenge: Students set up a single fixed pulley, then a single movable pulley, then a compound pulley system. For each, they measure the force required to lift a 5 N weight and the distance they must pull the rope. They calculate IMA and efficiency for each system and explain the trade-off.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Simple Machines and Mechanical Advantage. Exit ticket: A worker uses a 6 m ramp to push a 300 N crate to a platform 2 m high, applying 120 N of force. (a) Calculate the IMA. (b) Calculate the AMA. (c) Calculate the efficiency. (d) Explain where the 'lost' energy goes.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a simple machines reference card with diagrams of each type and formulas for IMA. Include a side-by-side comparison: 'Without machine: big force, small distance. With machine: small force, big distance. Same work.'
differentiation.on_level: Complete the ramp and pulley exploration and all calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Design a compound machine (combination of two or more simple machines) to lift a heavy object from the ground to a table. Calculate the theoretical IMA of the compound system and test it. Research how the Archimedes screw is still used for irrigation in developing countries.
differentiation.ell: Use hands-on exploration as the primary learning tool. Provide labeled diagrams of each simple machine in English and native language. Use consistent symbols in all formulas.
differentiation.iep: Provide a step-by-step efficiency calculation guide with fill-in-the-blank format. Focus on ramp and pulley problems only (skip the other four simple machines for now). Allow partner work on the exit ticket.

lessons.crse_connection: Explore how simple machines have been fundamental to every civilization's development — Archimedes' lever and screw in ancient Greece, the shaduf (lever-based water lift) in ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia, and the terrace systems of the Inca Empire that used inclined planes to manage water and agriculture across the Andes.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'mechanical advantage': A ramp makes it easier to push a heavy object to a higher elevation because___. A single fixed pulley changes the direction of force but does not reduce the effort, but a movable pulley reduces the effort by half because___. The efficiency of the ramp was only 83%, so___.

vocabulary.definition: A device that changes the magnitude or direction of a force; the six types are lever, inclined plane, wedge, screw, wheel and axle, and pulley
The mechanical advantage measured in a real machine; AMA = force_output / force_input
In simple machines, the exchange between force and distance — reducing the required force always increases the required distance

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: What Is a Simple Machine? — Changing Force, Not Energy
Section 3: Efficiency of Machines

Section 4: The Six Simple Machines — Examples and Applications

cer.phenomenon: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built with approximately 2.3 million stone blocks, each weighing about 2,500 kg. The pyramid is 146 m tall. Workers had no powered machinery. Archaeological evidence suggests they used long ramps with a gradual incline of about 7-8 degrees. An alternative theory proposes shorter, steeper ramps with a 20-degree incline wrapped around the pyramid.
cer.claim_starter: Based on mechanical advantage calculations, I claim that the longer, gentler ramp would have required less force per worker but more total distance, while the steeper ramp would require more force but less distance, because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the IMA for each ramp design. Determine the force required to push a 2,500 kg block up each ramp. Estimate the number of workers needed if each can exert approximately 500 N.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the 7-degree ramp has an IMA of approximately ___, requiring only ___ N of force (about ___ workers), while the 20-degree ramp has an IMA of only ___, requiring ___ N (about ___ workers). This illustrates the fundamental trade-off in simple machines.

lessons.title: Energy Conversions and Engineering Design (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: design, build, and refine a device that converts one form of energy to another within given constraints, and explain how to optimize its efficiency
lessons.circle_prompt: If you could invent a device that captures wasted energy from everyday life — body heat, vibrations from walking, sound from a crowded room — what would you create? How would you use the captured energy?
lessons.do_now: A wind turbine converts kinetic energy of moving air into electrical energy. If a turbine receives 500,000 J of wind energy per second and produces 175,000 J of electrical energy per second, what is its efficiency? What happens to the remaining energy?

dci: PS3.D: Energy in Chemical Processes and Everyday Life

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Energy Conversions and Engineering Design. Present the Regents sampler problem about a device that converts one form of energy to another (HS-PS3-3). Show the performance level descriptor: at Level 4, students must 'design, build, and refine a device that works within given constraints to convert one form of energy into another form of energy.' Set the challenge: Build a rubber band-powered car that converts elastic PE to kinetic energy and travels the farthest distance.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Energy Conversions and Engineering Design. Engineering design challenge: Groups receive identical materials kits and must build a rubber band-powered vehicle that travels as far as possible along the floor. Constraints: must use only provided materials, must fit within a 20 cm x 15 cm footprint, must start from rest. Groups have 10 minutes to build and 5 minutes to test and measure distances. Record initial elastic PE (estimated) and final distance traveled.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Energy Conversions and Engineering Design. Class debriefs: Which designs went farthest? Why? Discuss energy transformation chain: elastic PE (rubber band) -> kinetic energy (wheels) -> thermal energy (friction). What design features maximized efficiency? (Less friction, better axle design, optimal rubber band tension.) Connect to HS-PS3-3 PLDs: students must explain how their device could be refined and how a similar device could solve a real-world problem.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Energy Conversions and Engineering Design. Groups refine their designs based on first-round data. They make one modification, justify it in writing using energy concepts, and test again. They calculate the improvement in distance and efficiency. Students write a brief engineering report: original design, modification made, physics reasoning, results.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Energy Conversions and Engineering Design. Exit ticket: (a) Trace the energy transformations in your rubber band car from start to stop. (b) Identify where energy was dissipated. (c) Describe one design change you would make if you had additional materials, and explain why it would improve efficiency using energy concepts.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a pre-made chassis template that students can modify. Include a design checklist: 'Does your car have wheels? Is the rubber band attached securely? Can the wheels spin freely?' Offer an energy transformation chain template to fill in.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the design challenge with one refinement cycle as described.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the theoretical maximum distance using the elastic PE of the rubber band (measure k and x). Compare to actual distance and quantify the energy lost to friction. Propose a design that could achieve 50% or higher efficiency.
differentiation.ell: Provide labeled diagrams of sample car designs. Use hands-on building as primary learning. Pair with a strong English speaker for the written report but allow verbal explanation of design reasoning.
differentiation.iep: Pre-assemble a basic chassis and allow students to focus on the rubber band mechanism. Reduce the written report to sentence starters: 'My car converts ___ energy to ___ energy. I changed ___ because ___.' Provide extra building time.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how communities around the world are innovating with energy conversion technologies. Highlight William Kamkwamba, a Malawian inventor who built a windmill from scrap materials at age 14 to generate electricity for his village during a famine. Connect to how engineering design in physics can address real community needs, especially in areas without reliable power infrastructure.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'energy conversion': A rubber band car stores energy as elastic potential energy before release because___. Our first design traveled 3 meters, but after reducing friction on the axles it traveled 4.5 meters because___. The theoretical maximum distance was 6 meters based on stored PE, so our efficiency was approximately___.

vocabulary.definition: A machine or system that transforms energy from one form to another (e.g., solar panel: light to electrical; motor: electrical to kinetic)
A sequence showing the forms of energy as it is transformed through a system from input to output, including losses

lessons.circle_prompt: Share one connection you made between yesterday's topic and something in your daily life.

engage.description: Review warm-up connecting Day 1 vocabulary to a new example or context. Continuing: Present the Regents sampler problem about a device that converts one form of energy to another (HS-PS3-3). Show the performance level descriptor: at Level 4, students must 'design, build, and refine a device that works within given constraints to convert one form of energy into another form of energy.' Set the challenge: Build a rubber band-powered car that converts elastic PE to kinetic energy and travels the farthest distance.

explore.description: Structured practice — students work through increasingly complex problems with scaffolds. Continuing: Engineering design challenge: Groups receive identical materials kits and must build a rubber band-powered vehicle that travels as far as possible along the floor. Constraints: must use only provided materials, must fit within a 20 cm x 15 cm footprint, must start from rest. Groups have 10 minutes to build and 5 minutes to test and measure distances. Record initial elastic PE (estimated) and final distance traveled.

explain.description: Mini-lesson addressing patterns from practice; introduce additional complexity. Continuing: Class debriefs: Which designs went farthest? Why? Discuss energy transformation chain: elastic PE (rubber band) -> kinetic energy (wheels) -> thermal energy (friction). What design features maximized efficiency? (Less friction, better axle design, optimal rubber band tension.) Connect to HS-PS3-3 PLDs: students must explain how their device could be refined and how a similar device could solve a real-world problem.

elaborate.description: Partner work on application problems with real-world contexts. Continuing: Groups refine their designs based on first-round data. They make one modification, justify it in writing using energy concepts, and test again. They calculate the improvement in distance and efficiency. Students write a brief engineering report: original design, modification made, physics reasoning, results.

evaluate.description: Formative assessment — students solve 2-3 problems independently and self-check. Continuing: Exit ticket: (a) Trace the energy transformations in your rubber band car from start to stop. (b) Identify where energy was dissipated. (c) Describe one design change you would make if you had additional materials, and explain why it would improve efficiency using energy concepts.

differentiation.approaching: Provide completed examples from Day 1 as reference. Provide a pre-made chassis template that students can modify. Include a design checklist: 'Does your car have wheels? Is the rubber band attached securely? Can the wheels spin freely?' Offer an energy transformation chain template to fill in.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the design challenge with one refinement cycle as described.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the theoretical maximum distance using the elastic PE of the rubber band (measure k and x). Compare to actual distance and quantify the energy lost to friction. Propose a design that could achieve 50% or higher efficiency.
differentiation.ell: Provide labeled diagrams of sample car designs. Use hands-on building as primary learning. Pair with a strong English speaker for the written report but allow verbal explanation of design reasoning.
differentiation.iep: Pre-assemble a basic chassis and allow students to focus on the rubber band mechanism. Reduce the written report to sentence starters: 'My car converts ___ energy to ___ energy. I changed ___ because ___.' Provide extra building time.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how communities around the world are innovating with energy conversion technologies. Highlight William Kamkwamba, a Malawian inventor who built a windmill from scrap materials at age 14 to generate electricity for his village during a famine. Connect to how engineering design in physics can address real community needs, especially in areas without reliable power infrastructure.

cer.phenomenon: A school installs two energy systems: (1) Rooftop solar panels that convert sunlight to electricity at 22% efficiency. (2) A small wind turbine that converts wind kinetic energy to electricity at 35% efficiency. The solar panels receive an average of 5.0 kWh/m^2/day of solar energy and cover 100 m^2. The wind turbine intercepts an average of 800 kWh/day of wind energy.
cer.claim_starter: Based on efficiency and energy input calculations, I claim that the solar panels generate more total electricity despite having lower efficiency because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the daily electrical output of each system using efficiency and energy input data.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the solar panels produce ___ kWh/day while the wind turbine produces ___ kWh/day. Even though the turbine has a higher efficiency (___% vs. ___%), the solar panels receive ___ times more energy input, which demonstrates that both efficiency and energy input matter.

dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Unit 6 Review and Assessment. Kahoot or quick-fire whiteboard review: Display 6 rapid-fire questions covering key formulas and concepts (W = Fd cos theta, KE = 1/2 mv^2, PE = mgh, PE = 1/2 kx^2, conservation of energy, P = W/t). Students hold up whiteboards with answers. Address common errors immediately.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Unit 6 Review and Assessment. Problem carousel: Six stations around the room, each with a multi-step energy problem (Regents-style). Station 1: Work at an angle. Station 2: Work-energy theorem. Station 3: Conservation with gravitational PE. Station 4: Spring-launches and elastic PE. Station 5: Energy bar charts with friction. Station 6: Power calculations. Groups rotate every 2 minutes, solving one problem per station.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Unit 6 Review and Assessment. Teacher reviews the most commonly missed problems from the carousel. Focus on: (1) Remembering to include the angle in work calculations. (2) Setting up conservation of energy equations correctly — identifying what energy forms exist at each position. (3) Understanding when mechanical energy is NOT conserved (friction present). Display student work samples and discuss strategies.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Unit 6 Review and Assessment. Regents cluster practice: Students work through a complete bungee jumping-style cluster (5 questions) integrating gravitational PE, kinetic energy, elastic PE, conservation of energy, and energy dissipation. This mirrors the format they will see on the exam.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Unit 6 Review and Assessment. Self-assessment: Students rate their confidence (1-4) on each major skill: calculating work, calculating KE, calculating PE, applying conservation of energy, calculating power. They identify their weakest area and write one specific study action they will take before the exam.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a formula sheet organized by topic with example problems. Allow students to use the formula sheet during the carousel. Provide step-by-step solution guides for one problem at each station.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the problem carousel and cluster practice as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Create their own Regents-style cluster of 5 questions based on a real-world energy scenario of their choice (e.g., skateboarding, ski jumping, catapult). Include calculations for work, KE, PE, conservation, and power.
differentiation.ell: Provide problem sets with visual diagrams for every question. Include a bilingual formula reference. Allow extra time at stations.
differentiation.iep: Reduce carousel to 4 stations (skip the two most complex). Provide a completed energy bar chart example to reference. Allow extended time and calculator use on all problems.

lessons.crse_connection: Review the diverse scientists and cultural connections from the unit: Emilie du Chatelet, the physics of ancient construction, energy justice, and William Kamkwamba. Students reflect on how understanding energy empowers communities and individuals to make informed decisions about resources and technology.
lessons.hochman_activity: Summary writing: Students write a 4-sentence paragraph summarizing the unit using at least 6 vocabulary terms. Sentence 1: Define work and explain how it relates to energy transfer. Sentence 2: Distinguish between kinetic and potential energy. Sentence 3: Explain conservation of energy. Sentence 4: Define power and explain its importance.

guided_notes_outline: Section 3: Regents Exam Tips for Energy Questions

cer.phenomenon: A 70 kg pole vaulter sprints down a runway at 9.0 m/s, plants a flexible pole into a box, and is launched 5.8 m into the air, clearing the bar and landing on a soft mat 1.0 m above the ground. The pole bends significantly during the vault, storing elastic PE, then straightens, converting it to the vaulter's kinetic and gravitational PE.
cer.claim_starter: Based on energy conservation, I claim that the pole vaulter cannot clear 5.8 m using running speed alone and must rely on the pole's elastic energy storage and the additional push from their arms because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the maximum height the vaulter could reach using only their initial KE (ignore the pole). Compare this to the actual height cleared. Account for the additional energy sources.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because converting all of the vaulter's KE (= ___ J) to gravitational PE gives a maximum height of only ___ m, which is ___ m short of the actual 5.8 m clearance. The additional energy comes from ___ and ___, demonstrating that the pole vault is a complex energy conversion system.

units.title: Thermal Energy & Conservation
units.anchoring_phenomenon: On a hot summer day, a metal park bench feels much hotter than a wooden bench right next to it, even though both have been in the same sunlight for hours. Why do different materials feel different temperatures when they are actually at the same temperature?
essential_questions: What is the difference between temperature and heat, and how are they measured?
How does thermal energy transfer between objects at different temperatures?
How can we use the conservation of energy to predict the final temperature when two objects are combined?
units.crse_theme: Students explore thermal physics through cultural connections — the physics of cooking traditions from around the world (clay tandoor ovens, Korean stone pot bibimbap, Mexican earth ovens), the development of thermodynamics by scientists like James Joule and Sadi Carnot, and how access to heating and cooling technologies is an equity issue in communities experiencing extreme heat and cold.

formative: Exit tickets on specific heat calculations
summative: Investigation: Calorimetry and Conservation of Energy

investigations: Investigation 4: Thermal Energy Transfer in a Calorimetry System

lessons.title: Temperature, Heat, and Thermal Energy (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: distinguish between temperature, heat, and thermal energy, and explain how thermal energy transfers from hot objects to cold objects until equilibrium is reached
lessons.circle_prompt: What is the coldest you have ever been? What is the hottest? What did you do to warm up or cool down? How does your body know the difference between hot and cold?
lessons.do_now: A cup of hot cocoa at 80 degrees C and a swimming pool at 25 degrees C — which has a higher temperature? Which contains more total thermal energy? Explain why these are different questions.

dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

materials: Beakers (250 mL and 600 mL, 1 set per group)
Hot plate or access to hot water
Temperature vs. Time data recording sheets

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Temperature, Heat, and Thermal Energy. Touch test: Students touch a metal object and a wooden object that have been sitting in the room. Ask: Which feels colder? Are they actually at different temperatures? Use a thermometer to verify they are the SAME temperature. The paradox: How can two objects at the same temperature feel different? This introduces the difference between temperature and the rate of heat transfer.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Temperature, Heat, and Thermal Energy. Experiment: Pour 100 mL of hot water (60 degrees C) and 100 mL of cold water (10 degrees C) into separate Styrofoam cups. Predict the temperature when mixed. Mix them in a larger cup and record the temperature every 30 seconds until stable. Then repeat with 200 mL hot and 100 mL cold. Students observe that the final temperature is NOT always the average — it depends on how much of each.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Temperature, Heat, and Thermal Energy. Define key terms: Temperature — a measure of the average kinetic energy of particles in a substance. Thermal energy — the TOTAL internal kinetic energy of all particles (depends on temperature, mass, and type of substance). Heat (Q) — the transfer of thermal energy from a higher-temperature object to a lower-temperature object. Heat always flows from hot to cold until thermal equilibrium is reached. Introduce the Kelvin scale: K = C + 273. Clarify: heat is energy IN TRANSIT, not a property of an object.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Temperature, Heat, and Thermal Energy. Apply to the anchoring phenomenon: The metal bench and wooden bench are the same temperature, but metal conducts heat away from your hand much faster than wood, making it feel hotter (in summer) or colder (in winter). This is about the RATE of heat transfer, not the temperature. Students explain in writing using the correct vocabulary.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Temperature, Heat, and Thermal Energy. Exit ticket: (a) A bathtub of warm water at 38 degrees C and a cup of boiling water at 100 degrees C — which has more thermal energy? Explain. (b) Define heat and explain why it is incorrect to say 'an object contains heat.' (c) Convert 25 degrees C to Kelvin.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a comparison chart: Temperature (average KE, measured with thermometer, degrees) vs. Heat (energy transfer, measured in Joules, flows hot to cold) vs. Thermal Energy (total internal KE, depends on mass and temperature). Include visual diagrams.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the mixing experiment and vocabulary development as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research the difference between temperature and thermal energy at the molecular level. Explain why gases at extremely low densities (like in outer space) can have very high temperatures but very little thermal energy.
differentiation.ell: Use the physical touch test and mixing experiment as primary learning before vocabulary. Provide a bilingual vocabulary card with particle diagrams. Use arrows to show heat flow direction.
differentiation.iep: Provide a pre-labeled diagram showing particles moving at different speeds in hot and cold objects. Simplify the exit ticket to true/false with explanation for one item. Allow verbal response.

lessons.crse_connection: Explore how different cultures developed cooking technologies based on intuitive understanding of heat transfer — the underground earth ovens (hangi) of the Maori in New Zealand, the tandoor clay ovens of South Asia, and the Korean dolsot stone pots. Discuss how these traditional cooking methods demonstrate conduction, convection, and radiation principles.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'thermal equilibrium': Heat flows from the hot water to the cold water because___. The metal bench and wooden bench are at the same temperature, but the metal feels hotter because___. When two objects are placed in contact, heat transfers until they reach the same temperature, so we say they have reached___.

vocabulary.definition: A measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a substance; measured in degrees Celsius, Fahrenheit, or Kelvin
The total internal kinetic energy of all particles in a substance; depends on temperature, mass, and substance type
The SI unit of temperature; K = C + 273; absolute zero (0 K) is the temperature at which particle motion is minimal

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Specific Heat Capacity and q = mCdeltaT. Show a thermal image of a parking lot and a lake next to each other at midday — the parking lot glows red/white (very hot) while the lake is blue/green (cool). Then show the same image at midnight — the parking lot is cool but the lake is still relatively warm. Ask: Why does water resist temperature changes while asphalt changes rapidly? explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Specific Heat Capacity and q = mCdeltaT. explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Specific Heat Capacity and q = mCdeltaT. Define specific heat capacity (C): the amount of heat needed to raise 1 kg of a substance by 1 degree C. Units: J/(kg·C). Introduce the equation: q = mC(delta T), where q = heat gained or lost, m = mass, C = specific heat, delta T = change in temperature. Water has an unusually high specific heat (4186 J/kg·C) compared to most materials. Work through three examples: (1) How much heat to raise 2 kg of water from 20 to 80 degrees C? (2) A 0.5 kg piece of iron absorbs 5000 J — what is its temperature change? (3) An unknown metal of mass 0.3 kg absorbs 1200 J and rises by 10 degrees C — what is its specific heat?

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Specific Heat Capacity and q = mCdeltaT. Application: Explain why coastal cities have milder climates than inland cities at the same latitude. The ocean's high specific heat moderates temperature swings. Students calculate: How much heat is needed to raise the temperature of a 1 m x 1 m x 1 m cube of ocean water by 1 degree C compared to the same volume of granite?

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Specific Heat Capacity and q = mCdeltaT. lessons.title: Phase Changes and Latent Heat (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: interpret a heating curve, identify phase changes, and explain why temperature remains constant during a phase change as energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds
lessons.circle_prompt: Have you ever watched ice melt in a drink? The drink stays cold for a long time while the ice is melting, but once the ice is gone, the drink warms up quickly. Why does the ice hold the temperature steady?
lessons.do_now: Water boils at 100 degrees C. If you keep heating boiling water, does it get hotter than 100 degrees C? What happens to all the energy you are adding? Sketch what you think a Temperature vs. Time graph would look like.

dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Phase Changes and Latent Heat. Show a video of molten iron being poured into a mold. Ask: The iron starts as a solid, becomes liquid when heated to 1538 degrees C, and can become gas at 2862 degrees C. At each transition, something unusual happens to the temperature. Students predict what they think happens to the temperature during a phase change.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Phase Changes and Latent Heat. Lab: Groups start with 100 g of ice at approximately -5 degrees C and heat it steadily on a hot plate. They record the temperature every 30 seconds until the water has been boiling for 2 minutes. Students plot Temperature vs. Time (the heating curve). They observe two flat regions — one at 0 degrees C (ice melting) and one at 100 degrees C (water boiling) — where temperature stops changing despite continuous heating.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Phase Changes and Latent Heat. Interpret the heating curve: five regions — heating ice, melting (flat at 0 C), heating liquid water, boiling (flat at 100 C), heating steam. During phase changes, added energy goes into breaking intermolecular bonds, NOT increasing temperature. Introduce latent heat: q = mL, where L is the heat of fusion (L_f = 334,000 J/kg for water) or heat of vaporization (L_v = 2,260,000 J/kg for water). Note: L_v is much larger than L_f because vaporization requires completely separating molecules. Work through a complete heating curve calculation: total heat to convert 0.2 kg of ice at -10 C to steam at 110 C.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Phase Changes and Latent Heat. Application: Why do burns from steam at 100 degrees C cause more severe injuries than burns from water at 100 degrees C? Students calculate the heat released when 10 g of steam at 100 C condenses on skin vs. 10 g of water at 100 C cooling on skin. The steam releases the latent heat of vaporization IN ADDITION to the heat from cooling.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Phase Changes and Latent Heat. Exit ticket: Given a heating curve for a substance, students (a) identify the melting and boiling points, (b) label each region with the phase, (c) calculate the heat needed to melt 0.5 kg of ice at 0 degrees C using q = mL_f.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a pre-labeled heating curve with five regions clearly identified. Include a formula selection guide: 'Temperature changing? Use q = mC(delta T). Phase changing? Use q = mL.' Color-code regions on the heating curve.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the ice heating experiment and all calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Calculate the complete energy budget for converting 1 kg of ice at -20 degrees C to steam at 120 degrees C (five separate calculations). Create a stacked bar chart showing what fraction of the total energy goes to each step.
differentiation.ell: Use the hands-on experiment with real-time graphing as primary learning. Provide a bilingual heating curve diagram with phase labels in both languages. Use color-coding for each phase region.
differentiation.iep: Provide a pre-drawn heating curve template with axes labeled. Break the multi-step heating curve calculation into separate worksheet sections, one per region. Allow formula card use.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how understanding phase changes has practical applications in communities — from salting roads in winter (lowering the freezing point to prevent ice) to evaporative cooling used in traditional pot-in-pot refrigerators (zeer pots) in Nigeria and other parts of Africa, enabling food preservation in communities without electricity.

Steam at 100 degrees C causes more severe burns than water at 100 degrees C, so hospitals treat steam burns as___.

cer.claim_starter: Based on the three methods of heat transfer, I claim that House B is more energy efficient because its design features reduce conduction, convection, and radiation losses, specifically...

lessons.title: Calorimetry and Conservation of Energy in Thermal Systems (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: apply conservation of energy to calorimetry problems, calculating the final temperature when two substances at different temperatures are combined in an insulated system
lessons.circle_prompt: If you drop a hot stone into a bucket of cold water, the stone cools down and the water warms up. Will they ever reach the same temperature? How could you predict what that final temperature will be?
lessons.do_now: A 0.5 kg piece of iron at 200 degrees C is placed in 2.0 kg of water at 20 degrees C. Without calculating, predict: Will the final temperature be closer to 200 or closer to 20? Explain your reasoning using what you know about specific heat.

dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

materials: Calorimeters (Styrofoam cup nesting sets, 1 per group)
Various metal samples (aluminum, copper, iron — known masses)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Calorimetry and Conservation of Energy in Thermal Systems. Present the conservation of energy principle applied to thermal systems: in an insulated (closed) system, the heat lost by the hot object equals the heat gained by the cold object. Q_lost = Q_gained. No energy disappears — it just transfers. Show a diagram of a calorimeter and explain why we use insulated cups (to minimize heat loss to the environment).

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Calorimetry and Conservation of Energy in Thermal Systems. Calorimetry lab: Groups heat a metal sample (known mass, known material) in boiling water to 100 degrees C. They quickly transfer the metal to a calorimeter containing a known mass of room-temperature water. They record the initial water temperature and the final equilibrium temperature. Using Q_lost = Q_gained: m_metal × C_metal × (T_initial,metal - T_final) = m_water × C_water × (T_final - T_initial,water). Students solve for C_metal and compare to the accepted value from the Reference Table.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Calorimetry and Conservation of Energy in Thermal Systems. Formalize the calorimetry equation: Q_hot = Q_cold, or m_1 C_1 (T_1 - T_f) = m_2 C_2 (T_f - T_2). Note the sign convention: Q_lost is positive when written as (T_initial - T_final) for the hot object. Work through two examples: (1) 0.3 kg of copper at 150 degrees C is placed in 0.5 kg of water at 22 degrees C — find T_final. (2) An unknown metal of 0.2 kg at 95 degrees C is placed in 0.4 kg of water at 20 degrees C. T_final = 23 degrees C. Find C_metal and identify the metal.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Calorimetry and Conservation of Energy in Thermal Systems. Error analysis: Students calculate percent error between their experimental specific heat and the accepted value. Class discusses sources of error: heat lost to the cup and air, imprecise temperature readings, water splashing, metal not fully at 100 degrees C. Students suggest improvements to minimize each error.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Calorimetry and Conservation of Energy in Thermal Systems. Exit ticket: 0.8 kg of water at 90 degrees C is mixed with 1.2 kg of water at 10 degrees C in an insulated container. (a) Set up the conservation of energy equation. (b) Solve for the final temperature. (c) Explain why the final temperature is NOT 50 degrees C (the average).

differentiation.approaching: Provide a calorimetry problem-solving template: Step 1 — Write Q_lost = Q_gained. Step 2 — Expand: m_1 C_1 (T_1 - T_f) = m_2 C_2 (T_f - T_2). Step 3 — Plug in known values. Step 4 — Solve for the unknown. Include a worked example alongside.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the calorimetry lab and all practice problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Design a calorimetry experiment to determine the heat of fusion of ice. Students write a procedure, identify what to measure, and derive the equation needed. Discuss how this technique is used in food science to measure calories in food.
differentiation.ell: Use the hands-on calorimetry lab as primary learning. Provide a step-by-step lab procedure with diagrams. Use a bilingual variable identification guide. Allow partner work on calculations.
differentiation.iep: Provide a pre-set-up equation with blanks to fill in for each problem. Focus on water-water mixing problems before introducing metal-water problems. Allow formula card and calculator use throughout.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how calorimetry is used in nutrition science — the calorie content of food is measured by burning food samples in a bomb calorimeter and measuring the heat released. Explore how Wilbur Olin Atwater, an American chemist, developed the system for measuring food energy that is still used on nutrition labels today, and discuss food access and nutrition equity in underserved communities.

lessons.title: Entropy and Unit 7 Review (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: explain that entropy is a measure of disorder in a system and that natural processes tend toward increasing entropy, and apply all Unit 7 concepts to solve problems
lessons.circle_prompt: Your room naturally gets messy over time — you have to put in effort to clean it up. Does the physical world work the same way? Can you think of anything in nature that spontaneously becomes more organized without energy input?
lessons.do_now: An ice cube melts in a warm room. This is a natural process. The reverse — water spontaneously freezing in a warm room — never happens. Why not? Both processes conserve energy. What additional principle determines which direction processes go?

dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer
PS3.D: Energy in Chemical Processes and Everyday Life

materials: Food coloring and beakers of water (for diffusion demo)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Entropy and Unit 7 Review. Demonstration: Place a single drop of food coloring in a beaker of still water. Students watch it slowly diffuse throughout the entire beaker. Ask: Will the food coloring ever spontaneously gather back into a single drop? Why not? Conservation of energy allows it — but something else prevents it. Introduce entropy as the reason.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Entropy and Unit 7 Review. Students are given 10 coins. They start with all coins heads up (ordered state) and shake the container. After each shake, they count how many are heads and how many are tails. Repeat 20 times. Graph the results. Students observe that the system quickly moves toward ~50/50 and almost never returns to all heads. This models how systems naturally move toward more probable (disordered) states.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Entropy and Unit 7 Review. Introduce the Second Law of Thermodynamics: In any natural process, the total entropy of a system and its surroundings always increases. Entropy is a measure of the number of possible arrangements of a system — more arrangements = higher entropy = more disorder. Heat naturally flows from hot to cold because this increases total entropy. Refrigerators and air conditioners can move heat from cold to hot, but only by doing work and increasing entropy elsewhere. This is why perpetual motion machines are impossible and why no engine can be 100% efficient.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Entropy and Unit 7 Review. Unit 7 review: Students work through a set of mixed problems covering q = mC(delta T), q = mL, calorimetry, heating curves, and heat transfer identification. Focus on Regents-style problems that combine multiple concepts.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Entropy and Unit 7 Review. Exit ticket: (a) Explain in your own words why heat flows from hot to cold and not the reverse, using the concept of entropy. (b) Quick calculation: How much total heat is needed to convert 0.1 kg of ice at 0 degrees C to water at 40 degrees C?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a simplified entropy explanation: 'Things naturally spread out and mix. It takes energy to put them back in order.' Focus on the qualitative understanding rather than calculations. For review, provide a formula summary sheet organized by problem type.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the entropy activities and review problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research the connection between entropy and information theory. Explain Maxwell's Demon thought experiment and why it does not actually violate the Second Law. Calculate the entropy change for a simple heat transfer problem.
differentiation.ell: Use the coin demonstration and food coloring demo as primary learning. Provide visual before/after diagrams for entropy concepts. For review, include diagrams with all problems.
differentiation.iep: Focus entropy understanding on the qualitative level — 'disorder increases naturally.' For review, provide a problem-type identification guide: 'If temperature changes, use q = mC delta T. If phase changes, use q = mL. If two objects mix, use Q_lost = Q_gained.' Allow formula card use.

cer.phenomenon: A power plant burns coal at 600 degrees C to produce steam that drives a turbine, generating electricity. The overall efficiency is about 33% — for every 100 J of chemical energy in coal, only 33 J becomes electrical energy and 67 J is released as waste heat to the environment at around 30 degrees C. Engineers have tried for over a century to improve this efficiency but have never exceeded approximately 60% for any heat engine.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the Second Law of Thermodynamics, I claim that the maximum efficiency of any heat engine is fundamentally limited and can never reach 100% because...
cer.evidence_source: Apply the concept of entropy to explain why waste heat is an inevitable byproduct of converting thermal energy to work. Discuss how the temperature difference between the heat source and the environment limits efficiency.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the Second Law requires that total entropy must ___ in any real process. Converting 100% of heat to work would mean ___ entropy change, which violates ___. The waste heat at ___ degrees C carries the entropy that must be ___ to satisfy the Second Law.

units.title: Waves & Sound
units.anchoring_phenomenon: At a concert, you can hear the bass guitar from behind a pillar, but you cannot see the guitarist. Sound bends around obstacles easily, but light does not seem to. Both are waves — why do they behave so differently?
essential_questions: What are the properties that define and describe waves?
How do waves behave when they encounter boundaries, other waves, or different media?
How does the wave nature of sound explain the phenomena we hear every day?
units.crse_theme: Students explore wave physics through the lens of sound and music across cultures — the physics of instruments from the West African djembe to the Indian sitar to the Caribbean steel drum, how acoustic engineering shapes concert halls and recording studios, and the contributions of scientists like Maryam Mirzakhani (wave equations on surfaces) and Daniel Hale Williams (ultrasound applications in medicine).

formative: Exit tickets on wave calculations (v = f lambda)

investigations: Investigation 5: Determining the Speed of Sound

lessons.title: Wave Types and Properties (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: classify waves as transverse or longitudinal, identify wave properties (wavelength, frequency, period, amplitude), and calculate wave speed using v = f(lambda)
lessons.circle_prompt: What's the loudest sound you have ever heard? Where were you? Did you feel it in your body, or just hear it? What do you think was actually happening in the air to create that sound?
lessons.do_now: A wave on a string has a wavelength of 0.5 m and a frequency of 4 Hz. Sketch two complete wavelengths and calculate the wave speed. If the frequency doubles, what happens to the wavelength (assuming speed stays constant)?
materials: Long ropes or springs (1 per group)
Wave machine or wave demonstration spring

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Wave Types and Properties. Demonstration: Create a transverse wave on a long rope by shaking one end side to side. Then create a longitudinal wave on a Slinky by pushing and pulling one end. Ask: What do these have in common? (Both transfer energy without transferring matter.) What is different? (Direction of vibration vs. direction of travel.) Students identify which type each is.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Wave Types and Properties. Slinky lab: In pairs, students create transverse waves and longitudinal waves on a Slinky stretched across the floor. They measure wavelength (distance between consecutive crests or compressions) and frequency (count waves passing a point in 10 seconds, divide by 10). They vary the frequency by shaking faster or slower and observe how wavelength changes. Students calculate wave speed v = f(lambda) for each trial.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Wave Types and Properties. Formalize wave vocabulary: A wave is a disturbance that transfers energy through matter or space. Transverse waves: particles vibrate perpendicular to wave direction (examples: light, string waves, water surface waves). Longitudinal waves: particles vibrate parallel to wave direction (examples: sound, compression waves in a Slinky). Properties: wavelength (lambda) — distance of one complete cycle; frequency (f) — number of cycles per second (Hz); period (T) — time for one complete cycle (T = 1/f); amplitude — maximum displacement from rest position. Wave equation: v = f(lambda). Work through three examples using the Physics Reference Table.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Wave Types and Properties. Application: A radio station broadcasts at 98.5 MHz. All electromagnetic waves travel at 3.0 x 10^8 m/s. Calculate the wavelength of this radio wave. Then: A sound wave in air (v = 343 m/s) has a wavelength of 0.77 m. Calculate its frequency. What note does this correspond to? (Approximately A above middle C, 440 Hz.)

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Wave Types and Properties. Exit ticket: (a) A wave has a period of 0.02 s. Calculate its frequency. (b) If the wave speed is 340 m/s, calculate the wavelength. (c) Is this wave transverse or longitudinal if it is a sound wave? Explain.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a wave vocabulary visual reference card with a labeled diagram showing wavelength, amplitude, crest, trough, and equilibrium. Include the v = f(lambda) triangle (like the F = ma triangle). Provide the relationship T = 1/f on the card.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the Slinky lab and all wave calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research the electromagnetic spectrum and create a scale showing frequency, wavelength, and wave speed for different types of EM waves. Explain why all EM waves travel at the same speed in vacuum but sound speed depends on the medium.
differentiation.ell: Use the physical Slinky demonstrations as primary learning. Provide a bilingual wave vocabulary card with labeled diagrams. Use color-coding: red = transverse, blue = longitudinal throughout all materials.
differentiation.iep: Provide a wave property identification guide with visual cues. Break calculations into single-step problems with formula reminders. Allow use of the v = f(lambda) triangle card on assessments.

lessons.crse_connection: Explore the physics of sound and music across cultures — how the West African djembe drum produces deep bass tones through low-frequency vibrations of its goatskin head, how the Indian sitar uses sympathetic strings that resonate without being plucked, and how Caribbean steel drums are tuned by hammering different areas of a steel oil drum to different thicknesses, creating specific notes.
