lessons.title: The Electromagnetic Spectrum and Photon Energy (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: identify the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum by frequency and wavelength, calculate photon energy using E = hf, and explain the dual nature of light
lessons.circle_prompt: You cannot see radio waves, microwaves, ultraviolet, or X-rays, but they are all around you right now. What invisible waves are passing through this room at this moment? How do we know they are there if we cannot see them?
lessons.do_now: Visible light has wavelengths from about 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red). Calculate the frequency of red light and violet light. Which has more energy per photon? Use v = f(lambda) and E = hf.
materials: EM spectrum poster or reference chart

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: The Electromagnetic Spectrum and Photon Energy. Give each student a UV-reactive bead. Under indoor lighting, the beads are white. Take students near a window or under a UV lamp — the beads change color dramatically. Ask: What invisible radiation is causing this? Can you feel the UV light? Introduce the electromagnetic spectrum — visible light is only a tiny fraction of the full range of electromagnetic radiation.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: The Electromagnetic Spectrum and Photon Energy. Students use diffraction gratings to observe the spectra of different light sources: incandescent (continuous rainbow), fluorescent (discrete bright lines), LED (narrow band of color). They match the colors to approximate wavelengths using a reference. Then students calculate the frequency and photon energy for each color using v = f(lambda) (with v = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s) and E = hf (with h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J·s). They discover that violet/blue light has the highest energy and red has the lowest.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: The Electromagnetic Spectrum and Photon Energy. Present the full EM spectrum in order of increasing frequency: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma ray. ALL are electromagnetic waves traveling at c = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s in vacuum. They differ only in frequency and wavelength. Higher frequency = shorter wavelength = higher photon energy. Photon energy: E = hf, where h = 6.63 x 10^-34 J·s (Planck's constant). Introduce wave-particle duality: light sometimes behaves as a wave (diffraction, interference) and sometimes as a particle (photoelectric effect, discrete photon energies). Connect to HS-PS4-3: for some phenomena the wave model is more useful, for others the particle model is.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: The Electromagnetic Spectrum and Photon Energy. Application: (1) Calculate the photon energy of a dental X-ray (frequency 3.0 x 10^18 Hz) and a radio wave (frequency 1.0 x 10^6 Hz). Compare and explain why X-rays can damage cells but radio waves cannot. (2) Connect to the Regents HS-PS4-4 PLD: Evaluate claims about how different frequencies of EM radiation affect matter — UV causes sunburn, microwaves heat water, infrared is felt as warmth.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: The Electromagnetic Spectrum and Photon Energy. Exit ticket: (a) Arrange in order from lowest to highest energy: X-ray, visible light, radio wave, microwave, gamma ray. (b) Calculate the energy of a photon with wavelength 500 nm (green light). (c) Explain one situation where the wave model of light is more useful and one where the particle model is more useful.

differentiation.approaching: Provide an EM spectrum reference strip showing all regions with frequency, wavelength, and energy increasing in the correct direction. Include the equation E = hf with a worked example. Provide a 'wave or particle?' decision guide.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the spectral observation and all photon energy calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research the photoelectric effect and explain why Einstein received the Nobel Prize for demonstrating light's particle nature. Calculate the minimum photon frequency needed to eject an electron from sodium (work function 2.28 eV). Explain why red light cannot produce the photoelectric effect in sodium but ultraviolet can.
differentiation.ell: Use the UV bead demonstration and diffraction grating observations as primary learning. Provide a visual EM spectrum chart with bilingual labels and familiar examples for each type of radiation. Use consistent color-coding matching the visible spectrum.
differentiation.iep: Provide a pre-filled EM spectrum chart for reference. Focus on qualitative relationships (higher frequency = higher energy) before calculations. Break E = hf calculations into step-by-step guides. Allow formula and spectrum reference cards.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how different communities experience EM radiation exposure differently — from UV radiation risk in high-altitude equatorial communities to concerns about cell tower radiation in urban neighborhoods. Highlight Chien-Shiung Wu, a Chinese-American physicist whose experiments on beta decay contributed to our understanding of particle physics and the electromagnetic interaction. Connect to how EM spectrum knowledge empowers communities to evaluate health claims about radiation.

cer.claim_starter: Based on the relationship between EM radiation frequency, photon energy, and matter interactions, I claim that people at high altitudes face greater skin cancer risk because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the photon energy of UV-B radiation (frequency ~1 x 10^15 Hz). Compare to visible light photon energy. Explain how the thinner atmosphere at high altitude affects UV transmission.

lessons.title: Wave-Particle Duality and Unit 9 Review (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: evaluate claims about whether the wave or particle model better describes a given phenomenon, and solve review problems integrating all optics concepts
lessons.circle_prompt: Is light a wave or a particle? What if the answer is 'both' — how can something be two different things at the same time? Is there anything else in your life that seems to be two things at once depending on how you look at it?
lessons.do_now: Light shining through a narrow slit creates a diffraction pattern on a screen (wave behavior). The same light shining on a metal surface ejects electrons one at a time (particle behavior). How can light do both? Which model should we use when?
materials: Review problem sets covering all optics topics (printed)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Wave-Particle Duality and Unit 9 Review. Present three phenomena: (1) Double-slit interference pattern (wave). (2) Photoelectric effect — red light does not eject electrons from a metal but violet light does, regardless of intensity (particle). (3) A solar cell converts sunlight to electricity (particle absorption). For each, students decide: wave model or particle model? Establish that both models are needed and neither is wrong — they are complementary descriptions of the same reality.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Wave-Particle Duality and Unit 9 Review. Students work through a set of scenario cards. For each scenario, they identify which model (wave or particle) better explains it and provide reasoning: diffraction of light around an obstacle (wave), X-ray imaging showing photon absorption (particle), fiber optic total internal reflection (wave), photovoltaic cell converting photons to current (particle), radio antenna receiving broadcast (wave), fluorescence of atoms emitting specific photon energies (particle).

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Wave-Particle Duality and Unit 9 Review. Summarize wave-particle duality: phenomena involving propagation, interference, diffraction, and refraction are best described by the wave model. Phenomena involving emission, absorption, and energy quantization are best described by the particle model. Connect to the PLDs for HS-PS4-3: 'for some situations one model of electromagnetic radiation (wave or particle) is more useful than the other.' Neither model is complete alone — this is a fundamental aspect of quantum physics.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Wave-Particle Duality and Unit 9 Review. Unit 9 review: Comprehensive problem set covering law of reflection, plane mirrors, curved mirror ray diagrams and equations, Snell's law, total internal reflection, converging and diverging lens ray diagrams and equations, EM spectrum identification, photon energy calculations, and wave-particle duality reasoning. Focus on Regents-style question formats.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Wave-Particle Duality and Unit 9 Review. Exit ticket: (a) A beam of light passes through a narrow slit and spreads out. Which model explains this? (b) UV light causes a sunburn but visible light does not. Which model explains this? (c) Quick calculation: A concave mirror has f = 12 cm. An object is at d_o = 18 cm. Find d_i and describe the image.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a wave vs. particle model decision flowchart: 'Does it involve bending, spreading, or interfering? -> Wave model. Does it involve absorbing, emitting, or energy thresholds? -> Particle model.' Include a unit review formula sheet.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the scenario card activity and review problems as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research de Broglie's hypothesis — that matter also has wave properties — and calculate the wavelength of an electron moving at 1 x 10^6 m/s. Explain why we do not observe wave behavior for everyday objects like baseballs.
differentiation.ell: Use visual scenario cards with diagrams for each phenomenon. Provide bilingual model comparison chart. For review, provide problems with diagrams and visual supports.
differentiation.iep: Simplify wave vs. particle to a matching activity. For review, provide a topic-by-topic formula and concept summary with one example per topic. Allow formula card and calculator use.

lessons.crse_connection: Reflect on the diverse scientists encountered throughout the unit: Ibn al-Haytham's foundational work on optics, Shirley Ann Jackson's contributions to fiber optics and solar cells, and Chien-Shiung Wu's experimental brilliance. Discuss how scientific understanding is built through contributions from people of many cultures and backgrounds, and how ensuring diverse participation in science leads to better outcomes for all communities.
lessons.hochman_activity: Summary writing: Students write a 4-sentence paragraph comparing the wave and particle models of light. Sentence 1: Describe one phenomenon explained by the wave model. Sentence 2: Describe one phenomenon explained by the particle model. Sentence 3: Explain wave-particle duality. Sentence 4: Give a real-world application that depends on understanding both models.

vocabulary.definition: The fundamental concept that electromagnetic radiation exhibits both wave and particle properties; the appropriate model depends on the phenomenon
The smallest discrete unit of energy; a photon is a quantum of electromagnetic energy

cer.phenomenon: In a double-slit experiment, laser light passes through two narrow slits and creates an interference pattern of bright and dark bands on a screen (wave behavior). When the light intensity is reduced so that only one photon passes through at a time, each photon lands at a specific point on the screen (particle behavior). After thousands of individual photons are detected, the same interference pattern emerges.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the results of the single-photon double-slit experiment, I claim that light is neither purely a wave nor purely a particle, but exhibits both properties simultaneously, because...
cer.evidence_source: Describe how individual photon detections (particle property) collectively build up an interference pattern (wave property). Explain why this result cannot be explained by either model alone.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because each photon arrives at a ___ point on the screen (particle behavior), yet the probability of where it lands follows the ___ pattern predicted by the wave model. This means each individual photon somehow 'knows' about ___ slits, suggesting it behaves as a ___ when propagating but as a ___ when detected.

lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can explain total internal reflection and describe how it enables fiber optic technology.
lessons.circle_prompt: How does your internet get to your home? Has anyone seen a fiber optic cable?
lessons.do_now: When light passes from water to air, it bends away from the normal. What happens if the angle of incidence keeps increasing? At what point does the light stop leaving the water?

engage.description: Demo: Shine a laser into a semicircular glass block. Gradually increase the angle of incidence until the light no longer exits — it reflects back inside. Students observe the critical angle.

explore.description: Investigation: Students find the critical angle for glass-to-air by gradually increasing incidence angle. Then observe light traveling through a curved stream of water (light pipe demo).

explain.description: Define total internal reflection and critical angle. Explain conditions: light must travel from more dense to less dense medium, angle must exceed critical angle. Connect to fiber optics.

elaborate.description: Application: Students research and discuss how fiber optics transmit internet data. Calculate critical angles using Snell's law for different material pairs.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: Explain why diamonds sparkle using total internal reflection; calculate the critical angle for diamond (n=2.42).

differentiation.approaching: Provide step-by-step critical angle calculation using Snell's law with sin(θc) = n2/n1; visual diagram of TIR conditions.
differentiation.on_level: Complete investigation, calculate critical angles, and explain fiber optic applications.
differentiation.advanced: Research and present on medical applications of fiber optics (endoscopy); calculate how many reflections light makes in a 1 km fiber.
differentiation.ell: Visual diagram showing refraction → critical angle → total internal reflection progression with bilingual labels.
differentiation.iep: Focus on qualitative understanding of TIR; hands-on fiber optic cable demo; simplified calculation with support.

lessons.crse_connection: Shirley Ann Jackson — first African American woman to earn a PhD from MIT. Her telecommunications research contributed to the development of fiber optics, touch-tone phones, and solar cells.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So using 'total internal reflection': Light reflects back into the glass instead of refracting because___. Both reflection and refraction involve light hitting a boundary, but___. Fiber optic cables are made of glass with a higher index of refraction than the cladding, so___.

vocabulary.definition: The complete reflection of light at a boundary when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle
The minimum angle of incidence at which total internal reflection occurs
Thin glass or plastic fibers that transmit light signals using total internal reflection

lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can explain how objects get their color through absorption, reflection, and transmission of light.
lessons.circle_prompt: What's your favorite color? Have you ever wondered why that object appears that color?
lessons.do_now: A white T-shirt appears white in sunlight. What color would it appear under only red light? What about a blue T-shirt under red light?

engage.description: Demo: Shine white light through a prism to show the visible spectrum. Then use color filters to isolate colors. Place colored objects under filtered light — students observe color changes.

explore.description: Investigation: Students view different colored objects through different color filters. Record what color each object appears. Build a model explaining why objects appear different colors under different lighting.

explain.description: Explain selective absorption and reflection. White objects reflect all colors. Black absorbs all. A red object reflects red and absorbs other colors. Under blue light, a red object appears black (no red to reflect).

elaborate.description: Application: Stage lighting design — students plan colored lighting for a school performance, predicting how costumes will appear under different lights.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket: Explain why a yellow banana appears black under blue light.

differentiation.approaching: Color absorption/reflection chart provided; guided data table for filter observations; visual model template.
differentiation.on_level: Complete investigation, build explanatory model, and predict color appearances independently.
differentiation.advanced: Explain additive vs subtractive color mixing; design a color filter combination to produce specific colors.
differentiation.ell: Color-labeled diagrams showing absorption/reflection; visual explanation cards; hands-on exploration prioritized.
differentiation.iep: Focus on hands-on filter exploration with partner; simplified recording sheet; verbal explanation accepted.

units.title: Nuclear Physics
units.anchoring_phenomenon: The Sun produces enough energy every second to power human civilization for 500,000 years, yet it has been burning for 4.6 billion years without any chemical fuel. What process could possibly produce this much energy for this long?
essential_questions: What holds the nucleus together, and what happens when it breaks apart?
How do we use radioactive decay to determine the age of objects and diagnose diseases?
How does E = mc^2 explain the enormous energy released in nuclear processes?
units.crse_theme: Students explore nuclear physics through its profound impacts on human society — the science of nuclear energy and weapons, the debate over nuclear power in communities (Fukushima, Three Mile Island, and environmental justice in siting of nuclear facilities), contributions of Lise Meitner to the discovery of fission, and applications in medicine and archaeology.

formative: Exit tickets on decay equations and half-life calculations

lessons.title: Nuclear Structure, Stability, and Radioactive Decay (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: describe the structure of the nucleus, identify the three types of radioactive decay (alpha, beta, gamma), and write balanced nuclear equations
lessons.circle_prompt: Radioactivity is a word that can sound scary. Where have you heard it before — movies, news, science class? What do you already know about it, and what questions do you have?
lessons.do_now: Carbon-14 is radioactive and slowly decays over time. Carbon-12 is stable and does not decay. Both have 6 protons. What is different about their nuclei? Why might having extra neutrons make a nucleus unstable?
materials: Colored beads or balls (red for protons, blue for neutrons)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Nuclear Structure, Stability, and Radioactive Decay. Show a smoke detector — inside is a tiny amount of Americium-241, a radioactive element. It saves thousands of lives every year. Then show a medical PET scan image — radioactive tracers reveal brain activity. Radioactivity is not just about bombs and disasters — it has everyday applications that benefit society. Today we learn what radioactivity actually is at the nuclear level.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Nuclear Structure, Stability, and Radioactive Decay. Model building: Students use colored beads to build nuclei of several isotopes: H-1, H-2, H-3, He-4, C-12, C-14, U-235, U-238. They count protons (atomic number) and neutrons (mass number - atomic number). For each, they research whether it is stable or radioactive. Students look for patterns: very heavy nuclei tend to be unstable, nuclei with too many or too few neutrons relative to protons tend to be unstable.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Nuclear Structure, Stability, and Radioactive Decay. The strong nuclear force holds the nucleus together, overcoming proton-proton electrostatic repulsion. Unstable nuclei undergo radioactive decay to reach a more stable configuration. Three types: Alpha decay — nucleus emits a helium-4 nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons); reduces atomic number by 2 and mass number by 4. Beta decay — a neutron converts to a proton, emitting an electron (beta particle); increases atomic number by 1, mass number unchanged. Gamma decay — nucleus releases energy as a high-energy photon; no change in atomic number or mass number. Nuclear equations must balance: total mass numbers and total atomic numbers are conserved. Work through examples of each type.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Nuclear Structure, Stability, and Radioactive Decay. Students write balanced nuclear equations for: (1) Alpha decay of U-238. (2) Beta decay of C-14. (3) Alpha decay of Ra-226. They identify the daughter nucleus in each case using the periodic table. Then students rank the three types of radiation by penetrating power (alpha < beta < gamma) and ionizing ability (alpha > beta > gamma).

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Nuclear Structure, Stability, and Radioactive Decay. Exit ticket: (a) Write the balanced nuclear equation for the alpha decay of Po-210. (b) What type of decay increases the atomic number by 1 without changing the mass number? (c) Which type of radiation is stopped by a sheet of paper? Which requires lead or thick concrete?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a nuclear decay reference card showing the three types with particle symbols, mass number change, and atomic number change in a table. Include worked examples of balanced nuclear equations for each type.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the model building and nuclear equation balancing as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research the decay chain of U-238, which undergoes 14 sequential decays before becoming stable Pb-206. Identify each decay type in the chain. Calculate the total number of alpha and beta particles emitted.
differentiation.ell: Use the physical bead models as primary learning. Provide a visual decay diagram with bilingual labels showing the particle emitted and the changes in atomic and mass number for each decay type.
differentiation.iep: Provide a nuclear equation balancing template: 'Top numbers (mass) must add up the same on both sides. Bottom numbers (atomic) must add up the same.' Include a worked example alongside each problem. Allow periodic table use.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss Lise Meitner, an Austrian-Swedish physicist who was the first to correctly explain nuclear fission in 1939. Despite her critical contribution, only her male colleague Otto Hahn received the Nobel Prize. Meitner, who was Jewish, had fled Nazi Germany. Element 109, Meitnerium, was later named in her honor. Connect to the broader theme of how scientific credit has historically been denied to women and minorities.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'radioactive decay': Carbon-14 undergoes beta decay because___. Alpha particles and beta particles are both emitted during radioactive decay, but alpha particles are much more massive because___. A Geiger counter detected radiation from the sample, so the scientist concluded that___.

vocabulary.definition: The spontaneous emission of particles or energy from an unstable nucleus to reach a more stable configuration
High-energy electromagnetic radiation emitted from the nucleus; no change in atomic or mass number; highest penetrating power

cer.phenomenon: A nuclear medicine technician prepares three radioactive sources for different medical procedures. Source A (alpha emitter) is used in targeted cancer treatment by placing it directly on tumor cells. Source B (beta emitter) is injected into the bloodstream for thyroid treatment. Source C (gamma emitter) is used for external imaging scans where radiation must pass through the body to reach detectors outside.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the properties of each type of radiation, I claim that each source is matched to its medical application because of the differences in penetrating power and ionizing ability, specifically...
cer.evidence_source: Compare the penetrating power and ionizing ability of alpha, beta, and gamma radiation. Explain why each type is suited for its specific medical application.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because alpha particles have ___ penetrating power but ___ ionizing ability, making them ideal for destroying ___ cells. Beta particles can travel through ___ but not through ___. Gamma rays have ___ penetrating power, allowing them to pass through the ___ and be detected externally.

lessons.title: Half-Life Calculations and Applications (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: calculate the amount of a radioactive substance remaining after a given number of half-lives and use half-life data to determine the age of a sample
lessons.circle_prompt: How do scientists know that a dinosaur fossil is 65 million years old or that an Egyptian artifact is 3,000 years old? They cannot go back in time to check. What kind of 'clock' could nature provide?
lessons.do_now: A sample contains 100 g of a radioactive isotope with a half-life of 10 years. How much remains after 10 years? After 20 years? After 30 years? Graph the amount remaining vs. time. What pattern do you see?
materials: Pennies or M&Ms (100 per group, for half-life simulation)
Half-life data table (from Physics Reference Table)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Half-Life Calculations and Applications. Show an image of the Shroud of Turin. In 1988, radiocarbon dating showed the cloth dated to approximately 1260-1390 CE, suggesting it was medieval, not from the time of Jesus. This finding used C-14 half-life (5,730 years). Ask: How can measuring the amount of one isotope tell you when something was made? Students discuss.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Half-Life Calculations and Applications. Half-life simulation: Each group starts with 100 pennies (representing radioactive atoms). They shake the cup and pour out the pennies. Any penny showing tails has 'decayed' and is removed. They count the remaining heads (undecayed atoms) and record. Repeat for 10 'half-lives.' Students graph Number Remaining vs. Half-Life Number. They observe the exponential decay curve and calculate the fraction remaining after each half-life (1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16...).

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Half-Life Calculations and Applications. Half-life (t_1/2): the time for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. After n half-lives, the fraction remaining = (1/2)^n. Amount remaining = initial amount x (1/2)^n. Carbon-14 dating: living organisms absorb C-14 from the atmosphere. When they die, C-14 decays with t_1/2 = 5,730 years. By measuring the ratio of C-14 to C-12, scientists determine how many half-lives have elapsed and therefore the age. Work through examples: (1) A sample started with 80 g; 10 g remain. How many half-lives have elapsed? (2) A bone has 1/8 of its original C-14. How old is it?

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Half-Life Calculations and Applications. Application problems: (1) Iodine-131 (t_1/2 = 8 days) is used in thyroid treatment. A patient receives 200 micrograms. How much remains after 24 days? (2) A rock contains uranium-238 (t_1/2 = 4.5 billion years). Analysis shows 75% of the original U-238 has decayed to lead-206. How old is the rock? (3) Why can't C-14 dating be used for objects older than about 50,000 years?

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Half-Life Calculations and Applications. Exit ticket: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 20 minutes. Starting with 64 g: (a) How much remains after 1 hour? (b) How many half-lives have elapsed after 2 hours? (c) What fraction of the original sample remains after 2 hours?

differentiation.approaching: Provide a half-life calculation table template: columns for Half-Life Number (0, 1, 2, 3...), Time Elapsed, Fraction Remaining (1, 1/2, 1/4...), Amount Remaining. Include a visual halving diagram.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the penny simulation and all half-life calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Derive the continuous decay equation N = N_0 e^(-lambda t) and show it is equivalent to N = N_0 (1/2)^(t/t_1/2). Use it to calculate the amount remaining at non-integer numbers of half-lives.
differentiation.ell: Use the penny simulation as primary learning before calculations. Provide a bilingual half-life vocabulary card with a visual decay curve. Use a step-by-step number line showing each half-life.
differentiation.iep: Provide a half-life counting table pre-set-up with the halving pattern shown for the first few rows. Focus on counting half-lives before calculating amounts. Allow use of the table method rather than formula for assessments.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how radiocarbon dating has been used to correct historical narratives — dating Indigenous settlements in the Americas to much earlier than previously believed by European scholars, confirming oral histories of First Nations peoples. Also discuss how carbon dating of artifacts from the Kingdom of Aksum in Ethiopia revealed it was one of the most advanced civilizations of the ancient world, challenging Eurocentric historical narratives.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'half-life': After three half-lives, only 1/8 of the original radioactive sample remains because___. Carbon-14 dating works well for artifacts up to 50,000 years old, but for older samples it does not work because___. The bone sample contained 25% of its original C-14, so the scientist calculated that the bone was approximately___.

vocabulary.definition: The time required for half of the radioactive atoms in a sample to decay; a constant for each isotope, unaffected by temperature or pressure
A pattern where a quantity decreases by the same fraction in each equal time interval; described by N = N_0 (1/2)^n

materials: Pennies or M&Ms (100 per group, for half-life simulation)

engage.description: Brief review of Day 1 concepts through a warm-up problem or quick discussion. Building on previous days: Show an image of the Shroud of Turin. In 1988, radiocarbon dating showed the cloth dated to approximately 1260-1390 CE, suggesting it was medieval, not from the time of Jesus. This finding used C-14 half-life (5,730 years). Ask: How can measuring the amount of one isotope tell you when something was made? Students discuss.

explore.description: Students work through practice problems or applications in pairs or small groups. Building on previous days: Half-life simulation: Each group starts with 100 pennies (representing radioactive atoms). They shake the cup and pour out the pennies. Any penny showing tails has 'decayed' and is removed. They count the remaining heads (undecayed atoms) and record. Repeat for 10 'half-lives.' Students graph Number Remaining vs. Half-Life Number. They observe the exponential decay curve and calculate the fraction remaining after each half-life (1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16...).

explain.description: Address common misconceptions from practice; model problem-solving strategies. Building on previous days: Half-life (t_1/2): the time for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. After n half-lives, the fraction remaining = (1/2)^n. Amount remaining = initial amount x (1/2)^n. Carbon-14 dating: living organisms absorb C-14 from the atmosphere. When they die, C-14 decays with t_1/2 = 5,730 years. By measuring the ratio of C-14 to C-12, scientists determine how many half-lives have elapsed and therefore the age. Work through examples: (1) A sample started with 80 g; 10 g remain. How many half-lives have elapsed? (2) A bone has 1/8 of its original C-14. How old is it?

elaborate.description: CER activity connecting evidence to claims about the topic. Building on previous days: Application problems: (1) Iodine-131 (t_1/2 = 8 days) is used in thyroid treatment. A patient receives 200 micrograms. How much remains after 24 days? (2) A rock contains uranium-238 (t_1/2 = 4.5 billion years). Analysis shows 75% of the original U-238 has decayed to lead-206. How old is the rock? (3) Why can't C-14 dating be used for objects older than about 50,000 years?

evaluate.description: Exit ticket with application-level problems requiring multi-step reasoning. Building on previous days: Exit ticket: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 20 minutes. Starting with 64 g: (a) How much remains after 1 hour? (b) How many half-lives have elapsed after 2 hours? (c) What fraction of the original sample remains after 2 hours?

differentiation.approaching: Review key concepts from the full sequence before assessment. Provide a half-life calculation table template: columns for Half-Life Number (0, 1, 2, 3...), Time Elapsed, Fraction Remaining (1, 1/2, 1/4...), Amount Remaining. Include a visual halving diagram.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the penny simulation and all half-life calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Complete extension challenge connecting to real-world applications. Derive the continuous decay equation N = N_0 e^(-lambda t) and show it is equivalent to N = N_0 (1/2)^(t/t_1/2). Use it to calculate the amount remaining at non-integer numbers of half-lives.
differentiation.ell: Use the penny simulation as primary learning before calculations. Provide a bilingual half-life vocabulary card with a visual decay curve. Use a step-by-step number line showing each half-life.
differentiation.iep: Provide a half-life counting table pre-set-up with the halving pattern shown for the first few rows. Focus on counting half-lives before calculating amounts. Allow use of the table method rather than formula for assessments.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss how radiocarbon dating has been used to correct historical narratives — dating Indigenous settlements in the Americas to much earlier than previously believed by European scholars, confirming oral histories of First Nations peoples. Also discuss how carbon dating of artifacts from the Kingdom of Aksum in Ethiopia revealed it was one of the most advanced civilizations of the ancient world, challenging Eurocentric historical narratives.
lessons.hochman_activity: Kernel sentence expansion using 'Daughter Nucleus': Start with 'Daughter Nucleus is important.' Expand by adding when, where, why, and how details to create a complex sentence that demonstrates understanding of the concept.

vocabulary.definition: A technique for determining the age of organic materials by measuring the ratio of C-14 to C-12; useful for objects up to ~50,000 years old
The nucleus produced after a radioactive decay event; the decay product

guided_notes_outline: Section 2: Calculating Amount Remaining After n Half-Lives
Section 4: Other Dating Methods and Their Applications

cer.phenomenon: Archaeologists discover wooden tools at a site in North America. Carbon-14 analysis reveals that the wood contains only 6.25% of the original C-14 level. The half-life of C-14 is 5,730 years. Previous estimates based on artifact style suggested the site was approximately 10,000 years old.
cer.claim_starter: Based on half-life calculations, I claim that the site is significantly older than the style-based estimate because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the number of half-lives elapsed (6.25% = what fraction?). Multiply by the half-life of C-14 to determine the age.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because 6.25% = 1/16 = (1/2)^___, meaning ___ half-lives have elapsed. At ___ years per half-life, the site is approximately ___ years old, which is ___ years older than the style-based estimate of 10,000 years.

lessons.title: Fission, Fusion, and Mass-Energy Equivalence (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: compare nuclear fission and fusion, explain mass-energy equivalence (E = mc^2), and evaluate the benefits and risks of nuclear energy applications
lessons.circle_prompt: If you could harness any form of energy to power your home and community, what would you choose — solar, wind, nuclear, or something else? What are the trade-offs of each? What factors would be most important to you?
lessons.do_now: The Sun converts 4 million tons of matter into energy every second using E = mc^2. Calculate the energy produced: E = (4 x 10^6 kg)(3 x 10^8 m/s)^2. How does this compare to the total US energy consumption in a year (~10^20 J)?
materials: Binding energy per nucleon curve (poster or handout)

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: Fission, Fusion, and Mass-Energy Equivalence. Show two images side by side: a nuclear power plant peacefully generating electricity and the mushroom cloud of a nuclear explosion. Same physics, vastly different applications. Ask: What nuclear process powers both? How can the same science be used for energy and for destruction? This is the dual-use dilemma of nuclear physics.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: Fission, Fusion, and Mass-Energy Equivalence. Students examine the binding energy per nucleon curve. Iron-56 is at the peak (most stable). Elements lighter than iron can release energy by fusing (moving toward the peak). Elements heavier than iron can release energy by splitting (also moving toward the peak). Students identify which elements undergo fission (heavy, like U-235) and which undergo fusion (light, like H isotopes). They compare the energy released per nucleon in each process and discover that fusion releases MORE energy per nucleon.

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: Fission, Fusion, and Mass-Energy Equivalence. Nuclear fission: A heavy nucleus (U-235) absorbs a neutron and splits into two smaller nuclei plus additional neutrons, releasing enormous energy. Chain reaction: each fission releases 2-3 neutrons, which can trigger more fissions. Controlled in reactors (fuel rods, control rods, moderator), uncontrolled in weapons. Nuclear fusion: Two light nuclei (hydrogen isotopes) combine to form a heavier nucleus (helium), releasing even more energy per unit mass. Powers the Sun and all stars. Not yet achieved for sustained energy production on Earth. Mass-energy equivalence: E = mc^2. In both fission and fusion, the total mass of the products is slightly LESS than the reactants. This 'missing mass' (mass defect) has been converted to energy. Even tiny mass changes produce enormous energy because c^2 = 9 x 10^16 m^2/s^2.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: Fission, Fusion, and Mass-Energy Equivalence. Students calculate: (1) The energy released when 0.001 kg of mass is converted to energy in a nuclear reaction using E = mc^2. Compare to the chemical energy in 1 kg of coal (~3 x 10^7 J). (2) Connect to HS-PS1-8 PLD: students use models to explain the changes in composition of the nucleus during fission, fusion, and radioactive decay, and compare the scale of energy released. Discuss: nuclear power produces no CO2 during operation but creates radioactive waste. Is it a solution to climate change?

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: Fission, Fusion, and Mass-Energy Equivalence. Exit ticket: (a) Compare fission and fusion in terms of what they split/combine and which powers the Sun. (b) A nuclear reaction has a mass defect of 3.0 x 10^-28 kg. Calculate the energy released. (c) Give one benefit and one risk of nuclear power for a community.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a fission vs. fusion comparison chart with rows for: process, starting materials, products, energy released, where it occurs, controlled applications. Include a worked E = mc^2 example.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the binding energy curve analysis and all calculations as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research the current state of fusion energy research (ITER, NIF). Explain the technical challenges of sustaining fusion on Earth. Calculate the energy that would be released if all the deuterium in 1 liter of seawater underwent fusion.
differentiation.ell: Use the binding energy curve as a visual tool — students see that both fission and fusion move toward the peak. Provide bilingual comparison charts. Use visual diagrams of fission (big splitting to small) and fusion (small combining to bigger).
differentiation.iep: Focus on the qualitative comparison of fission and fusion. Provide E = mc^2 as a single calculator step (m x c x c). Allow reference cards for all calculations.

lessons.crse_connection: Discuss the nuclear energy debate in communities — the Fukushima disaster and its impact on Japanese communities, Three Mile Island and its effect on the surrounding Pennsylvania community, and the pattern of nuclear waste storage facilities being disproportionately sited near Indigenous and low-income communities (environmental justice). Also highlight the positive applications: nuclear medicine saving lives through PET scans and radiation therapy, and carbon-free electricity generation.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'nuclear energy': Nuclear fission releases enormous energy from a small amount of fuel because even a tiny mass defect corresponds to a huge energy release according to E = mc^2 because___. Both fission and fusion release nuclear energy, but fusion has not yet been harnessed for power plants because___. Nuclear power produces no carbon dioxide during operation, so some scientists advocate for it as a climate solution, but opponents argue that___.

vocabulary.definition: The splitting of a heavy nucleus into two lighter nuclei, releasing energy and additional neutrons; used in nuclear power plants and weapons
Einstein's principle that mass and energy are interchangeable; E = mc^2, where c is the speed of light
A self-sustaining sequence of fission reactions where neutrons from one fission trigger additional fissions

guided_notes_outline: Section 1: Nuclear Fission — Splitting Heavy Nuclei
Section 3: Mass-Energy Equivalence — E = mc^2
Section 5: Nuclear Applications — Power, Medicine, and Societal Impact

lessons.hochman_activity: Kernel sentence expansion using 'Mass Defect': Start with 'Mass Defect is important.' Expand by adding when, where, why, and how details to create a complex sentence that demonstrates understanding of the concept.

vocabulary.definition: The combining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy; powers the Sun and stars; releases more energy per unit mass than fission
The difference between the mass of a nucleus and the sum of the masses of its individual protons and neutrons; this mass has been converted to binding energy
The energy required to completely separate all protons and neutrons in a nucleus; equivalent to the mass defect times c^2

cer.phenomenon: France generates approximately 70% of its electricity from nuclear fission, while Germany has decided to shut down all its nuclear power plants by 2023 in favor of renewable energy. France has one of the lowest carbon emission rates per kWh in Europe. Germany's carbon emissions per kWh are higher because it still relies partly on coal. However, France must manage radioactive waste storage, while Germany does not face this issue with its renewable infrastructure.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the physics of nuclear fission and the data on carbon emissions and waste management, I claim that the choice between nuclear and renewable energy involves significant trade-offs that depend on a community's priorities because...
cer.evidence_source: Compare the carbon emissions, waste products, and energy reliability of nuclear fission versus renewable sources. Consider the scale of energy needed and the physics of each source.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because nuclear fission produces ___ carbon emissions but generates ___ waste that remains dangerous for ___. Renewable sources produce ___ waste and ___ carbon emissions but face challenges with ___ and ___. The 'best' choice depends on whether a community prioritizes ___ or ___, demonstrating that physics informs but does not dictate policy decisions.

units.title: Engineering Design & Course Review
units.anchoring_phenomenon: Every year, natural disasters, energy shortages, and transportation challenges affect millions of people worldwide. Engineers use the same physics principles we have studied all year to design solutions — from earthquake-resistant buildings to electric vehicles to renewable energy systems. How can we apply physics to solve real problems in our own community?
essential_questions: How do engineers use physics principles to design solutions to real-world problems?
What criteria and constraints must be considered when evaluating engineering designs?
How can we apply the physics we have learned to address challenges in our community and beyond?
units.crse_theme: Students apply physics to community-relevant engineering challenges — designing for resilience in the face of climate change, sustainable energy solutions for underserved communities, and transportation innovation. They learn about diverse engineers who have used physics to improve lives: Fazlur Rahman Khan (skyscrapers), Ellen Ochoa (optical systems and first Latina astronaut), and Lonnie Johnson (inventor of the Super Soaker and pioneering work on solid-state batteries).

summative: Course Final Exam / Regents Exam Preparation Assessment

lessons.title: The Engineering Design Process (Day 1 of 2)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and identify key concepts related to: define a problem in terms of criteria and constraints, and propose a physics-based solution that accounts for societal needs and trade-offs
lessons.circle_prompt: If you could solve one problem in your community or school using what you have learned in physics this year, what would it be? Think about energy, transportation, safety, buildings, sound, light, or any other physics topic.
lessons.do_now: A school wants to reduce energy costs by 30% without reducing comfort. List three possible solutions and identify at least one trade-off (positive and negative) for each. What physics principles apply to each solution?

dci: ETS1.A: Defining and Delimiting Engineering Problems

materials: Laptops or tablets for research (if available)
Poster paper and markers for proposals

engage.description: Introduce the phenomenon and driving question. Students make initial observations and predictions. Topic focus: The Engineering Design Process. Present three real-world engineering challenges: (1) Designing buildings that survive earthquakes (forces, energy absorption). (2) Making electric vehicles with longer range (energy, efficiency, power). (3) Providing clean water in remote communities (thermal energy, filtration). For each, students identify which physics concepts from Units 1-10 apply. Introduce the engineering design process as a systematic way to solve these problems.

explore.description: Hands-on exploration or guided investigation to build initial understanding. Topic focus: The Engineering Design Process. Students work in groups to define an engineering problem from a list of community-relevant options: reducing heat loss in older homes, designing a safer intersection, creating an emergency power system for a community center, improving acoustic quality in the school auditorium, or designing a solar water heater. Groups complete a problem definition worksheet: What is the problem? Who is affected? What are the criteria for success? What are the constraints (cost, materials, time, safety, environmental impact)?

explain.description: Teacher-led instruction introducing key vocabulary and foundational concepts. Topic focus: The Engineering Design Process. Formalize the engineering design process: (1) Define the problem — identify criteria (what success looks like) and constraints (limitations). (2) Research — review relevant physics principles and existing solutions. (3) Brainstorm solutions — generate multiple ideas. (4) Select and design — choose the best option based on criteria and constraints. (5) Build and test (or model). (6) Evaluate and refine. Connect to HS-ETS1-1 through HS-ETS1-3 PLDs: students must analyze global challenges, specify criteria and constraints, and evaluate solutions accounting for societal needs, trade-offs, and impacts.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity connecting new vocabulary to prior knowledge. Topic focus: The Engineering Design Process. Each group brainstorms at least three possible solutions to their defined problem. For each solution, they list: the physics principles involved, the expected benefits, the potential drawbacks or trade-offs, and the constraints it must satisfy. Groups then select their best solution and prepare a brief proposal to present to the class.

evaluate.description: Quick formative check — exit ticket with 2-3 questions on key definitions and concepts. Topic focus: The Engineering Design Process. Exit ticket: (a) Define 'criteria' and 'constraints' in engineering design and give one example of each for a specific problem. (b) Why is it important to consider trade-offs when selecting a design solution? (c) Identify one physics principle from this course that could be applied to a real-world engineering problem and explain how.

differentiation.approaching: Provide a problem definition template with sentence starters: 'The problem is ___. The people affected are ___. A successful solution must ___ (criteria). The solution is limited by ___ (constraints).' Include a checklist of physics topics from each unit.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the problem definition and brainstorming activities as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Research an actual engineering project that addresses their chosen problem. Analyze the criteria, constraints, and trade-offs the real engineers faced. Evaluate the effectiveness of the existing solution and propose improvements.
differentiation.ell: Provide visual examples of engineering problems with labeled physics connections. Allow verbal presentation of proposals. Provide bilingual engineering vocabulary cards.
differentiation.iep: Pre-select a manageable problem for the group. Provide a structured proposal template with specific prompts. Allow extra time for brainstorming and focus on one solution rather than three.

lessons.crse_connection: Highlight diverse engineers who used physics to solve community problems: Ellen Ochoa used optical physics in her patents for optical systems before becoming the first Latina astronaut and later director of the Johnson Space Center. Lonnie Johnson, an African American nuclear engineer, invented the Super Soaker and is now pioneering solid-state battery technology that could revolutionize energy storage. Discuss how engineering impacts different communities differently and the importance of diverse perspectives in design.
lessons.hochman_activity: Because/But/So sentences using 'engineering design': An engineering solution must account for multiple constraints because___. Solar panels and wind turbines both generate renewable electricity, but they have different trade-offs because___. The group identified reducing heat loss as the top priority, so they focused their design on___.

vocabulary.definition: The requirements that a successful engineering solution must meet; what defines success (e.g., reduces energy use by 30%, costs under $500)
A situation where improving one aspect of a design requires accepting a disadvantage in another aspect (e.g., increasing strength may increase weight and cost)

cer.phenomenon: A coastal community experiences frequent flooding. Two engineering firms propose solutions: Firm A proposes a concrete sea wall (cost: $5 million, protects against storms but blocks ocean views and damages local ecosystems). Firm B proposes restoring natural wetlands and dunes (cost: $3 million, provides habitat for wildlife and recreational space but offers less protection against extreme storms). The community must choose one.
cer.claim_starter: Based on the criteria and constraints analysis, I claim that the better solution depends on the community's priorities because...
cer.evidence_source: Compare the two solutions across multiple criteria: cost, effectiveness against flooding, environmental impact, aesthetic impact, long-term maintenance, and resilience to extreme events.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because Firm A's solution excels in ___ but fails in ___, while Firm B's solution excels in ___ but fails in ___. The 'best' choice requires the community to decide whether ___ or ___ is the higher priority, demonstrating that engineering design is not just about physics but also about ___.

lessons.title: Applying Physics to Real-World Design Challenges (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: build, test, and refine a physics-based engineering solution and use data from testing to optimize the design
lessons.circle_prompt: Think about a time you built something, fixed something, or found a creative solution to a problem. What worked? What did not? What would you do differently next time?
lessons.do_now: Your group's engineering project is due at the end of this lesson series. Review your problem definition and selected solution. List three specific measurements or tests you will use to determine if your solution meets its criteria.
materials: Materials specific to each group's project (varied)
Measuring tools (rulers, thermometers, spring scales, stopwatches)
Presentation materials (poster paper, markers, or slides)

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Applying Physics to Real-World Design Challenges. Brief review: Each group shares their problem statement and proposed solution in one sentence. Teacher confirms that each group has a clear test plan and knows what data to collect.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Applying Physics to Real-World Design Challenges. Build and test phase: Groups build their prototypes or models and conduct testing. cer.phenomenon: A group of students designs a solar water heater for their school's greenhouse. Their first prototype uses a black-painted metal container exposed to sunlight. It heats 2 liters of water from 15 degrees C to 28 degrees C in one hour of direct sunlight. After adding a glass cover (to trap heat by the greenhouse effect) and insulating the bottom and sides, the same amount of water reaches 42 degrees C in the same conditions.
cer.claim_starter: Based on heat transfer principles, I claim that the modifications improved the heater's performance because...
cer.evidence_source: Calculate the thermal energy gained by the water in each trial using q = mC(delta T). Determine the improvement as a percentage. Identify which heat transfer methods (conduction, convection, radiation) each modification addressed.
cer.reasoning_frame: This evidence supports my claim because the glass cover reduces heat loss by ___ (trapping warm air), the insulation reduces heat loss by ___ (minimizing thermal transfer through the bottom and sides), and together these modifications increased the thermal energy delivered to the water from ___ J to ___ J, an improvement of approximately ___%. This demonstrates how understanding ___ transfer principles leads to better engineering designs.

lessons.title: Course Review and Regents Exam Preparation (Day 1 of 3)
lessons.learning_target: At the end of 42 minutes I can define and describe key concepts related to: apply concepts from all units of the Physics course to solve multi-step problems in the format of the Regents examination
lessons.circle_prompt: As we look back over the whole year, what is the one physics concept that changed how you see the world? What will you remember from this course five years from now?
lessons.do_now: Quick review challenge: Solve one problem from each major unit — (1) A vector problem. (2) A kinematics problem. (3) A Newton's law problem. (4) A momentum problem. (5) An energy conservation problem. (6) A wave problem. (7) An optics problem. You have 5 minutes.

dci: PS3.B: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

materials: Comprehensive review packets organized by topic
Index cards for student-generated study aids

engage.description: Anchoring phenomenon presentation. Students record initial observations and questions. Topic focus: Course Review and Regents Exam Preparation. Regents exam overview: The exam tests four claims — Forces and Interactions, Energy, Waves and EM Radiation, and Engineering Design. Questions come in clusters (like the bungee jumping and automotive optics samplers we studied). Review the test format: multiple choice, constructed response, and investigation-related questions. Emphasize: the Reference Table is your best friend — know where to find every formula and constant.

explore.description: Guided discovery activity — students investigate the concept through hands-on work. Topic focus: Course Review and Regents Exam Preparation. Topic rotation review: Students move through stations, each covering one major topic area. Station 1: Kinematics and forces (free body diagrams, F = ma, projectile motion). Station 2: Momentum and impulse. Station 3: Work, energy, and power. Station 4: Thermal energy and calorimetry. Station 5: Waves, sound, and Doppler effect. Station 6: Optics (mirrors, lenses, Snell's law). Station 7: EM spectrum and nuclear physics. At each station, students solve 2-3 Regents-style questions and check answers immediately.

explain.description: Direct instruction introducing core vocabulary, principles, and relationships. Topic focus: Course Review and Regents Exam Preparation. Teacher addresses the most commonly missed question types from the practice rotation. Focus on: (1) Reading the Reference Table efficiently — finding the right formula. (2) Setting up multi-step problems — what do you know, what do you need to find, which equation connects them? (3) CER-style constructed responses — making a claim, citing specific evidence, and connecting with physics reasoning. (4) Cluster questions — reading the stimulus carefully and answering each question independently.

elaborate.description: Hochman writing activity using new vocabulary in Because/But/So sentences. Topic focus: Course Review and Regents Exam Preparation. Students create personal study cards: on one side, write a concept or formula they find challenging. On the other side, write a worked example with the solution steps. Students share their toughest topics with a partner and teach each other. This metacognitive exercise helps students identify their weakest areas before the exam.

evaluate.description: Exit ticket — match terms to definitions, identify key relationships. Topic focus: Course Review and Regents Exam Preparation. Final self-assessment: Students rate their confidence (1-4) on each of the four Regents claims. They write their top three study priorities and one specific strategy for each (e.g., 'Practice ray diagrams by drawing 5 per night' or 'Re-do all conservation of energy problems from Unit 6').

differentiation.approaching: Provide a topic-by-topic formula and concept summary with one worked example per topic. Highlight the most-tested formulas. Provide a Reference Table navigation guide showing where to find key information.
differentiation.on_level: Complete the topic rotation review and practice exam questions as designed.
differentiation.advanced: Work through a complete practice Regents exam under timed conditions. Analyze their results to identify patterns in errors (conceptual vs. computational vs. reading errors). Create a study plan targeting specific weaknesses.
differentiation.ell: Provide review materials with visual supports for every problem. Include a bilingual key terms list organized by unit. Allow extra time at review stations. Focus on understanding the question before solving.
differentiation.iep: Provide a reduced review set focusing on the most heavily tested concepts. Allow use of all reference materials during practice. Focus on multiple-choice strategies and one constructed response format. Provide extended time accommodations as per IEP.

lessons.crse_connection: Final reflection: Throughout this course, we have encountered scientists and engineers from every continent, every culture, and every background — from Ibn al-Haytham to Emilie du Chatelet, from Katherine Johnson to Shirley Ann Jackson, from the Polynesian wayfinders to the engineers of the Inca terraces. Physics is a human endeavor that belongs to everyone. The principles you have learned this year empower you to understand and shape the world around you.
lessons.hochman_activity: Reflection writing: Students write a 5-sentence paragraph reflecting on their physics learning journey. Sentence 1: Describe the physics concept you found most challenging and how you overcame it. Sentence 2: Describe the concept you found most fascinating and why. Sentence 3: Connect one physics principle to your daily life. Sentence 4: Identify one way physics knowledge could help your community. Sentence 5: Set one goal for how you will use scientific thinking in the future.
